subsubtopic: DREDGING CONTRACTS-CALL FOR PREFERENCE TO BE GIVEN TO CANADIAN COMPANIES-MOTION UNDER S O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43 to propose a motion of urgent importance, in view of the fact that large foreign dredging cartels are being given a decided advantage in bidding on multimillion dollar federal dredging contracts in the Canadian Arctic, in the Miramichi Channel and at the Roberts Bank superport in my riding, and whereas these dredging projects should instead be carried out by Canadian contractors using Canadian crews and vessels manufactured and registered in Canada, 1 move, seconded by the hon. member for York-Sunbury (Mr. Howie):
That the Minister of Public Works and the Minister of Transport, together with the responsible officials in the National Harbours Board, be directed to stop giving favoured status to foreign dredging companies, for example, those of Dutch origin, which seem to be popular with some government officials, and that the government be required instead to show clear preference for Canadian-owned dredging companies, many of which are presently working at only a 20 per cent utilization factor.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, we are making our views known, but not through that channel. The problems of Poland are for the Poles to solve and not for any other country. We have stated publicly on many occasions in the last number of weeks and months-we stated this clearly to the Soviet government-that the problems of independent countries of the world are to be solved by those countries and not by the Soviet Union.
December 4, 1980

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Leader of the Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Madam Speaker, if I might attract the attention of the Prime Minister-
Oh, oh!
He is not interested in this subject.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
The Prime Minister smiles while the danger to world peace accentuates in Europe. We now have it clear that the Government of Canada is not prepared to speak out strongly in the way that other governments have. It is clear now that the Secretary of State for External Affairs has not yet called in the Soviet ambassador. The Secretary of State for External Affairs tells us that the government is doing things but that those things are too important and too secret for the people of Canada or for the Parliament of Canada to know what they are.
Will the Prime Minister of Canada tell us what the Government of Canada is doing in the name of trying to preserve a situation of peace and trying to prevent the conflagration that could occur if Canada and other nations that want to speak for freedom and for peace do not defend the values for which this country stands?
Hear, hear!

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I understand the impatience of the opposition to see some public stand taken by the government. I think the Secretary of State for External Affairs was right in indicating that we were acting but in ways that we did not yet want to indicate publicly.
If the Leader of the Opposition insists, I suppose I can recite some of the concerns we have and the concerns I have shared with Helmut Schmidt, the Chancellor of West Germany, with the Premier of France and with the President of France, and since then in correspondence with every other summit leader.
And an old camel driver?

speakerposition: Prime Minister
speechtext: Madam Speaker, the Tory opposition is concerned with camel drivers and this is not an occasion for me to answer that type of snide remark.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Madam Speaker, what the House of Commons and the people of Canada would like to know is this. In a situation where the leaders of other countries-the United Kingdom, the United States of America, and leaders of the European community-have spoken out on this matter, why is the Prime Minister of Canada adopting such a position of silence? Why is the Secretary of State for External Affairs of Canada afraid to call in the Soviet ambassador?

speakerposition: Prime Minister
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I will again attempt to explain to the Leader of the Opposition that action is being taken. We would not like to see a repeat of the situation at the time of the Afghanistan invasion by the Soviet Union when
Oral Questions
most western nations acted on their own to condemn that invasion and to indicate that they were not only opposed to the invasion but that detente was severely threatened, that they would take various measures to protest that invasion. The Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition was then prime minister and I do not have to remind him that we succeeded less in showing our condemnation of the Soviet Union than showing the extent to which the western nations were divided, whether it was over the Olympics, the grain boycott, or the interruption of visits and of detente with the Soviet Union.
If the members of the opposition want greater elaboration on that, I will gladly do that, but I think the events are clear enough in the memories of the former prime minister and the former secretary of state for external affairs. In this very serious time for the peace of the world we in Canada do not care to show again that kind of division which existed when the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition was prime minister. We are hoping that the western nations will be able to react in a more united way to this very serious threat. That is all I want to say.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Madam Speaker, the fact is clear that most of the nations of the western world are acting in a united way but that there is one nation standing alone. The nation which is standing alone is Canada. Canada is standing alone in silence. Why is Canada standing alone in silence?

speakerposition: Prime Minister
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I cannot accept the premise of the question of the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition when he says that all of the western nations except Canada are acting in a united way. For instance, I will ask him if he knows how the various nations are reacting to the very serious economic difficulties in Poland brought about by the fact that to achieve peace with the trade unions a few months ago the Polish government had to make undertakings which it will find very difficult to keep. Does the Leader of the Opposition know which countries are wanting to help Poland through its near bankruptcy and which are taking the opposite position, that we should let it flounder? Does he know what position the NATO countries are taking on this and to what extent they are united?
Do you know?

speakerposition: Prime Minister
speechtext: He was being completely fallacious and it was just a sign of ignorance which the Leader of the Opposition showed when he was prime minister when he assumed we were all united on Afghanistan, or when ours was one of the countries which was party to a boycott which most of the other countries could not carry out. We do not want the same kind of division, disunity and chaos to be shown in the west as was shown when he was leader of the government.

Hear, hear!

December 4, 1980
Oral Questions

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Madam Speaker, what we know is that the leaders of Great Britain, the United States and other countries in the European Economic Community have spoken out, but Canada has stayed silent. We do not know what Canada is doing because the Prime Minister of Canada and the Secretary of State for External Affairs for Canada will not tell us, except to say that they have not even taken the elementary step of calling in the Soviet ambassador to this country.
Question.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: What action, other than silence, is the Government of Canada taking? Why is the Secretary of State for External Affairs for Canada reluctant to call in the Soviet ambassador? Why is the Government of Canada not joining with other nations in a public way to try to bring pressure which might stop dangerous events from occurring in the world? Why the silence? What is being done?

speakerposition: Prime Minister
speechtext: Madam Speaker, 1 thought 1 had indicated in my first answer that I had been in personal meetings with at least three of the leaders of the western nations and that I had been in contact by personal correspondence with the others. If the Leader of the Opposition chooses to call this inaction and silence, that is fine. It would be easy for us to break the silence, as other nations have done, by saying we condemn any danger or pressure arising from the Soviet Union; but what would we be doing collectively to take steps in a united way to show that if the worst threatens or happens we will be acting in a united way? Docs the Leader of the Opposition suggest that we boycott some other things, or does he suggest that we help Poland financially, or that we-
You can do both.

speakerposition: Prime Minister
speechtext: 1 wish the hon. member for wherever he is from -
Saskatoon West.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: It is in the west; that does not matter to you.

speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
speechtext: Come on, Joe.

speakerposition: Prime Minister
speechtext: I think the Leader of the Opposition has made his effort. If he wants to condemn us for not making great statements, that is his privilege.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I want to condemn you for abandoning our allies.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member for Regina West.

subsubtopic: REPORT RESPECTING MIRABEL PERIPHERAL LAND HOLDINGS
speechtext:
Thank you, Madam Speaker, finally. 1 would like to address a question to the
Minister of Public Works, about which the Minister of Transport no doubt also has concern. I would like to ask the Minister of Public Works about a report which the press in Quebec has been dealing with recently concerning 79,000 acres of land owned by the Government of Canada called "Mirabel peripheral land holdings". The report says, among other things, that the local residents have suffered significant losses due to the destabilizing of the area, that budgets have allowed only for hasty and superficial repairs in most cases, which has resulted in a vicious circle, and that these residents do not have any security of tenure. The government has spent $130 million to buy the land and $42 million to repair buildings and properties.
Has the minister made any decision as a result of that report? What measures does the government propose to give the people who live there more security of tenure, so that they can fix up their homes and farms?

speakeroldname: Hon. Paul J. Cosgrove (Minister of Public Works):
speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
subsubtopic: REPORT RESPECTING MIRABEL PERIPHERAL LAND HOLDINGS
speechtext: Madam Speaker, the report to which the hon. member refers was indeed prepared for the Ministry of Public Works in preparation for a cabinet submission. The cabinet committee involved is charged with taking a long-term look at the problems which have continued in the Mirabel area. I might say that the control and management of an area of 79,000 acres is no easy task. I met residents of the area as late as Monday of this week and received briefs from them. I also met the local members of Parliament who had input into that decision-making process. That report will be before the committee on government operations on December 12. It sets out a number of long-range options which we hope will be a long-term look at what the problems will be in trying to accommodate an international airport in any section of this country.

subsubtopic: REPORT RESPECTING MIRABEL PERIPHERAL LAND HOLDINGS
speechtext: Madam Speaker, the minister still cannot make up his mind. In addition to the acreage the government owns, the government spent another $10 million developing an industrial park which nobody will use. Mirabel ranks forty-sixth of all the airports in Canada in terms of take-offs and landings. It is No. 10 in terms of passengers handled. Nobody will use the industrial park on which that $10 million has been expended. In addition to doing something about security of tenure for individual residents and farmers on those lands, what does the minister intend to do to have some use made of that industrial park? Will he consult the Minister of Transport with respect to following the recommendations of the Canadian Institute of Guided Ground Transport which could move people to Mirabel airport by fast rail at a cost of $4 per person?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
subsubtopic: REPORT RESPECTING MIRABEL PERIPHERAL LAND HOLDINGS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am happy to say that the Ministry of Public Works has been in close consultation with the ministry of transportation and communications. We cannot approach this problem in isolation. A number of ministries have had input into this decision.
The question of industrial use, of course, goes hand in hand with the security of tenure of people in the area. People who would move into the area and put in industrial plants would, of

December 4, 1980

Oral Questions
course, want to know where their labour market is. They would want to know where their sales market is. At the same time they have to know what is the general stability or otherwise of the community. It is a complicated land use and community development concern that we have and, as 1 say, we cannot forget at all that this land surrounds an international airport. We do not want to have a repeat of the problems, for example, that we have in connection with the Toronto International Airport, where there are conflicting uses and conflicting problems which persist to this day.

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF PETROLEUM RESEARCH PLANT IN MONTREAL-GOVERNMENT POSITION
ESTABLISHMENT OF PETROLEUM RESEARCH PLANT IN MONTREAL-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, 1 wish to ask a question of the hon. Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources.
To begin with, 1 would like to remind everybody that Montreal is a petroleum products refining centre of extreme importance for the eastern part of the country and that in the Montreal area there are many people who would like to have a heavy oil upgrading plant built there. The hon. minister will recall that some time ago a request was made for a feasibility study regarding the construction of such a plant in Montreal.
Could the minister let us know if this study is now completed? What are its main conclusions? Can Montrealers expect soon the establishment of such a heavy oil upgrading plant in their city?

speakerposition: subtopic

subsubtopic: DREDGING CONTRACTS-STEPS TO ENSURE CANADIAN TENDERING
speechtext: Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Public Works; 1 am sorry 1 did not have an opportunity to give him notice. Like his predecessor, I suspect the minister is concerned that in the interests of consistency and national development we help Canadian companies develop a capability in Canada for doing their own dredging operations, despite the unfortunate history of some Canadian companies. Will the minister tell the House what steps, if any, he will take to assure Canadian participation in dredging, in view of the fact that tenders have recently closed on some multimillion dollar dredging contracts?

speakeroldname: Hon. Paul J. Cosgrove (Minister of Public Works);
speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
subsubtopic: DREDGING CONTRACTS-STEPS TO ENSURE CANADIAN TENDERING
speechtext: Madam Speaker, 1 too am sorry the hon. member did not give me notice of his question. The objective of the ministry is exactly as he indicated, that is, to attempt to ensure that Canadian companies are protected and that labour and management specialties in this area are given secure opportunity for competition. I will be happy to take the member's submission under notice, and if the tenders are being processed, 1 am sure it is an item the ministry will take into consideration and review.

subsubtopic: DREDGING CONTRACTS-STEPS TO ENSURE CANADIAN TENDERING
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, 1 thank the minister for his answer and look forward to the supplementary information.
My supplementary question is much simpler and does not require notice. While the dredging of the Miramichi River in New Brunswick has been postponed-on several occasions it has been sought after and very much promised-will the minister be making a tender award for this project soon, and could he tell us when it will commence? Will the project be cost-recoverable, or will the government, in its great wisdom, treat it as a development project, as it should be?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
subsubtopic: DREDGING CONTRACTS-STEPS TO ENSURE CANADIAN TENDERING
speechtext: Madam Speaker, the short answer is that it is not a cost-recovery project. The question of cost recovery is still a policy under consideration by the government. The project is under way and the efforts of the hon. member should not go unnoticed. As many members of the House know, the member has pushed for this for a long time.

speakeroldname: Hon. Marc Lalonde (Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subsubtopic: DREDGING CONTRACTS-STEPS TO ENSURE CANADIAN TENDERING
speechtext: Madam Speaker, the government had asked Petro-Canada to complete a study during the summer regarding the creation of a heavy oil upgrading plant of the Montreal refineries. This study was completed some time ago and according to its conclusions, such a plant should be built and peferably in Montreal. Since then, a committee has been formed with the Montreal refineries for the purpose of concluding the details of this study by April 1 of next year. This project could cost up to $1 billion and the recommendation is to the effect that such a plant be built as soon as possible.

subsubtopic: DUMPING OF TOXIC CHEMICALS BY UNITED STATES COMPANIES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of State for Science and Technology and Minister of the Environment. Given the already serious pollution problems in the Niagara River, a situation which has been known to politicians and public servants for several years, and in light of the recent announcement that dioxins, the most toxic chemical known to man, have been found in gull eggs in the Great Lakes, will the minister

December 4, 1980
Oral Questions
finally reverse the passive position both he and the previous minister of the environment have taken with respect to the pollution of boundary waters and initiate the toughest measures possible, including court action if needed, to prevent American chemical companies from using the Niagara River and the Great Lakes as a sewer for toxic chemical waste products?

subsubtopic: DUMPING OF TOXIC CHEMICALS BY UNITED STATES COMPANIES
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakeroldname: Hon. John Roberts (Minister of State for Science and Technology and Minister of the Environment):
speakerposition: Minister of the Environment; Minister of State for Science and Technology
subsubtopic: DUMPING OF TOXIC CHEMICALS BY UNITED STATES COMPANIES
speechtext: Madam Speaker, the hon. member mischaracterizes the position the government has taken. We have been forceful in our representation to the American authorities and have repeated those representations on an extraordinarily frequent number of occasions. We are exploring every possible means at our disposal to try to ensure that limitations are brought to bear against those in the United States who are guilty of this kind of pollution, including an examination of the possibility of applying procedures by which legal action might be taken.

subsubtopic: DUMPING OF TOXIC CHEMICALS BY UNITED STATES COMPANIES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, 1 am glad to hear the minister is considering possible court action. I hope he will cease his passive attitude and also oppose the action of SCA Chemical Waste Services Inc. which will pour millions of gallons of toxic waste into the Niagara River.
My supplementary question concerns the discovery of chlorophenoxy acid herbicides, such as 2, 4-D; 2, 4-DP; and 2, 4, 5-T which contain dioxins, in surface waters in western Canada, the highest concentration being recorded in the Qu'Appelle River district of Saskatchewan. Given the fact that these toxic chemicals are being introduced into the environment through agricultural spraying as well as municipal and industrial effluents in urban areas such as Winnipeg, Regina and Edmonton, what specific steps will the minister take to prevent further contamination of the environment of western Canada with these toxic substances and to alert the public of any possible dangers to health?

speakerposition: Minister of the Environment; Minister of State for Science and Technology
subsubtopic: DUMPING OF TOXIC CHEMICALS BY UNITED STATES COMPANIES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, perhaps I could refer the hon. gentleman to my answers in the House of Commons two days ago in relation to these issues. If he has not received the press release and the background information which 1 released two days ago, I will be happy to ensure that they are sent to him, including all the information we have in relation to western Canada.
The problem concerning the dioxin question is that the generation of dioxin does not come through the utilization of herbicides and spray, it comes through the manufacture of 2, 4, 5-D and phenoprop. The origin of that as a problem arises as a byproduct of manufacture, and perhaps springs as well from combustion, in all aspects and not simply in relation to the destruction of these chemicals. As far as we know, if properly used there is no consequential hazard from the utilization of these herbicides at the present time.

subsubtopic: INQUIRY WHETHER CANFARM WILL CONTINUE OPERATION
speechtext: Madam Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Agriculture but as he is not in the House 1 shall put it to his parliamentary secretary. Since the Agricultural Producers' Union has adopted an aid policy in order to give its regional tax agents responsibilities as developers with a view to helping the financially depressed Canfarm organization, can the parliamentary secretary tell us, in light of the discussions held the day before last with the board of the organization, whether the department is considering helping this co-operative pursue its activities, which are important to the farmers in my riding as well as to those all over Canada?

speakeroldname: Mr. Marcel Ostiguy (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture
subsubtopic: INQUIRY WHETHER CANFARM WILL CONTINUE OPERATION
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, last Tuesday night we met with the heads of Canfarm. The organization is now asking the government for a $2.5 million grant. In view of the financial slump in which Canfarm finds itself, because of lack of participation by Canadian farmers, we have asked its directors and its chairman, Mr. Peter Hannam, to try to find people who would be interested in buying the corporation in the near future.
Within a week, the department should be able to give a satisfactory answer so that Canfarm employees can be paid before the end of the month. Last Friday in Montreal, we met with APU chairman Pierre Gaudet, and it would appear that the union is now quite interested in making Canfarm an offer to purchase.

speechtext: Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources. I was encouraged by the comment he made in answer to a question asked earlier in the House regarding Alsands that discussions are taking place to resolve this very tense situation. Will the minister give his absolute assurance that satisfactory negotiations will be completed to ensure that this project does not die, since this would be absolutely catastrophic for the nation?

speakeroldname: Hon. Marc Lalonde (Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subsubtopic: ALSANDS PROJECT-REQUEST FOR ASSURANCE OF COMPLETION
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I must tell the hon. member that I cannot give him that assurance, for the good reason that he asked me whether we will have a satisfactory agreement or a resolution of the differences at the present time. I cannot speak for the government of Alberta. I can tell him that if he looks at
December 4, 1980

the record, particularly with regard to tar sands plants, he will find the federal government has always been very forthcoming and ready to make sure those projects will take place. If there has been any delay it has not come from the federal government in the past and I do not think it will come from us in the future.

subsubtopic: ALSANDS PROJECT-REQUEST FOR ASSURANCE OF COMPLETION
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, in a serious situation like this the minister of energy blames the government of Alberta, when he knows full well that blame lies equally in his court.
1 would like to ask the minister if he can confirm something for me. In a recent interview the minister indicated he does not feel that time pressures are against him because of the potential production from Canada lands offshore and in the high Arctic. Does the minister feel that the high Arctic and these Canada lands production projects coming on-stream would make oil sands development unnecessary? Is that the position of the minister? If he confirms that it is, would he table in the House information he might have which would give credence to that position?

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subsubtopic: ALSANDS PROJECT-REQUEST FOR ASSURANCE OF COMPLETION
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I have always taken the position that Canada needs all these projects, whether they are offshore, in the Arctic or in the tar sands, the heavy oil area. That is the position we have taken and it is the position 1 have taken consistently.
I have indicated, however, that there may be large discoveries taking place offshore, or in the Arctic, which may change the general context of the situation and might reduce some of the pressure to proceed immediately with some of those plants. 1 can only tell the hon. member that this is speculation, but speculation which arises out of very public facts released by the companies concerned about the potential which exists in the offshore and the Arctic. I hope we will be able to proceed with all those projects.
I remind the hon. member that in the National Energy Program we forecast self-sufficiency in this country before 1990, without taking into account any discoveries offshore or in the Arctic. If those discoveries were made in the meantime that would again improve the situation very considerably indeed.

subsubtopic: ASSURANCE OF ENERGY SUPPLIES FOR FOOD PROCESSORS AND FISHERMEN
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources. In view of the great dependence on energy supplies, particularly by Canadians in the Atlantic region involved in the processing of essential, perishable food products and commercial fishing, could the minister indicate to the House if he is in the position to give some assurance with respect to energy supplies for these food processors, and can he guarantee protection for commercial fishermen?
Privilege-Mr. Flis

speakeroldname: Hon. Marc Lalonde (Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subsubtopic: ASSURANCE OF ENERGY SUPPLIES FOR FOOD PROCESSORS AND FISHERMEN
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I am happy to confirm that the Energy Supplies Allocation Board, following numerous representations from farming groups, fishermen's groups and in particular from many members of Parliament on this side of the House, has come to the conclusion that the highest priority should be given to agricultural products and fisheries products. I welcome this decision of the board.

speakerposition: subtopic
Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: MR. McKNIGHT-LETTER WRITTEN BY MR. DE CORNEILLE
speechtext:
The hon. member for Kindersley-Lloyd-minster (Mr. McKnight) on Tuesday rose on a question of privilege concerning a letter written on House of Commons stationery, in which the hon. member for Eglinton-Lawrence (Mr. de Corneille) solicited support for A National Committee for a Human Rights Charter, of which he is chairman. The hon. member for Kindersley-Lloydminster suggested it was improper to use House of Commons stationery for such a purpose.
I have examined the matter carefully and I cannot find any grounds upon which the Chair ought to intervene. There are no grounds upon which privilege might be claimed in this case, nor would the House expect me to act as a censor for any hon. member. There are rules regulating the contents of the householder mailings, but members must take full responsibility for material mailed under their frank and written on official stationery.

speechtext: I have a question of privilege in the name of the hon. member for Parkdale-High Park (Mr. Flis).

subtopic: MR. FLIS-REMARKS REFLECTING ON POLISH HERITAGE
speechtext: Madam Speaker, my question of privilege arises from questions, and answers given in this House with regard to the situation in Poland. My heritage, which happens to be Polish, was disgraced in this House because of the official opposition reference to camels and what-have-you. Madam Speaker, I would like to read the "blues" before speaking further on this question of privilege.

breach of his privilege, then I am afraid it is probably a bit far-fetched. 1 do take note of his point but I do not feel that he has a question of privilege. We will leave it at that.

speechtext: Madam Speaker, it being Thursday 1 wonder if the government House leader is able to tell us, following this six-day period for the consideration of estimates under the special order, the government's legislative program between now and the time he estimates we will be rising for Christmas. speechtext: Madam Speaker, 1 rise on a point of order to thank you for trying to correct a severe imbalance which was occurring during question period. I hope you will continue to do that. speechtext:
House again in Committee of the Whole on Bill C-47, an act for granting to Her Majesty certain sums of money for the Government of Canada for the financial year ending March 31, 1981. When the committee rose on Wednesday, December 3, 1980, Vote no. 1 under Transport was under consideration, and the hon. member for Mississauga North had the floor.
DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORT:
Vote No. 1.

Thank you, Mr. Chairman. Before we ended our discussion yesterday I had some questions that I directed to the Minister of Transport to learn from him our progress following the passage of the bill dealing with the transportation of hazardous goods. At that time I pointed out to him that questions had been raised in Mississauga about the follow-up to that bill and there had been comments made, particularly by the mayor, that a year ago the federal presence was not adequate. It is my feeling that considerable progress has now been made. 1 posed some questions to the minister about inspection procedures, about negotiations with the provinces, about budgets, and about a variety of other areas. I hope that the minister will take this occasion to answer these questions.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I will do so as rapidly as I can in order to release more time for any of my hon. friends who care to have it.
We are talking about transportation of dangerous goods. The member for Mississauga North asked me a number of very specific questions. He asked me if the bill had been proclaimed, and it has. I think November 1 was the date. He asked me if other provinces had adhered to the legislation because this is what is meant to happen, as he knows. This is legislation that is open to the provinces to come into, not only legislatively but administratively. There was a meeting of
December 4, 1980

ministers of transport in Toronto some weeks ago at which time I pleaded-1 didn't sink to my knees, but almost-that they would come in, that they would pass their own legislation or orders in council in order to satisfy the objective of this legislation which is a co-operative federal-provincial approach to matters of transportation for dangerous goods.
Ontario is going ahead and I understand B.C. is preparing itself for that too. I am using this opportunity again to remind them although I am sure they have not forgotten, and to plead with my provincial colleagues that they will move as rapidly as possible in order to give this legislation the full federal-provincial use it is meant to have.
The regulations are in their fourth draft. Final consultation is taking place with interested groups and we hope to have the regulations gazetted-I do not know where the accent is-by next summer.
The hon. member for Mississauga North asked me how many inspectors we would have, and here we are witnessing an evolving situation. The legislation is not applicable yet in terms of the regulations not being available yet, but the department and the transport commission are preparing themselves for the time when it will be. By way of illustration, I understand that the CTC had seven specialists, experts, inspectors, and we have added four to that, so now there are more than 11 altogether. They are going to be specialists in the transportation of dangerous goods. Similarly, I understand the department is hiring, or has hired, six air inspectors who are already in position in the different regions of the country. They are going to be specialists in the transportation of dangerous goods by air. This is just to indicate that progress is being made. I want to use this opportunity to thank members of the transportation committee who have worked extremely well during the last part of the session to bring about this result.

Because the regulations are still being negotiated with industry, and because the minister and the CTC are still trying to set their priorities on these matters, I would like to stress now the importance of what I think is a crucial element, the importance of good inspection, particularly with the railroads. It seems to me that our policy up to this point has been to trust the railroads and to trust the companies, and it seems to me, as well, that that places an unfair burden on the companies. The companies exist to make a profit, to provide good service for their customers, and to keep their trains rolling on time. They have a variety of other concerns, and safety has to fit in with those concerns. It seems to me that the question of safety must be the first concern for any public body. That has to be the fundamental question that we examine.
The minister mentioned that the Ontario government has already committed itself to follow our legislation and to cooperate with it. They have already started with problems associated with truck shipments. I would like to use that as an example. When trucks in Ontario are carrying dangerous goods, they will be subjected to a wide range of inspection. They will be regularly examined at weigh stations. They will be subject to inspection by provincial police authorities and by
Supply
local police authorities. The companies will be able to maintain their own standards and they will be able to seek their own goals to try to get a profit, but the public will also be assured that the trucking industry will have a degree of safety because of the regular inspections that will occur. I am not so sure that we can make that same claim today about our railroad system.
We do not inspect our trains as thoroughly as Ontario will be inspecting the trucks that run on its highways. I think the public should be given the assurance that we will upgrade inspection procedures, because public safety is such an important question. I would very much appreciate a few comments from the minister about his plans to improve the inspection and general safety procedures of the railways.

speechtext: Mr. Chairman, the only comment I can make is that we are moving similarly on the question of the safety of railway transportation.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, similar movement is taking place with respect to railway safety, which is more of a preoccupation of the CTC. My understanding is that the CTC expects to increase their force by 30 inspectors. I thought I had referred already to the presence of 11 dangerous goods inspectors. However, as my hon. friend knows, all these things are subject to national priorities as well as to the approval of Treasury Board. Much as I would like to be more enthusiastic, I must throw some cold water on these expectations because I know this hope will be subject to very close analysis.
On the subject of railway transportation, there was some news in yesterday's newspaper which I must rectify. It was reported that the Grange report had been tabled. The Grange report concerns the railway derailment at Mississauga, and my hon. friend is aware of that. We have, however, received the draft of the report of Mr. Justice Grange, who is using the facilities of the department for printing and translation purposes. I want to emphasize that I have not seen it nor will I look at it because I understand Mr. Justice Grange wants to present his report to me personally early in January. If there are leaks, they will not be from me, my office, or from officials in the Department of Transport. This is a service which the Department of Transport is giving to Mr. Justice Grange. He requested this service, the purpose being to use administrative facilities which exist, instead of creating new ones.

Mr. Chairman, I want to underline what the minister has just said. Inspection for railroads is indeed a question of priorities. When we take a look at the issues, the

December 4, 1980
Supply
expense involved in providing numerous and proper inspectors is not as great an expense as providing for some of the other facilities in the ministry. Perhaps the minister will take as my representation this comment about the importance of the inspectors. More people benefit from adequate rail inspection than would benefit from some of the other facilities which his department finances.
When the Mississauga accident happened, it covered a geographic area extending approximately one-half mile away from the railway tracks. According to Statistics Canada there are some 250,000 people living one-half mile from the CPR tracks between Streetsville and Agincourt. Those people are vulnerable whenever a train carrying dangerous goods runs along that track. When we start to examine vulnerability in that sense, we begin to see how important is the question of public safety.
1 want to congratulate the minister for increasing the number of specialists, but I hope that he will take a look at the whole question of rail safety and inspection and increase the number of inspectors, perhaps at the sacrifice of other facilities until he can provide funding for them as well.

Mr. Chairman, I have a short intervention. First, 1 would like to express my thanks to the member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain for allowing me to speak at this time because I have a commitment to keep later on this afternoon. His courtesy is most appreciated.
I want to talk briefly about the movement of grain by rail all across southern Alberta in 1980. As I am sure the minister is aware, southern Alberta is served almost entirely by the Canadian Pacific Railway. There is only a short CNR branch line coming into the northern part of that whole southern area.
Nineteen-eighty has not been a good grain shipping year, particularly when it comes to the railways. It should have been much better. After all, most of the usually severe winter months were wide open. There were no reasons why almost
normal summer rail movement could not have been maintained. So, it was not because of the weather. However, there were two main situations which contributed to this poor grain movement throughout most of 1980. First, there was the labour situation on the Revelstoke subdivision line which is in the interior of British Columbia which went on for months. The Revelstoke line is part of the main line of the CPR.
There was hardly any mention of the labour strike in the newspapers. It did not make headlines, and the public at large were not aware of the situation. Perhaps even those in southern Alberta did not realize it was a most serious factor until the situation was almost over. However, I am sure the minister is aware of this. The situation was caused by a small portion of a railway union. There were perhaps as few as 20 members who objected rather strenuously to the fact they had difficulty in getting one hot meal a day away from their base. That seemed to be the main thrust of the complaints. As a result, there was a horrendous holdup of massive amounts of prairie grain shipments which should have gone forward throughout the several months this strike was in progress.
The Grain Transportation Authority had suggested a goal of 1,500 unloads per week for this main line of the CPR of which the Revelstoke subdivision is a part. The 1,500 unloads of grain, not total, per week was their objective. During the strike that unload figure dropped to between 600 and 800, less than half the objective. By week number ten, the Revelstoke labour strike situation caused a shortfall of up to 5,000 cars of grain. That, of course, was in addition to all other commodities which were held up during the same period because of the strike. It made a fantastic difference to the shipments out of southern Alberta as that is the one rail system which serves us most of the time. It is true some of our grain is shipped through Thunder Bay, but most is over the CP mainline through the Revelstoke subdivision.
The second factor which contributed to this was that, when the new hard red spring quotas were announced at the beginning of the current crop year, there were no quotas allocated to the four shipping blocks which covered all of southern Alberta. This really hurt the grain shippers at that time. I need not dwell on it too long because I am sure the minister and his parliamentary secretary are aware of how urgently needed these early quotas are in order for farmers to have their cash requirements, meet their accounts payable, and so on. For some considerable time there was no quota for all for southern Alberta. In fact it was the only region in the designated Wheat Board area where there were no quotas for hard red spring wheat.
There are two questions I wish to ask the minister. First, there must be some built-in routine to deal with selected key railway strikes, such as that in the Revelstoke subdivision which tied up millions of bushels of grain movement to the west coast. It tied it up at the most critical time of the year when normally the maximum volume of grain should be moved. It could not have happened at a worse time with
December 4, 1980

respect to the traditional volume moving time. Will the minister indicate what action he has taken on this specific situation, and what policy changes he feels would be appropriate to prevent such critical holdups in our grain handling situation in the future?
The second question arising out of this dissertation I have been enlarging on with the minister is with regard to grain quotas or, more properly, the lack of grain quotas in southern Alberta. What for?

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader
speechtext:
I appreciate the help that the public servants are giving to the minister, but I am very serious about this. I would like the Minister of Transport to quit being a messenger boy who reports to the president of Canadian National Railways and the president of Canadian Pacific Railway that certain members in the House of Commons are raising issues about the pensions of railway workers. After all, both of those railways owe their existence to the government and the Parliament of Canada, and both of those railways get all kinds of financial assistance from the taxpayers of Canada through this Parliament and through the government.
I think the Minister of Transport has the responsibility to discuss seriously with those railways their unfairness to their
pensioners and the several aspects of the matter. I have gone over this issue so many times that I hardly need to go over it again, but let me sketch the main points which are disappointing to railway pensioners.
First may I say that we have lost a decade on this issue. Back in the early 1970s we were pressing pretty hard. Motions were passed by various committees, we thought something would happen, and then the present Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development, who was then minister of labour, arranged-and we welcomed it-for the setting up of an industrial inquiry commission into railway pension plans. He did this at a time when we were trying to settle a railway dispute and, since pensions were not included in the settlement, the setting up of this industrial inquiry commission was supposed to relieve our minds.
It took two or three years for that commission, headed by Dr. Noel Hall, to produce a report. It finally came down in 1976. By that time we had lost two or three years in the seventies, and then that report did what so many reports do- it began to collect dust.
Here we are four years later, and very little that was recommended in that report has been implemented. For example, it urged very strongly that the Canadian Pacific Railway be called upon to put its pension arrangements at least on a par with those of Canadian National Railways, and then it called on both railways to improve their pension plans. There was a proposal for the setting up of a heritage fund-this was even before that name became so well known in Alberta in another connection-out of which moneys might be available to index, escalate, or supplement the pensions of retired railway workers.
Back in the early days of escalation when some pensions were being indexed by a percentage point, or by two percentage points, the railways did it for a while. Canadian National did it first, and Canadian Pacific did it a little, but there never has been an acceptance of the proposition that railway pensions ought to be escalated automatically year by year in accordance at least with the rise in the cost of living, and in recent years things have fallen so far behind that older pensioners are way out of line in their incomes with what has happened to the rise in the cost of living.
As 1 say, I think it is time that the Minister of Transport played a role more than that of a messenger boy. He should talk to the railways about their responsibility to meet the retirement needs of their former workers. The ones who are still working, of course, have a chance through collective bargaining to try to win certain improvements in their pension plans, and they have won some improvements. The main desire on the part of those who are still working is that there be provisions for early retirement without penalty for such early retirement but, as I say, the main group of persons on behalf of whom I plead are the retired railway workers at both Canadian National and Canadian Pacific whose pensions have gone way out of line with the cost of living.
December 4, 1980

I urge very strongly that the minister act on this. If I repeat myself, I apologize, but I will do it anyway. So often when we raise matters like this the minister simply stands up and says, "I will make this known to the president of Canadian National or the president of Canadian Pacific". Well, it is time they were told what they ought to do.
In this connection there is a reform in pensions which simply has to come. I assert that it has to come in all pension plans, not just in those of railway workers, but what better place to start than with the railway workers, since the railways receive so much assistance from the taxpayers and the people of Canada generally? I refer to the provisions in both railway pension plans regarding widows. It is a rule that is in many other plans, but that does not make it right. That does not detract from the fact that it is antiquated and does not fit modern thinking at all.
Both railways have the provision that if a pensioner dies there is a 50 per cent pension for his widow, but if the wife dies first and the old man lives on as a widower, his pension is 100 per cent. Compared with the days when pension plans did not provide any survivor benefit, of course that was something to crow about, but surely in this day, when we say we believe in equality between men and women, there is no justification for continuing that arrangement in a pension plan under which, if the woman dies first, the husband receives a 100 per cent pension, but if the husband dies first the woman receives only a 50 per cent pension.
Various suggestions have been made about this. Some suggest that it should be 100 per cent for the first year, and then something like 75 per cent. Any improvement would be an improvement. I suppose one could say that we do not look for the ultimate right off the bat, but I suspect that if I were a woman standing here I would say, why not? If it is fair to do it, and to put women in an equal place with men in this respect, why not do it now? Why wait for a decade or two down the road? I urge very strongly that the minister press upon both railways that it is time to recast their plans so far as the pensions of widows are concerned.
As I have already said, if I were a woman I would plead for the perfect plan right now, but surely at least there should be a provision for widows to get 75 per cent of the pension instead of only 50 per cent, and if it meant that there would have to be some adjustment to put it on an equal basis, such that either survivor would get 90 per cent instead of one getting 100 per cent and the other 50 per cent, something like that might be worked out.
I have discovered in my work in the field of pensions that this has become an issue across the board which is felt pretty strongly. More people have pension plans now than was the case when I first came to this House of Commons, so they are aware of these things. Workers are getting older. Veterans are getting older, and they are getting more concerned about their widows than they were some years ago. But this is one of the important things railways workers do press, and I would like to see the minister go to the mat with the two railways on it.

Speaking of widows, there is another provision which still exists and which seems to me out of date, and that is the provision which says that the widow of a railway worker gets no pension if she married the worker after he retired. In most cases where this happens, she is the second wife. I have quite a job trying to explain to some of these widows that it is not because they are the second wives but because they married after the husbands retired. However, they still come back with the point that the contribution was made. It was there. There are cases in which the second marriage lasted longer than the first marriage, and yet we have the older railway worker having contributed to the plan and facing the prospect that he might die first and leave his widow, in the knowledge that if that widow was married to him after he retired, there is no pension for her at all. If this requires some adjustment in the rates, or some actuarial changes, let us make them, but surely it is time for us to move forward in this area.
1 know a few years back there were pension plans which had no survivor benefit at all, so it was a great thing to achieve a survivor benefit of 50 per cent. But surely we do not stop there. Surely fairness, and the concept that men and women should be equal, should apply.
Someone may come back and say, "What about the other way when it is the wife who works, dies, and leaves a pension?" I am for that too, but the experience so far is largely that it is the man who is the wage earner and who is out there in industry or out there in the workaday world. But surely we do not have to argue any more that what he is able to do is very largely made possible by the support of his wife and by her maintaining of the home and raising the family, and there should not be any second-class status so far as the wife is concerned.
I want to leave the minister time to answer these points, and for me to answer him if that should be necessary, so I will leave it at that. I would be glad to have his comment on the first point I raised, even though some colleague of mine will raise it later today. That first point was the unfairness to the people of my constituency, as a result of granting the permit for the Sherbrook-McGregor overpass. However, in the main I would like to hear from him now on what he is going to do in terms of talking turkey to Canadian Pacific and Canadian National about putting the indexing of railway pensions on an automatic basis fully equal to the rise in the cost of living, and about doing something to put pensions to the widows of railway workers on a basis that is fair and equal.

Mr. Chairman, I welcome the opportunity to participate in discussion on these estimates. I should like to open my remarks by congratulating the backbench members of the Liberal party for taking advantage of this long lost opportunity of bringing up problems not only affecting their own constituencies but of the country as a whole, because this is the only occasion that parliamentarians have to put their viewpoints and their problems before the minister with a chance of them being heard. However, I should like to congratulate in particular, on behalf of all backbenchers of every parliament in the world, the young member for Manicouagan for the contribution he made yesterday.
Hear, hear!

I do not
think that any person who heard his remarks could have failed to hear that he was speaking for every backbencher of every party which has ever sat in parliament. The trouble we have as members of Parliament in breaking through this tremendous
mess of an overloaded bureaucracy, and in trying to resolve simple problems, is one of the heaviest loads we bear, so I think the hon. member for Manicouagan is owed a debt by all of us for speaking so frankly.
It is expected of us in the opposition to try to put our best foot forward on these estimates and to try to get our points across, so I will attempt to do the same thing. I think you will notice, Mr. Chairman, that the points made by the opposition yesterday and today have been largely constructive and helpful to the minister. This gives the minister arguments which he can use with his officials and with his colleagues in cabinet and the Treasury Board to get some changes made a little more expeditiously.
I should like to speak on two subjects. The first one deals with the Canadian Wheat Board. Even though I address my remarks to the minister, I know the parliamentary secretary will be listening. My remarks are very brief. It is a request to the parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Transport to ask the minister in the other place in charge of the Canadian Wheat Board to put before his legal officials an amendment to the Canadian Wheat Board Act to correct an injustice which takes place from time to time in the administration of that act. I am referring to the fact that a regulation of the Canadian Wheat Board Act gives the farmers the right to ask if they may transfer their payments from the pool in one crop year to the next pool. That right was granted by Parliament through this regulation of the Canadian Wheat Board to all producers under the Wheat Board's jurisdiction. In effect, that right is denied to farmers who hold permits under the Canadian Wheat Board Act because of a condition which occurs periodically.
I have the details on what I am now saying but I will put it in general terms. Under the Canadian Wheat Board Act, every farmer has the right to deliver to the elevator of his choice a number of bushels of grain up to the amount of the quota allocated to him. The technique of doing that is that the Wheat Board asks the leading elevator company how much space is available for a certain type of grain. When the report comes in and the railway cars are dispatched to pick it up, every producer in that elevator area has the right, equal to that of every other producer, to deliver that grain.
When a mistake is made, and the figures given as to the amount of space that is available and the amount of grain on the farms do not match up so that a number of farmers in the area cannot get the allocated bushels into the elevator in that crop year, then the Wheat Board Act allows for an extended delivery period. But the Canadian Wheat Board Act says very precisely that if a person delivers grain during an extended crop period beyond July 31, he must become part of the pool of that crop year which ends on July 31, which takes away from that producer, through a mistake made by someone else, his right to deliver that grain during that crop year and put the grain into the elevator in the next crop year for pooling purposes of the final payment. It is not a deliberate and evil contradiction, it is a normal thing which happens in the
December 4, 1980

administration of a complicated marketing system such as we have.
The minister knows all about this. He has spoken to producers who have had trouble in that regard, and he knows that these matters were brought to the Canadian Wheat Board, which treated the matter facetiously and said, "You lost out in the gamble." I am asking the parliamentary secretary to take this up with the minister in charge of the Wheat Board and to tell him that the first thing to do is to adopt a simple amendment to the Canadian Wheat Board Act. The second thing to do, in my view, is that when an injustice is done and mistakes are made, the principle of compensation should be considered and accepted.
The incident I spoke about happened in 1978, over two years ago. One company, which I will not name, found out about this injustice because several farmers who had delivered grain to their elevator could not get their grain in, as they had the right to do on an order of the Canadian Wheat Board, and had to deliver their grain during an extended marketing period. So they lost their right to go to the next pool. The company compensated those producers for their loss. But another grain company said to its customer in the same situation, "No, you lost the gamble, you did not get it in." We know that it must have been either the fault of the grain company that it had not informed the Wheat Board accurately, or it was the fault of the Wheat Board that they issued the order without knowing exactly what the situation was. The fault does not lie with the producer.
It is no use going to the Canadian Wheat Board and asking for their advice in this matter.
No civil servant at any level ever wants to disclose a mistake. So I am asking the parliamentary secretary to speak very candidly to the minister who understands this type of thing, and ask him whether he could get his legal officers to correct an error which exists in the present Wheat Board Act and which makes it impossible to carry out the regulation dealing with joining in the second pool. I think that is fairly simple to those people who understand the situation.
If the Hansard record is shown to the minister, I am sure he will consider my requests. The first request is for an amendment to the Canadian Wheat Board Act, and the second request is to consider compensation being paid by whoever is responsible for the mistake. Either the Wheat Board or the grain company, either one or the other, should compensate the farmer who loses out through no fault of his own.
I should like to deal with railway transportation and the Hall commission report. When the report came down, speaking on behalf of the official opposition 1 stated that it was the magna carta of western producers. One reason why I made that statement was that the government periodically was under heavy pressure to change the Crowsnest rates which farmers consider to be a moral agreement that should not be destroyed. The Hall commission recommended that the Crowsnest rates
Supply
be retained, but it laid down a positive, constructive proposal, showing how it would not cost the railways anything.
In very simple, blunt terms, the proposal was that railways should haul more than just grain. Every Canadian knows that the bulk of the wealth of Canada comes from the area west of the Great Lakes. Not only grain produces that wealth. Every year there is a rise in the number of shipments of every type of product. The products about which I am talking at this moment are the bulk ones which are most suitably carried on railways, particularly potash and coal.
The Government of Canada, along with the government of the United States, signed an agreement in good faith on approximately February 18, 1980. It committed the coal reserves of the United States and Canada to Europe and Japan. We will do all we can to supply their desperate need for coal over the next 40 or 50 years. If one looks at where the coal is located and the quantities necessary to meet the rising demands of Japan, Taiwan, South Korea and the entire Asian theatre, as well as the demand in Europe, one realizes that it amounts to many millions of tonnes per year and that this coal for Europe can only come from Saskatchewan and Alberta. Of course the coal for the Pacific market will come from British Columbia. I am talking about thermal coal, but it applies also to metallurgic coal.
If one looks at where coal is located in Saskatchewan and Alberta, one will soon find out that it is in the southern part of Saskatchewan and in the northwestern part of Alberta. I am not talking about the Crowsnest deposit which is orientated toward the Pacific market. In order to make it physically possible, we need a north-south railroad, from southern Saskatchewan going north into Churchill. All the parts of that railway are in place now as joint sections between the east-west lines going into Churchill, except for three little gaps.
If we want to send ten million tonnes of coal a year to Europe, it means the Churchill port will have to be kept open eight to ten months a year. We can do that, and the department is working on it. If we take ten million tonnes of coal out of Alberta and Saskatchewan at a freight rate several times per tonne greater than that at which wheat is carried, we will provide an income for the railways as great as the income from carrying all grain. If we ship an extra four or five million tonnes of potash a year through Churchill, which is the direct route, to the European market, the railways will earn four or five times more than they would carrying the same weight in wheat.
The incomes of the railways sharing in that carriage will be doubled or tripled by the simple act of completing the railway from southern Saskatchewan up to Churchill. The cost of building these little links is small, except for the engineering difficulties of crossing the Qu'Appelle River. It fits into the Hall commission report to build a new grain terminal elevator in Yorkton so that the dry protein grain of the south can be mixed with the lower protein grains of the north in order to increase the standards of grain to the levels wanted by the European market. It will be a direct route to Europe, so we

will double the wheat movement, not to mention feed grains which are increasingly needed in Europe.
The minister knows about this. He has indicated a favourable attitude toward it, but his only hurdle to overcome is to convince one railway company that the rewards of getting across the Qu'Appelle River are far greater than the cost of getting across it. Engineers have known for some time how to do it.
The government of Saskatchewan is very anxious to move coal and potash into the markets of the world. Because of the surveys conducted in the last five years, we now know more thoroughly how much potash and coal there is in Canada. I think the plans of the provincial government of Saskatchewan for developing the Qu'Appelle River could be combined with the needs of the railway to get across the river, and the solution would be beneficial to the province of Saskatchewan and to all the people of Canada. We would be able to complete our obligations under the agreement to provide coal to Europe and Japan.
What I have just described is not mentioned in the Hall commission report. In chapter 9 or 10 it deals with how we can make the railways pay for themselves by hauling more products. I have given, in quantative amounts, the rough parameters on how to make a north-south railway in eastern Saskatchewan pay for itself. Not only will it help the entire country, but certainly it will relieve the pressure on western grain producers which hangs over their heads like the Sword of Damocles, that some silly ass some day will say that we must change the Crowsnest rates.
In 1966 the minister of transport admitted in the House that there was no necessity to change the Crowsnest rates if the railways were making money out of hauling. So, let us make money for the railways in spite of themselves, but it must be done with the strong, strong support of the Minister of Transport. We cannot talk to the railways as we would talk to a group of music teachers. They must understand just one thing-they must be able to explain to their directors and shareholders why they are turning down the opportunity to make money. Once we have said that loud and clear to the railway company heads, they will agree, because they would not dare to stand before their directors and shareholders denying that they should make money.
I would think my remarks are sufficient and hopeful enough to get the minister really interested. He should not take the attitude that he wants to learn more; he should simply get out there and say, "This is what we want to do; let us find the difficulties and clear them up one after the other". In so doing there are several small things he must remember. There is an application before the Board of Transport Commissioners now to pull out one of those little lines which run north and south, on the grounds that it is not economic. This rail line is called the Corning subdivision. It was recommended for abandonment by the Hall commission report and it was turned down by the other study which followed, but it did not consider the subdivision as part of this north-south concept I have just outlined.
Both the Hall commission people and the later study failed in their responsibilities to bring into the over-all global picture what we are trying to do. This matter was put before the so-called Neil study under the authority of the then minister of transport, who gave the solemn promise that if any grain company would say they would keep their elevators in place on these lines which were up for abandonment, then the government would guarantee they would be put on to the permanent lines of the railway system until the year 2000.
Several railway lines were given this status by orders in council as a result of this policy by the former minister of transport. Two of these lines were late in getting their information in, and the then minister of transport promised that he would pass on the recommendation in writing to the new minister of transport, which he did. He asked the new minister to honour his commitment to these producers, in view of the fact that the government was changing. ing them. I hope he will continue them and expand them in the future.
There is hardly another department of the government which can carry out this vital work which is so important in our area. As well, the boater safety programs are equally important in preventing accidents. For instance, the inshore rescue program has two stations, one located in Batchawana on Lake Superior and one in Blind River on Lake Huron, in which young students carried out important search and rescue programs and boater safety programs during this past summer.
I would also like to raise a number of concerns that have surfaced in my constituency relating to airports and air safety. This past summer the Department of Transport carried out an important paving program on the apron of the Manitoulin Island airport, which serves the entire Manitoulin Island and district. However, this was carried out late in the season and some problems have been identified with the paving program. If the program which was carried out this past year is to be fully beneficial to that airport I think it is important that the paving of the main runway be carried out during 1981-82 so that the full benefits of this improvement will be realized. We are hoping that those airport facilities, which particularly serve the tourist industry of Manitoulin, will be increased, because the customs service has agreed to expand their program in the coming year, which will provide customs service right from the airport and, as well, will hopefully provide the direct phone-in service. The phone-in customs service has been operating in the Sault Ste. Marie area for the past year, and will be especially beneficial to Manitoulin airport if established there. I am hoping those two improvements will take place in 1981. That would move up the date for the paving of the main runway, which is scheduled for 1982, from 1982 to 1981. This would enable the necessary remedial work to be done to the apron improvements which were carried out this past summer.
I also want to mention the Sault Ste. Marie airport, which is also located in the Algoma constituency. I mention it because during the next couple of years there will have to be important improvements carried out there as well. The services have outgrown the size of that airport. We have several carriers in there now, including Nordair, whose facilities will be expanded next spring. This will result in the manager of the airport being removed right out of the airport into an auxiliary building. Air Canada has two or three auxiliary buildings as well, which points to the need to expand the facilities of that airport terminal building. In the next couple of years, not only for additional carriers, but to improve the baggage area which is very poorly set up at present. The restaurant facilities, too, are totally inadequate and in need of improvement.
I also want to mention the third airport which is located in the Algoma constituency. It is located at Elliot Lake. The town of Elliot Lake is growing rapidly from some 15,000 people to what is projected to be close to 25,000 by the middle of this decade. This is due to the expansion of the uranium mines in that community. Along with this increase in population has come an increase in the use of the airport.
Supply
The federal government spent some $300,000 in 1979 to expand the runway from 2,500 feet to 3,500 feet. Included in the $300,000 figure was the provision of lighting to the runway. The air boardings and the use of the airport have expanded dramatically since 1976 when there was something in the range of two boardings a month as compared with over 1,000 boardings a month between the two commercial carriers which operate there now. Last month there were over 120 charter flights operating out of that airport. We actually have four communities feeding services into the Elliot Lake airport: Chapleau, Sault Ste. Marie, and Sudbury to Toronto, with nine scheduled flights a day.
Plans are going forward in the next fiscal year to improve the taxi way, the lighting on the taxi way and the car park at the airport. Other needs will become apparent with the expansion of the use of the airport during the next three or four years. Certainly in the next couple of years the small metal building which serves as the terminal will require expanding as the town grows. 1 know that proposals will be coming forward from the Elliot Lake airport committee and the town council for the expansion of that facility. The expansion is necessary because of the growth of the community and in the general area, the growth of air traffic, the development of the Eldorado uranium refinery at Blind River, and the general expansion in the uranium mining industry.
Another problem which the town has faced for the past two or three years is with regard to the atmospheric environmental service at the airport which is currently being provided under an arrangement with Norontair, the principal air carrier in the area. However, the way in which this arrangement works out means that a small town of 15,000 people ends up subsidizing by $75,000 a year the atmospheric environmental service which is normally provided at airports by the federal government through the Department of the Environment. Surely, as the traffic grows this airport will grow, and the responsibility for this service should be assumed by the federal government rather than maintained by a community of this size. It is interesting that this weather information is fed into the national weather service. Obviously the responsibility ultimately lies with the federal government.
More urgently, I want to raise the matters of navigational aids, air traffic control, and radio communication at the Elliot Lake airport with the Minister of Transport. There is a large amount of air traffic at this airport every day, which has nine commercial scheduled flights. At the present time MOT plans are going forward to instal a new non-directional beacon by the summer of 1981 and I understand that negotiations are taking place to have this beacon located at an appropriate spot west of the airport. I also understand that there are plans going forward to move the peripheral UHF radio station from Blind River, some 15 miles or 20 miles away, to the airport to help air traffic control cover this airport.
I am told that we have quite a dangerous situation at the present time because we do not have air traffic control.
