Considering the number of flights and considering the bad weather during the winter months, a great deal of concern is being expressed by the airport committee, pilots and the commercial air carriers, that because there is not proper air traffic control, action should be taken immediately. I hope that the minister will see that action is taken to provide air traffic control, better navigational aids and better communications aids, because they are essential to this airport.
1 would like to congratulate the minister on the action which was taken to provide a new air navigational aid at Wawa, which is just west of my constituency. The device was installed this past year at a cost of some $800,000. It will be very useful to that entire area on the north shore of Lake Superior, north of Sault Ste. Marie. I understand that this is the first air navigational aid of its type to have been installed outside the Rocky Mountain area of western Canada. Certainly it is important to air safety in that area on the north shore of Lake Superior.
1 would like to leave some time for the minister to respond to the several questions which I have raised about airport facilities and air safety in the Algoma constituency, namely, an earlier start to the improvements at Manitoulin-Gore Bay, the terminal facilities in the Sault Ste. Marie, and an increase in the number of navigational aids and the safety facilities at the Elliot Lake airport. I think that it is important that the minister respond to these matters.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, 1 will respond to the remarks made by the hon. member for Algoma on the needs, both air and marine, in his constituency. At the same time 1 would like to take this opportunity to inform the hon. member on what the life of the Minister of Transport entails. I can in all honesty say that the sort of representation he has made is reiterated by almost all the 282 members in this House, including the hon. member for Ottawa-Carleton, who occasionally decides that his riding also has an airport.
My department pays attention to all the matters which are raised, and I am particularly sensitive to those representations. I wake up in the morning thinking about such matters, or go to sleep at night dreaming about radar, ELTs, runways, aprons, parking concessions, and so on and so forth. It has become a major preoccupation.
Mir. Hnatyshyn: Tell us more about your dreams.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
speechtext:
Strangely enough, there has been a change in values. On the subject of safety, the hon. member for Algoma made some comments with which I agree. The preoccupation will be great and the department is very much concerned about safety. When one listens to what is said on air safety, one forgets to look at the record in Canada, particularly with respect to regular scheduled carriers. We have been very fortunate because the number of accidents in Canada is extremely low, and in most years it has been zero. I am looking at my air administrator for his blessing as I am speaking, but most years the fatalities have been zero. This would suggest
that there is a lot of good equipment and much attention given to such matters.
I would like to report very rapidly that the first operating station of the joint en route terminal system at Moncton was opened last summer. This is the first of seven such terminals which will be located across Canada. A rather expensive radar modernization program has been developed which will cost, if I remember correctly, $147 million.
I would like to use this opportunity both to agree with the representations of my friend and to say how expensive this equipment is. The department and the minister try to be as fair as possible in distributing the advantages around the country, but the demand is almost unlimited. I welcome the kind of interventions made this afternoon and last night, particularly by the hon. member for Manicouagan who laid it all out on the floor of the House with regard to his frustration, to which I replied in part by saying a few words on the frustration of the minister.
I also welcome what the hon. member for Algoma said about the coastguard auxiliary program. This has been very, very helpful, and it is one of the main objectives of the department to continue that expansion.
I wish I had more time to deal with the matter of search and rescue, but I want to tell members what is happening. There has been an increase in the number of accidents, particularly on the west coast, due to the increase in fisheries, the increase in commercial transport and the increase in the number of recreational boats. This applies to the Great Lakes as well. Accidents have increased. The Department of National Defence has the primary responsibility in this matter but the Department of Transport has the marine responsibility, and it is spending a lot more money on this particular aspect of its responsibilities as years go by.
1 want to thank the member for Algoma and tell him that I will be particularly mindful of Manitoulin, Elliot Lake, and the coastguard auxiliary force.

Mr. Chairman, I want to apprise the minister-I am sure if he was here last November when we had that problem in Mississauga-that certain representations were made in the House by the member for Mississauga North, and I think they should be corrected.
The tragedy of Mississauga occurred at 11.50 p.m. on November 11. On November 12 at two o'clock in the afternoon when the House opened, this House unanimously directed the minister of transport to have a full and independent inquiry into the activities that happened in Mississauga. As soon as possible the minister organized a public inquiry under Justice Grange. As the minister knows, it is not easy to get a public inquiry going. You have to get a judge, then counsel, and so on. The then minister moved as expeditiously as was possible.
Secondly, the minister directed the CTC to have a Mr. McGee at the site throughout all of the investigation problems, and throughout all of the period when the evacuation was
December 4, 1980

taking place. If the member for Mississauga North lived in Mississauga, if he had even recognized where Mississauga was on November 11, he would have known that. The member is talking through his hat. He does not know what the minister of transport in the last Parliament did. That minister of transport did everything for the benefit of Mississauga that could conceivably be done.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Chairman, I want to direct a question to the minister about air transport. The minister will know that in Mississauga we have probably one of the most profitable airports in Canada, and certainly one of the most busy airports in Canada. The minister will also know that study after study has been made of this airport. I refer him to the last study, the Southern Ontario Modal Passenger study, completed in September, 1979. That study recommended all sorts of things be done. If the minister would direct his attention to Malton, 1 would like to know what the minister has done with respect to a terminal that was supposed to be built within 12 months from the date of that study. Fourteen months have passed and nothing has happened.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I am surprised at the ferocity of the tone. I am flabbergasted, as a matter of fact. I am not used to it. But the short answer was already given to a member from the Toronto area some days ago in the House when I said that the terminal is the subject of a study at the present time. Unless my air administrator contradicts me as I am speaking, the decision on the terminal is expected to be made early in the year.
Tell us when construction will commence.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
speechtext:
First of all, the matter has to come before cabinet and Treasury Board. After that we start planning with architectural designs and that sort of thing. I would think that it will be anywhere between two or three years before the actual construction will take place. Another subject which is being explored now is the financing. A number of people have suggested that in view of the limited financial capacity of governments these days, and in view of the tremendous need across the country for facilities of this kind, we should consider other forms of financing for airports.
As my friend already knows, my department has been through a study exercise on airport management. Unfortunately, its recommendations have not met with unanimous support in all parts of the country, so we are trying to adjust it in order to make it more acceptable to a greater number of people. Thus, there is all this talk under way about both the third terminal at Malton and the financing of it.

I must say that three or four or five years is not acceptable. There is terminal crowding now that is seriously interfering with service in Toronto. The terminal could be financed without any expenditure of public funds. Indeed, the terminal would make a profit from day "go", and the minister knows that. There seems to be no reason whatever for the
Supply
holdup and delay in getting on with this needed terminal building. I would like to have a better commitment than three, four or five years, and study after study, from the minister on this matter. It is about time that the minister took his responsibility for this problem seriously.
This airport presently takes in airplanes like the Cessna 172, and it even rents out space to people in which to park their Cessna 172s. Can the minister tell me what it costs to tie down a Cessna 172 at Toronto international airport?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
speechtext:
I am very familiar with the increase in the recent landing fees. I have good reasons-something like 67 good reasons-judging from the number of letters I received from members of this House. I answered in kind, in the sense that I sent an explanatory note to my hon. friends to explain what had been happening. I am familiar with the increase in landing fee from $1.65 to $5. I explained that and a great number of other things to hon. members, in my letter. The first thing is that this is not vengeance. This is not an attack on general aviation. This is simply an effort to make sure that people using these facilities at the four major airports, namely, Mirabel, Dorval, Malton and Vancouver, make a just and fair contribution to the cost of operating these airports. I have inquired about the price elsewhere in the world and I am told that in Boston and New York it is closer to $50 than it is to $5. Unless my memory does not serve me well, it is more expensive in other airports in Canada also.
Another argument which I have used is the fact that people who are using these airports-and that applies to the four already mentioned, and to the others-should be mindful also that the department does have to recover some of the investments it makes. Why does it have to do it? Because there are other locations in Canada, other groups of people, who would like to have small airports or big airports, and don't. It is a question of fairness.
On the subject of the timing for the construction of the third terminal in Malton, if I was slightly reluctant to indicate a date-and by the way, my hon. friend transformed the two to three years, which I used, to three to four years. Suddenly there was a year added to my timetable. If the terminal were built by private enterprise it could be built more rapidly than if built by government. So I go along with the argument he is trying to make. I suggest to him that we are investigating that possibility now.

Mr. Chairman, may I ask the minister about tie-downs. A tie-down is a place where a person can rent a space at the airport to tie down their airplane so that it will not blow away. Does the minister know you can, in fact, rent a tie-down for a Cessna 172 cheaper at Malton than at the Brampton Flying Club?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, that proves how difficult it is to assess what people actually pay for the services they get. People who own aircraft have to pay a number of fees. For example, there are fees on fuel, and there is this one on

December 4, 1980
Supply
tie-downs. There are landing fees, and so on. Presumably there is the cost of alcohol at the bar, too. However, this should be seen as a general proposition. In the letter which I sent to members I explained the very substantial rise in the cost of landing fees at Malton and three other airports. 1 indicated fees have not been increased in other areas of the airport.

I was not really concerned about the landing fee charges. It is my feeling that a major airport should not be used when there are problems with respect to runway capacity, as there is in Toronto. In my opinion, people should not be allowed to fly in and out of a major airport in private single engine aircraft which are unable to land at speeds comparable to jet aircraft. Toronto international airport is probably our busiest airport in Canada. It certainly has most of our commercial traffic. By allowing planes which have to land at less than 70 knots per hour, this delays all sorts of jet traffic.
When is the minister going to treat Toronto international airport as an international airport? When is the minister going to supply general aviation with other facilities away from the jet-age traffic so that general aviation can have a place from which it can operate with proper IFR facilities? If he handles it that way, he could leave the capacity at Toronto for regular commercial flights and regular business activity using jet aircraft which can land at speeds appropriate to the jet age.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I can only say that the argument which my friend is using is one which I refrain from using. This argument is qualified as unfair by a number of people. It is all right to say that you should use Cartierville if you are in Montreal instead of Dorval, or St. Hubert; to say you should use Buttonville or Maple if you are in Toronto. I was told this is not a very good argument. It is possible that a person who has a plane may not be in a position to use those satellite airports. I did not want to make that as a part of my argument, but if my hon. friend wants to, he can suit himself.
I think it makes some sense in these big international airports used by the larger aircraft, and although I am not an air traffic controller it would appear to me that getting in all the pipsqueaks at the same time must delay the operations of the big planes. I was told not to use that argument because it would not wash well, both intellectually and psychologically.

Mr. Chairman, the minister knows that you cannot use the argument of small aircraft being permitted to land at Toronto international as an excuse to go through a big process of building an airport at Pickering. Would the minister give us a commitment to supply the satellite airports with the IFR facilities so those airports can be used to their fullest extent? The problem is that you cannot fly into Toronto Island airport in all weathers. That is why a person cannot leave his aircraft there. That is why business cannot use that airport to its fullest extent. You cannot use the Maple, the Brampton Flying Club airport or the Oshawa airport the way one would like, simply because the air control facilities are not there. The traffic protection facilities for IFR flying are not there. Will the minister do something to make it possible for people in
general aviation to have an airport to go to so they do not have to take their lives in their hands and compete with the jumbo jets?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, that just proves demand is great. I was going to use the word "unlimited," but that may be an exaggeration. My predecessor used the formula at Vancouver when he offered Boundary Bay airport to private investment. That is an idea.
It is a good idea.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
speechtext:
The idea has been explored. Yes, I said that even in the absence of the hon. member for Vegreville. Even when he is not in the House, I say kind things about him.
My air administrator says that consideration is being given to limit the use of Malton by small aircraft on the basis of pilot licences and weight of plane. This makes sense, and we have just agreed on that. As a counterpart to that, maybe we can try to pay particular attention to the improvement of facilities at the satellites so we can have a compensating balancing factor.

Mr. Chairman, the minister will recall that I asked him in the House about the estimated cost of putting navigational aids into the Toronto Island airport. I suggested to him that it would be about $5 million. Will the minister confirm his investigations with respect to what he has done about my question on the Toronto Island airport?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I have these figures somewhere. Apparently $5 million is correct. However, if I recall, there are two amounts of $5 million; one is for the airport itself and one is for the facilities leading to the airport. If the two are put together, it makes sense. If the Toronto community and the relevant authorities-metropolitan, the city and the government of Ontario-are interested enough to put the STOL project into operation at Toronto Island, then there might be a division of labour and expenditures between the federal government and the other interests and orders of government.

Mr. Chairman, I appreciate there is a $5 million charge to put a bridge or a tunnel into the airport, but it is not necessary to build a bridge or a tunnel because there is a ferry service available. It is my understanding from the minister's figures that $5 million spent on navigational aids would indicate a repayment of the $5 million in about four years with any STOL service. Will the minister confirm that is the case? Will he confirm that if he spent the money on navigational aids there is enough business ready to go there, particularly if he gives the licence to people who want to run the STOL service, and he will get the money back in four years?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I tiptoe into this debate because there are so many ifs in the air. The first if, as the hon. member for Mississauga indicates, is the participation of whoever is going to get the licence from the Canadian Transport Commission. I do not know who it is. One of the
December 4, 1980

difficulties of the decision is by not choosing, because of the uncertainties, the Transport Commission made it more difficult for me to bring this matter to a conclusion.
Had a candidate been selected by the CTC, we could have talked to that person to find out to what extent financially he could get involved in the costs of developing the facilities which my hon. friend has mentioned. That has created difficulties. It is now an "apres vous Alphonse, apres vous Ernest" situation. I now have to do the work. That will start in the coming days. I will find out what other orders of government are willing to do to get this project on the road. I make puns voluntarily. I will then find out to what extent the successful applicant could be involved in this. We will get through it.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: This is the last question for the hon. member for Mississauga South.

The minister will know the government has spent a great deal of money supporting STOL technology in de Havilland. There were at least three applicants who want to use the airport facility at Toronto Island.
Five.

Five. I suspect the minister will know that every member representing Toronto from his side of the House is probably in favour of it, and I suspect that almost every member from the Toronto area on this side is in favour, with the possible exception of the hon. member for Beaches. The new mayor of Toronto is in favour, as is the chairman of metropolitan Toronto and the Toronto Board of Trade.
Will the minister now tell me why he has to talk to more people about that possible airport, which could conceivably pay for this service in four years, before he interferes, and does something to make STOL technology available to Torontonians and others in the Toronto area?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member's time has expired. Possibly the minister can reply briefly.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
speechtext: Just a couple of sentences, Mr. Chairman. I am perfectly aware of the distribution of intelligence or lack of it in this House and elsewhere. With the possibility of one or two, I know who is for and who is against. If I am doing it this way, it is because the steering group had been created for that purpose by my predecessor once removed. I believe my immediate predecessor had the same intention. Therefore, there seems to be some wisdom around the decision to develop a consensus among the different parties. We will talk money at the same time. That is why I am doing it in this fashion. If I were not doing it that way, the hon. member would say 1 am being despotic and Napoleonic, or something of that nature.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, it is a pleasure for me to speak during these estimates debates. I want to mention first that I feel the Department of Transport is probably one of the most difficult departments of the federal government over
Supply
which to gain administrative control. It is my feeling that the present minister has done an excellent job from the point of view of Atlantic Canada. He has had to cope with matters which have been very difficult to oversee.
In recent years Crown corporations have been turned over to their own control so that at the present time the federal government does not exert much jurisdiction over them. One such corporation which is gaining strength, power and authority, and which ought to be very mindful of the needs of Canadians, is Canadian National. CN has a great influence on the lives of Atlantic Canadians.
VIA Rail has recently become a separate company. Although it is no longer a part of the CN system, it is no less important. The maintaining of passenger rail service in the maritime provinces is of the utmost importance. I was glad to see that VIA has put new coaches on the Nova Scotia runs and has made its rail cars considerably more attractive.
In recent years, probably within the last 12, there has been a very disturbing problem in my constituency. That is the erosion of CN Marine, which provides ferry service from North Sydney to Newfoundland. That service is guaranteed under the terms of union with Newfoundland.
This very important service has deteriorated to the extent that approximately five years ago it employed about 1,000 men on the wharves and today employs less than 500. Of these 500, a great many are not working full time and are merely on call. This has been a source of concern to the communities of North Sydney and Sydney Mines, and to me personally as the member of Parliament for that area.
This deterioration continued through the years. This year, with the help of the minister, we were able to obtain a study on the problems of CN Marine. I want to thank the minister very much for interceding in this very desperate situation. The study has not yet been completed. We are hopeful it will point out where the problems have been in this industry and with this community. Once we know the source of the trouble, I am hopeful that steps will be taken to rectify a good part of the difficulty. With this report the minister has provided to the people of North Sydney the feeling that the Department of Transport is not only interested in the future of this very valuable asset, but in the well-being of that community.
The most current and pressing difficulty regarding the CN system is CN Express. I do not need to tell of the difficulty the closure of CN express terminals in Atlantic Canada is creating, particularly in my constituency. The CN Express terminal in the city of Sydney will be closing completely. This will mean a loss of 52 jobs. The economy there, without the closure of CN Express, is very, very shaky. Therefore, this is a very bad time for the economy of that area. The economy will improve with the coming of the mining industry and steel industry, but at this critical juncture the loss of jobs and services will be very damaging.
In the last month, three businesses on the main street of Sydney ceased operation, and rumours are that other businesses will be following suit. These are difficulties that busi-

December 4, 1980
Supply
nesses are facing before Christmas. Imagine what it will be like after Christmas. The difficulties facing these businesses, particularly the merchants, with the closure of CN Express will be absolutely devastating. I ask the consideration of the Department of Transport in that regard.
The additional cost of unloading parcels at Stellarton, the closest terminal, but many miles away, and loading them on to another truck owned by another company will drastically increase the cost of shipping from other points to Cape Breton Island. The economy of Sydney cannot absorb that additional burden.
In view of the hardships facing the merchants of Sydney, is the minister prepared to assist the community in overcoming this very bleak scenario?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
speechtext: The hon. member for Cape Breton-The Sydneys puts me in a very difficult situation. The difficulty is really the behaviour of the minister with Crown corporations. It is not a new problem. Every minister who has been around has experienced this. In the case of CN, it is a schedule D corporation and has a great amount of freedom. That is the way the system works. When Crown companies have less freedom and independence, they are put in different category from that one. The minister must be aware of that. My predecessors have taken the same position as I, that is, we do not tell them what to do. We discuss with them, we try to bring forward other points of views manifested by members of Parliament, bring factors to their attention, and so on.
What about the president's salary?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
speechtext:
Well, even at that, the present salary he receives is probably half of what he would get elsewhere. That applies to us too, but we have special dedication.
In this particular case, I have agreed with the purpose of CN Express and have said so on the floor of the House, because CN Express indicated that they could not do a good job of competing in small parcel express. They tried it and, because of the nature of the beast, they cannot. There are various truckers and others who are more keen and capable of doing it. It is a confession on the part of CN Express that for small parcels they are not able to compete with other companies which are lighter, specialize in certain areas, and do a better job.
Another reason why I cannot agree is the behaviour of CN Express with workers in terms of pre-retirement, relocation, pre-pensioning and retraining. Another reason was the attitude they are taking with respect to communities, in that they will not leave the responsibility to fly-by-night operators but try to accommodate the communities by way of developing subcontracts, interlining and so on. So, they were mindful of their responsibility.
What we are witnessing now is that CN Express is trying to accommodate, in a civilized fashion, the interest of the communities. What we are hearing now is that there might be some accommodations for Charlottetown, Prince Edward
Island, and Cape Breton-The Sydneys, in particular. Maybe they can develop another modus operandi so that there would be only one centre, Moncton, but there would be trailer facilities going from Moncton to those other areas which would reduce the number of employees who would be laid off. Again, I do not want to tell CN Express how to do it. They are, very conscientious people and I told them to do the best job they could in the light of the philosophy that they expounded when they told me that they intended to retrench the small parcel business. I hope the end result is acceptable to the greatest number of people.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion
speechtext:
I am sure the minister appreciates the seriousness of the situation. As I mentioned to him, it is not only a question of jobs in this particular case but the actual survival of a downtown area, an area which is, at this particular time, undergoing considerable hardship.
I think probably very kindly, CN Express is providing pre-retirement pensions and has offered to give displaced employees job opportunities in other branches of CN. In many areas this might be satisfactory. Unfortunately, in an area in which all arms of CN recently laid off employees who are now on call and on standby, to take men from CN Express and to give them the first opportunity for employment in another branch of CN is merely postponing the opportunity for people in that other branch of CN once again to obtain gainful employment. In the context of the high level of unemployment in industrial Cape Breton, I think what should be considered very carefully when Dr. Bandeen, CN and CN Express look at this question, as I think they must, is what the final situation for the CN Express facility in industrial Cape Breton is going to be.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the hon. member has made his case very eloquently. It used to be said of CN that it is both a business and a responsibility. That is the balancing act it has to do regularly.
CN is a business, and it is not there to lose money. I heard an hon. member say this morning that this was the first time he could report that Crown corporations were making money. But if every time they make money-and in business circles this is one of the indications that you are doing a good job-we say they have to lose that money, we take it away, what then? It is this balancing of responsibility between business enterprise, efficiency and so forth that those schedule D corporations must achieve. They must reconcile themselves between being in business and exercising responsibilities, and there is no formula in the textbooks of this House or in the government which will give us a good definition once and for all. In every instance that balancing takes place, and hopefully it will be done well again this time.

Mr. Chairman, I have listened carefully to the minister's replies to the various questions put to him today. I

I had the opportunity to inquire in the House on two or three occasions about the future of Nordair. Could the minister tell us quickly how the matter stands and whether the sale will be completed before January 1?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, if the hon. member can settle the matter, why did he not do so when his party was in power? Obviously, I would have been the first one to be relieved. If he did not act himself with his colleague the minister of transport at the time, it is because the problem is particularly difficult. Some people refuse to accept that, but I feel that in this case especially they are not showing much sense of responsibility. The matter is extremely complex and has become symbolic in a way. But once again, I tell myself that it is not of my own doing.
Compromises should be made by the shareholders in the matter of the balance between shareholders within what is known as Regionair, a holding company grouping various persons and companies. They should come to terms among themselves; the Quebec side and the Ontario side of the group should come to an agreement. Now, if the hon. member insist that I should take care of the Quebec group only, which I doubt he will do because it would be a disservice to the cause, I would remind him that though Nordair has its head office in Montreal, it does in fact operate in Ontario. So it is quite proper for the Quebec government to be interested in the case, just as it is for the Ontario government to be concerned with it too. What is good for one is good for the other. All those aspects have to be taken into account and it is with that rather tricky balancing act that we are now busying ourselves. 1 met once again the Regionair group a few days ago and I shall surely do so again in the next few days. We are trying to find a balance in the matter. It is not just a matter of the shareholders coming to terms, but also that of accommodating the people who work for the companies and the people who
Supply
manage them. They are entitled to some attention too. In many cases, they are responsible for the success of the company. Their interests deserve some consideration.
A third group must also be accommodated: the unions. They have a say in this as well and they have a right to be concerned about the outcome. I feel it is our duty to respond to that too. In addition, we have to think of the future of the company, future investments and the services it will offer its passengers, and so on. So I think this is a very serious matter. Some of my friends have told me that I agonized too much over it, but I would rather be accused of agonizing too much than too little. So, that is why it has taken so much time and is still taking time, but I do think the problem will be solved one of these days.

Mr. Chairman, the minister tells me that this is a serious matter. Of course, it is a serious matter. We considered that matter. We did a lot of work on that case. Mr. Chairman, this is the question I ask the minister today.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, the hon. member knows that I am favourably disposed towards him. But if he wants to contribute to that debate, why does he not tell us this afternoon how he would have solved the problem? I shall listen with the greatest interest.

Mr. Chairman, today we have an opportunity to put questions to the minister responsible, and the fact the minister is asking me questions astounds me as well as the Canadian people. It is his responsibility to provide answers, it is his responsibility to make decisions. He has not decided anything in ten months. speakerposition: Minister of Transport
speechtext:
I cannot say. And in this matter as in many others, I discharge my responsibilities. If some of my friends feel that I am not going fast enough in this matter, it is their privilege to criticize me. The hon. member is exercising his privilege now. 1 have consistently stated that matters have to settle in the Nordair case, and this is now taking place. Some may feel that the process is too slow, that I am not, should I say, bold enough, gambler enough, that I should decide and things would settle down once a decision had been taken. Be that as it may, everyone plays that game with his own gut feelings, and mine would be rather cautious in that kind of thing, especially in a case like this when there is a symbolic significance. We must be especially cautious when a case like this takes on a symbolic significance, which this one has had right from the beginning, and do not blame me for that.
So I tried to be nice this afternoon as I told the hon. member he was missing a golden opportunity to indicate how he would have solved the problem. Because when I took over this department, all the problems were not solved. Yesterday, my friend from Vegreville seemed to be saying that the only problems to have been solved were those he had solved himself. But such was not the case; many problems had not been solved when he took over the department, and 1 inherited many from him. This is normal. It is a classic situation.
As I was saying to the hon. member for Joliette, he missed a good opportunity to contribute to the solution of the problem if he so wished, but he did not. He asked me a question and I replied by pointing out how difficult it was to solve the problem. He is now asking me to tell him what is my deadline, but I cannot do so because the negotiations are still going on. However, I am giving this matter all the attention it deserves.

I can assure the minister that we respect the principle of giving priority to the interests of Quebec without, however, neglecting Ontario.
What I can tell the minister if he will not or cannot reply today, is that what concerns the hon. member for Laprairie and many others is the priority given to Quebec's interests. I want the minister to know this.
Another matter of great interest to Quebec is the confidential report submitted last September 29 to the federal Minister of Public Works, and since it concerns the famous Mirabel project, the Minister of Transport is certainly involved to a large extent. Has the minister seen this document, as I imagine he has, and would he care to comment on what I would call the nearly disastrous situation outlined to the Department of Public Works concerning Mirabel? Nearly all those who live or work there are shocked to see that the initial plan has yet to be carried out. There is much concern because of the amounts that would still be needed to improve all aspects of this project which was supposed to bring about great economic and social benefits and which has fallen far short of its goals. Could the minister comment briefly on this report if he has read it?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, if my hon. colleague is referring to my department's report, I have indeed read it. I do not know whether there is another report. There may have been another on the peripheral zone, on Mirabel's cattle exporting potential. I do not know exactly what he is talking about, but my department has indeed produced a report, to which I have referred in the House, which deals with the situation at Mirabel, the reasons behind the problems.
There are reasons, the main one being Montreal. For reasons which would be too long for me to explain today- because I do not want to take up the hon. member's time- Montreal has simply not been as booming as one could have expected when the building of Mirabel was being considered. That often happens. Forecasters are wrong sometimes one way or another. For example, in Calgary, the department of the day was accused of lacking vision, and volume has increased twice as fast as forecast. What I mean essentially is that economic conditions explain the situation. There are some purely technological conditions, if you want. Aircraft are getting bigger and bigger and cover ever greater distances.
I saw a few days ago that Iberia, which used to route all its flights to Mexico via Montreal, has now routed part of its flights directly from Madrid to Mexico without going through Montreal. This is another one of the factors which have caused the expectations concerning Mirabel to fall through. Several departments are involved in this issue. The Minister of Public Works has a responsibility as concerns the peripheral lands, the Department of Agriculture has some responsibilities concerning the use of the airport for cattle exports, and there is a committee which regroups all of this.
I should perhaps say a few words about the Department of Transport report which I mentioned earlier. I said that the department is studying the factors which have brought about the present situation and that it then makes certain hypotheses. There are now seven scenarios, from moving only a few elements to moving the whole facilities, and each of these scenarios is then analysed on the basis of seven factors, such as passengers, cargo, carriers, and so on. This report should be made public in the next few weeks. The reason I have waited is that three aspects which I consider extremely important are not covered in this report. These are the costs for the passengers, the costs for the carriers and the costs for the governments. I thought that a study which did not cover these three elements left a lot to be desired. This will make up the second phase of this study, and this is what my department is now working on.
December 4, 1980

Mr. Chairman, some time ago, following a speech made by the Secretary of State, a newspaper reported that after a commitment on the part of the Liberal caucus during the election campaign concerning the second phase of the project, the Secretary of State himself had abandoned this project, and 1 would like to know if he was stating the position of the minister and the government and whether it is true that the second phase, which included, I believe, an airport and a runway, will be definitely postponed as the newspapers have reported?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
speechtext:
No, Mr. Chairman, that is not true at all. Perhaps what was meant was-well I do not know what was meant, but the investigation is going on. The cost analysis concerning the three components that I mentioned earlier is going on. What we have done is to eliminate some of the possible scenarios that I mentioned earlier. We have kept only the first, which was the status quo, the sixth, which concerns the transfer of everything except the shorter routes, and the seventh which is a complete transfer. This has narrowed the analysis to be made and the study is now much more limited. It is within this more restricted context that we shall now know what the costs would be.
For my part, 1 do not know whether my colleagues think that I am too careful. Perhaps I am, but I have always been this way. I have not changed. However, I believe it is very important to make cost analyses, before making such vital decisions, because even though many people were willing three years ago to move everything from Dorval to Mirabel, many others are not. Many people would like Dorval to develop as it has been since the second year of the project. Before undertaking any move, the government wants to ensure that there will be some industrial development in the Dorval area to replace the people who will work elsewhere. This is what is going on and it takes a certain time; becoming impatient will not solve anything. I want to accommodate as many people as possible, but in such a matter, I believe that the public will agree that it is better to look twice before leaping.
The whole situation is undergoing a maturing process, a certain evolution. Of course, after what happened in the last few years at Dorval, if the plan continues, if new facilities are provided, the next few years will see new growth, new balance and, in the final analysis, people will not be perturbed to any great extent. At least, that is what I hope.

Mr. Chairman, the minister is surely aware of some of the comments of the hon. member for the area who, for instance, is concerned about the delays, that long overdue development, the projects that could be integrated at Dorval, at Mirabel; he even wonders if the civil servants may not be somehow responsible for those delays. In light of the study on train services between Mirabel and Montreal, the future use of Dorval versus possible progress and changes at Mirabel, is the minister in a position, for instance, to indicate whether or not
Supply
he intends to conduct public hearings at which all interested parties, in Montreal, and Mirabel, as well as probably all hon. members who are interested in the Mirabel project, can be heard, through his own committee or a special committee that could be instructed to look into the matter and see what changes are indicated? There is doubt about it: the viability of Mirabel is important to the government and, as a consequence, to the voters, the citizens. Can the minister tell us whether he would consider an open study of the matter to allow all those whom the project interests to comment on it and participate in it?

speechtext: The time of the hon. member has now expired. If the minister wants to reply very briefly, he may do so.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, the study is in progress. It is the type of question that could lend itself to open discussion once the study has been completed. With regard to the use of Mirabel, I would like to refer to the recent change that happened when First Air received the mandate to cover Ottawa-Mirabel, while Air Canada had only one daily service. First Air will have three round trips. This is the kind of optimal utilization the ministry is striving for in the case of Mirabel to improve utilization, to encourage people in Ottawa to use Mirabel when travelling abroad, to the Caribbean or elsewhere, so they will go there rather than elsewhere.

Mr. Chairman, I am pleased to take part in this debate on the estimates of the Department of Transport. The minister stated he wanted to add additional information to the matters raised by the hon. member for Joliette. I will give him later an opportunity to do so, because 1 also have certain questions for him.
I am amazed to see how eager the hon. member for Joliette was to get answers he already knows. It will be remembered that when he was minister for the northern region, wherein Mirabel lies, his remarks or press conferences earned him nothing more than a reputation as a minister for patronage, because he stated he was ensuring that people doing the census came from the Tory organization. Certainly everyone must remember that speech by the hon. member for Joliette. He looked more anxious to ensure that the people doing the federal 1981 census would be members of the Tory organization.
On his second contribution to this debate, Mr. Speaker, the member for Joliette is suggesting another public study, but as far as I am concerned it seems to me that we have had enough of them, and when the minister says that he is very careful, I can only agree with him about that.
However, I am quite conscious of the complex nature of the responsibilities of our Minister of Transport. He is responsible for maritime, air and land transportation in this country. I

have had an opportunity to learn a bit about his activities when I was parliamentary secretary and at that time I had mentioned, like other colleagues, that the present structure of responsibilities within the Department of Transport which covers the field of air, maritime and land transportation, not to mention the Canadian Wheat Board, made it humanly and physically impossible to ask a minister to be responsible before the House for the management of all its activities and I have not changed my mind on this subject.
Mr. Chairman, we are speaking of the Department of Transport, of its activities. Because of its strategic location in the northeastern corner of North America, Montreal has become a natural hub of all modes of transportation: surface, rail, water, and air, both domestically and internationally. As member for Laval, in greater Montreal, I am convinced, having seen them speak in caucus, that all my colleagues agree we must take this opportunity to make the minister and his staff aware of our concerns as members of Parliament for the development of greater Montreal in the transport sector.
There are 80 million people in a 1,000 kilometre range around this city of three million residents. Because of its privileged position in eastern North America, Montreal has become one of the most industrialized and richest cities in America and since the beginning of aviation in this country, it has become the main port of entry to the rest of the country and the main jumping off point for Europe and the rest of the world. Air, marine, rail and road transport operators converge on the city to make it into an international transport centre. With that objective in mind, we Liberal members of that area will continue to call on the minister to ensure the development, as was mentioned earlier, of Mirabel international airport. Situated 1,500 kilometres from the ocean, the Montreal harbour allows large ocean going vessels to get to the heart of the continent; well situated at the head of the St. Lawrence Seaway, it controls all movements from the ocean to the Great Lakes.
World aviation capital, Montreal houses the seat of the International Civil Aviation Organization and the International Air Transport Association. Situated at the heart of the most travelled rail corridor in the country, Montreal is also where two transcontinental railway systems have their head offices. From all directions, major highways penetrate Montreal's urban fabric whose topography is criss-crossed by all sorts of expressways.
It is, therefore, recognizing Montreal's strategic importance in international transportation, that I rise tonight to speak in this debate. It is obvious that these characteristics were taken into account when the site of Mirabel airport was originally chosen. I do not intend to go over all the points that have been made thus far, but I would like to take this opportunity to find out in what direction Mirabel international airport is headed.
For months, not to say years, the members who are working at the regional level have studied several departmental papers to ensure the development of Mirabel. However, it seems to be almost impossible to know what direction will be taken. I was wondering this evening when the Minister of Transport was answering the member for Joliette and listing the number of
departments involved at Mirabel if he does not think that the present structure was not too cumbersome. The minister said that when a decision concerning the peripheral areas of Mirabel was made the Department of Public Works had its say. When livestock exports are concerned, the Department of Agriculture gets in the act. The Department of Transport, as well as the Department of Finance, Treasury Board, etc. are, of course, involved in the development of Mirabel.
It seems to me, Mr. Chairman, in light of the facts acquired after almost ten years of experience, while the economic context is different, that the planning and development schemes have been altered, but I feel that the structure is too cumbersome and that decisions are not taken because studies are multiplied and consequently Mirabel is endangered.
If the minister is willing to hear me, I would like to make a suggestion. Unlike the member for Joliette I will not refer once again to another public inquiry or anything else. The member of the area, Mr. Chairman, have been considering the problem for many months. Given the complexity of the structure and the fact that the Department of Public Works, the Department of Transport and the Department of Agriculture all have their say in any decision, I take this opportunity to suggest to the minister that we should lighten the structure, set up a board of directors at the airport who would be responsible to the Minister of Transport and would co-ordinate the activities of Mirabel, Dorval and Saint-Hubert. In addition, the board of directors at the airport would endeavour to develop the area and the trade at the industrial park of Pica. The board of directors would also be asked to organize step by step the implementation of the Mirabel plan. It is a suggestion I am making to the minister. The present organization seems to me to be extremely heavy. Decision-making takes an enormous amount of time and we now find ourselves in a dilemma. When a minister becomes responsible for the administration of the airport, new studies are undertaken and it causes further delay. I make that suggestion. The problems seem to have been identified.
I am thinking about the problem of transferring flights from Dorval to Mirabel, of completing the development of a road transport system, of rapid transit on rail or otherwise. I have made perhaps ten speeches in the House on the importance of developing roads to Mirabel. A very modern airport for passengers as well as cargo has been built, but there is no road system and the province of Quebec under a PQ administration does not have any confidence nor any interest in developing Mirabel. We have been told Mirabel did not rate as a priority. It seems to me it is up to us to ensure the development of a road system to try to improve the situation.
I should like to ask the minister a question about commuter trains. I am addressing the minister, Mr. Chairman. With regard to commuter trains, I asked in October what the policy of the Canadian government would be, while abiding by the fact that urban transportation comes under provincial jurisdiction. We have had the sad experience of the abandonment of

road transportation, of CP rail service. The province of Quebec refused to take responsibility for providing service to users. Then the Quebec transport minister wrote to the CP Rail director once again to express pious thoughts, and not only was the service discontinued but after my conversation with CP Rail authorities, it was suggested that the Lakeshore service could also be discontinued in December if the provincial government, that is the government of Quebec, does not fulfil its responsibilities in that area. speakerposition: Minister of Transport
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I must say that to be able to make a comment on the administrative structure, on the structure the hon. member for Laval is suggesting for Mirabel, I should ask him first two questions: Does he suggest the establishment of an executive board or an advisory board? I have to know that. And I have to know what kind of source of financing he has in mind. What will be the financial responsibility of that board?

Mr. Chairman, I am pleased to answer that question. To me, that board should be administered somewhat like the National Harbours Board; it should be a kind of board of administrators with such powers that decisions would be a little closer, we would have a much closer centre of decision. I made that suggestion because it seems to me that as far as current structures are concerned, given the involvement of three or four departments in the decision-making process, the results we have seen so far fail to indicate that the present structure is the most efficient. There are some Crown corporations- 1 refer to schedule C-whose board of directors reports directly to the minister, and 1 am now thinking of a board like Canadair's, class C. That board has some powers and is directly responsible to the minister.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, if the hon. member for Laval did not see the study the department made on airport management, that will demonstrate that great minds think alike because that study advocates something along the lines of the hon. member's suggestion. It even indicates how we could conciliate the local board with the management of the Department of Transport since the department must assume some reponsibilities for the security aspects, for example. According to this study, which proves that studies are sometimes very useful, the Department of Transport and that local board could share the responsibility and the authority. I could go on, but I will not. This study also shows how the financing could be shared, how some taxes could be earmarked for these airports and how the airport administration could raise funds to extend the runway, to build a roadway or a parking lot, which goes to prove that great minds think alike.
But the problem is that this study made by the department met with quite a bit of opposition in the country and it is interesting to note that it has a lot to do with psychology and culture. In some areas, people say that these airports-I am talking about Mirabel for instance-are too fraught with responsibility to be entrusted to ordinary people who are not

qualified to assume these responsibilities. It is therefore very difficult for me to sell this policy by showing to what degree it is applied across Canada.
But to encourage the hon. member I would say that the second part of his speech is also very pertinent because some people suggested at the same time that it might be risky to entrust the local administration with this responsibility, that it might be advisable to establish the equivalent of the harbours board at the national level, with subsidiaries at the local level and this body would be the same across the country. That, I think, is what the hon. member for Laval was saying at the conclusion of his speech.
In any event, we will try that line of action with harbours. Because as I stated yesterday we have a document addressed to my colleagues in which we are trying to establish a structure which would consider the National Harbours Board as a strong super-corporation with mini-administrations in Montreal, Vancouver and elsewhere. We will test that system. We will see if the response of cabinet to this approach is positive and if its application to harbours can be extended to airports. I thank the hon. member for his contribution to our consideration and this area.
