There are always people, and we read about it every day in the press, who will say that a certain piece of equipment is the greatest invention since sliced bread. Then others will attack that same piece of equipment as if it were of no use at all. There is a similar debate on the quality of the equipment purchased by the department, or by any other department for that matter.

1 am not talking about the quality of the equipment; I am talking about the obsolescence of the equipment and the technology that is involved. The minister should be aware that the equipment is at least 20 years old. I find it very strange that the department would continue with the installation of obsolete equipment while putting across to the general public the illusion that it is modernizing or bringing up to date the radar system across Canada. Is the minister prepared to comment on that point?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
speechtext: I am not prepared to give advice on what is the best equipment. The department has a lot of qualified people for that particular purpose, and they have discussions. I take the advice of my officers on these matters. I am not competent to judge, nor do I know anybody in the cabinet who is, what is the best radar available in the market now. I really do not know what the member from Esquimalt-Saanich expects me to say at this particular moment. Does he want to say that I have personal views on this matter? I have none. I take the advice the air transportation administrator gives me when he says that this is the most modern piece of equipment available. We could have a debate on the importance of rail compared to buses, or buses compared to airlines, or big jets compared to STOL aircraft, and so on and so forth.
I think we were talking about radar. I wonder whether the minister could tell us to which corporation the contract was given to develop this system for installation.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
speechtext: It has not been given. I have also received correspondence from Raytheon to the effect that they should be given the contract without competition, but this is not the view of the department, and this is being attended to now.
Perhaps the minister could tell us whether CAE Electronics is in this operation in any form.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
speechtext: Well, that sort of proves the point I was making, that another company feels it should be given this contract, I understand, almost automatically. Others would like to participate in it too and, of course, this is what is happening now. It will be an open tender.

Will it be given to those who have expertise in the development of radar equipment, or
Supply
will it be given to those who have been developing simulator equipment for training pilots? I wonder whether the minister is aware of that part of it.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
speechtext: If I were aware of all these questions I would be senior air adviser. I am sorry, but my hon. friend is old enough, he is experienced, he is a former diplomat, he is a great intellectual, he is a great thinker, and so on and so forth, and he knows very well that there is no minister on earth who can explore and find out all about the different pieces of radar equipment. The answer is that there is an interdepartmental committee involved in ensuring open competition and that all developments and purchases are in accord with government policies and practices.
Does the minister become involved in this committee once it has decided what it is going to do, or does the minister have any say whatsoever in this?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
speechtext: I would not care to give advice to Mr. McLeish on which of the radar systems would give the best bang for the buck in Canada at this time. Really I am at loss to find out what the role of a minister is. I read MacGregor Dawson and he tells me on page so-and-so that the minister should not be an expert. I do not want to teach political science to my hon. friend. I am not supposed to be an expert. 1 am not going to say, "Hey, McLeish, buy this radar, it is the one I like", because it is red or blue or whatever it is. Is that the role of a minister, according to my hon. friend?

I wonder if the minister has ever been brought up to date on some of the problems confronting air traffic controllers at Victoria international airport? Is he aware, for example, that within the last six months there have been near misses reported at the rate of at least one a month? I also hope he is aware-if he is not, he has not been listening to my question-that there is no radar in use at Victoria international airport.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
speechtext:
I am certainly aware of it because my hon. friend has taken very good care to make me aware of it. As to the radar system, he asks me the question every time he sees me-on elevators and everywhere. So how can I not be obsessed by it? I have consulted people who know about these things and they have assured me, on a stack of Bibles, that Victoria is not in trouble now, that the service is covered from Vancouver, that the distance is not an abnormal one, and that this is done in all other civilized parts of the world. There is nothing abnormal about it. I keep repeating that to my hon. friend, and he keeps not believing what is being said.
On the subject of misses, near misses, separation, or whatever you want to call it, he brings all of these cases to my attention. I pass the information on. The department makes inquiries, surveys, analyses, investigations, and what-not, on location. I am assured that this is not the case. I pass on the news to my hon. friend who keeps not believing what he is being told. Maybe that is why he was such a distinguished ambassador. He never believes what he sees but prefers to go

December 4, 1980
Supply
and find out for himself. So, be my guest. Is there anything else I can humanly do to satisfy his curiosity? Am I not being responsible in what I am doing?

I hope on the next visit to Victoria international airport the minister does not have a near miss. Has he had any feedback from his officials, from Mr. McLeish or anyone else, about aircraft going into Victoria international airport through parachutists-through 20 or 30 parachutists?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, that report was verified. I read it. Radar would not pick up parachutists, even if we had radar that was operating at that time. That question from the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich has been brought up several times. The term "near-miss" is an expression used by the media. There is great variance between what a civilian considers a near miss and the certain minimal loss of separation that is required to be reported to Transport Canada.

I would like to ask the
minister one final question with regard to civilians. One of these incidents was reported by an RCMP officer, and I think his testimony could be relied upon. I suggest to the parliamentary secretary that parachutes and parachutists do not grow up out of the ground; they are dropped from aircraft. The aircraft, at least, would be picked up by radar if radar were being used. These were American parachutists and they were over American soil. Why is there no co-ordination in that area, particularly on a flight path? I think this situation is worth inquiring into. Why is there no co-ordination with Vancouver when there is going to be a parachute drop on the flight path to Victoria international airport, which is presumably controlled by Vancouver? Why is there no co-ordination between Vancouver and the military in the EJnited States which are going through an exercise? Has there been no report on that? If there has, why has it not been made public?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
speechtext:
I am sure there is such co-ordination between the United States authorities and Canada.
I just want to say I am sorry I showed a bit of impatience a moment ago. It is part of the exercise, presumably; I apologize. What made me a bit impatient is that I thought I had done my job in these matters. I had brought these situations to the attention of the officials who had conducted the inquiry in the Victoria situation. I remember regularly signing correspondence to my hon. friend on these matters. I want to philosophize for half a second. It is strange the way things are seen. The last time I was in Victoria-which was in recent times-I forgot to go and see the radar system. I must say I regret that, though I would not have understood it anyway.
It is not there. There is no radar.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
speechtext:
I remember the baggage tray located outside the airport. I thought it was beautiful. I thought it was remarkably poetic, pretty, useful, convenient and what-not. I took it that
the assumption was that it never rained in Victoria, and 1 regretted not having accepted an invitation some years ago to teach there.
I was not talking about that.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
speechtext: I thought you were talking about baggage facilities.
Yes, but behind the baggage counter.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
speechtext: That is what I am talking about. If that is not what the hon. member is talking about, I am sorry.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order, please. I did permit a last question, but with the news that the question and answer are dissociated from one another, I have no choice but to recognize the hon. member for The Battlefords-Meadow Lake.

Mr. Chairman, I have a number of questions I would like answered. These concern the closure of express offices throughout Canada. There was an article in The Globe and Mail on November 18, 1980, which reported a decision of CN Express to close about half its 70 terminals in Canada, many before the end of 1981, starting with 15 express terminals in the Atlantic region.
I have a letter with me from employees of CN Express in Nova Scotia in which they express their concern at the reduction of about 40 per cent of the services. This will result in the loss of 254 jobs in the maritime provinces alone and over 1,100 jobs across Canada. At the same time someone from Newfoundland phoned me. He was concerned about what was happening to the rail service in that province and its turnover to Terra Nova Transport, the company now responsible for rail services in Newfoundland.
My first question is this. When the ten-year period is up- the amount of time which was given by a previous minister of transport, the Hon. Otto Lang, to prove whether the rail service in Newfoundland was a profitable venture or not-will the rail service be pulled out completely? What will happen to the fellow who called me with 35 years' seniority in CN? Will he be out of a job along with many others? At the end of the ten-year period which Mr. Lang talked about when he was minister of transport, will you reassess the situation and look at the service which is called for under section 262 of the Railway Act, or will you close down the rail system in Newfoundland?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I welcome this participation. I meant to speak about the railway situation in Newfoundland in my opening remarks but I did not finish my remarks because of the time limit. The hon. member for Regina West knows all about the railway and he is always on track.

Don't use my time on him.
December 4, 1980

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
speechtext:
If my memory serves me correctly, the Sullivan report came out in 1977. One of its recommendations was the elimination of the railways in Newfoundland, not because that board did not like railroads, but because the railroads did not fit into the transportation system. Since then there have been a number of debates and federal-provincial meetings. There have been only a few in the last year or so because of the two elections, among other reasons. However, the officials were still in contact, but the warmth of the relationship was not as good as that which normally exists.
A few weeks ago I went to St. John's. I met the premier and the minister of transport for that province. We had a very good conversation. 1 tried to sell him the idea of trade-offs. This idea of trade-offs is in the Sullivan report. One of the fears provinces have, particularly in the east, is that the federal government will not continue to support them financially as well as they have in the past. My hon. friend is aware of the tremendous sums of money which go into the subsidization of transportation in the Atlantic provinces.
The idea is to create a transportation envelope, a sum of money going from Ottawa to province X. The province, then being assured of that minimum sum of money, could then begin to allocate money, in consultation with the federal government, to the best form of transportation for the province. That is the philosophy. In other words, envelope, tradeoff, multimodal and so forth.
That is the notion I was trying to sell to the province of Newfoundland. In that context, knowing that the money which goes to the railway now would not be lost, it might be that the province could look at transformation or maintenance in a slightly different light. Anyway, that was my purpose. I was trying to convince the authorities in Newfoundland to accept a five-year global transportation plan and a five-year railway plan, with an experimental phase to find out whether the railway was a viable proposition. It was with the thought that, if the province itself realized that it was not a viable proposition, the money would not be lost; it could be used to build roads, buy buses, or whatever.
So much for your energy program.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
speechtext: It is debatable which is more costly, a full bus or an empty train. Officials have met since that time. I have not had a report because I have been too busy here. In any event, this exercise will be continued in the coming weeks.

Mr. Chairman, I take it that we will not know what is to happen when the ten-year period is up, as announced by the Hon. Otto Lang. He said that the rail service would terminate under Terra Nova Transport. However, I am still concerned about the closure of the CN Express stations across Canada. I have mentioned the people who will be losing their jobs in the maritime provinces. At the same time, I am also concerned about western Canada.
Prior to the announcement on November 18, as reported in The Globe and Mail, I knew that the express station in The Battlefords community in which I reside had closed on Octo-
Supply
ber 24. Even after much protest from the community and from myself as a member of Parliament, the station closed. We asked for a hearing to be held. We made reference to section 262 of the Railway Act. We mentioned the erosion of services in the area over the past number of years. We wanted all of this looked into very closely. If I look back over the years I have lived in The Battlefords-Meadow Lake area, which is a part of western Canada, I have seen the rail service deteriorate, even in my young years. The constituency of The Battlefords-Meadow Lake covers over one-third of the geographic area of the province. There is no point in the constituency where you can have rail passenger service. The train goes through there, but there is no passenger service at any point in the constituency. There is no mobile operator in The Battlefords. There is one mobile operator in the Meadow Lake area. Then we had the closure of the CN Express station in The Battlefords. There is no service at all in The Battlefords-Meadow Lake constituency from rail, other than for the movement of grain, which has not been very effective either in past years. There is a story of plugged grain elevators from Medstead to Robinhood, Meadow Lake and many other points in the constituency. I am concerned about this.
My next question on this erosion and closure of service is whether this is because the service is too costly to upgrade and keep in place. Are these closures a money saving item, or are they because of the bad service provided by the railways in the past. Which of those two is it?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
speechtext: With regard to CN Express, Mr. Chairman, I have already answered a number of questions today and on previous days. I emphasize that even if money was an important consideration, it was not the only one. It may not even have been the most important. However, the money aspect is there. CN Express lost $14 million in 1970. It is now losing $57 million or $58 million yearly. If it goes on, it will lose more and more money. I explained that this afternoon. As I said earlier, because of the nature of the beast, being relatively heavy in administrative terms, it is not in a position to compete with smaller operators, operations of ten guys with five trucks. They can operate faster, working weekends, off hours and so on.
CN used to do it, and they quit.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
speechtext:
The argument being made is an understandable one. In any event, they are not in a position to compete because the smaller companies can specialize, carrying smaller parcels and so on. CN decided to get out of this area while continuing with larger shipments. There is a technical word which escapes me at the moment-less than carload, I am told. We are witnessing the consequences of this.
Some people will lose their jobs. I stated previously that CN Express has guaranteed that up to 90 per cent of those affected by these moves will be pre-pensioned, relocated or retrained. They are going out of their way to act in a humanitarian fashion.

December 4, 1980
Supply
Will 1,100 people across Canada be retrained and put in other jobs?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
speechtext: Yes. CN says they are guaranteeing the employment of all those people.
Can you promise those 1,100 people they will not lose their jobs?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
speechtext: I am repeating the guarantee CN has given to the union which, by the way, is co-operating in this. The president of the union is co-operating with CN Express.
He is not very happy with 1,100 people losing their jobs.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
speechtext: I am saying that co-operation with the union is a fact. The hon. member can verify that if he wants. The 90 per cent figure is one that CN used in a communique they issued on this matter. The biggest problem, accepting the fact that employment is an important one, is with the communities. A number of communities feel they will be affected too harshly by this. Discussions are now going on. This afternoon I raised the question as to whether it would be possible for CN Express to maintain one point in Prince Edward Island, to establish a slightly different kind of relationship between Moncton, which will be the headquarters for CN Express operations in the maritimes, and Halifax, Sydney, and so on. This is the sort of adjustment which is now taking place.

I thank the minister for that reply. 1 have a couple of questions following up on that. Will the minister agree that the services I describe to places such as The Battlefords have decreased over the years? Second, does he relate the closure of the express stations to an expenditure item, the fact that the railways will save money? I would like to know how money would be saved by the closure of express stations. The minister must keep in mind it cannot be a total saving. Other carriers have to be paid, such as Kindersley Transport which does the interlining in the area of Saskatchewan I represent. How much money will be saved? Does the minister agree there has been an erosion of service over the years?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, in all of these discussions there is a bit of a philosophical base. The hon. member appears to believe the government should play a major role in all of these matters. He has been well trained by the hon. member for Regina West in believing that section 262 of the Railway Act orders the railways to deliver wherever in the country there is something to be sent. That has been contradicted by the Supreme Court, yet the hon. member for Regina West will believe it "until death do us part". This is the debate.
What happens when CN Express leaves a community because it cannot compete as it operates differently than it used to, is that somebody picks up the work. It may not be the same person who gets the work. That is why CN is offering pre-pensioning and relocation. However, the work does not disappear. Somebody else does it. It is no longer the Government of Canada through CN Express. That is why so much of the debate is in the minds of the two members. I do not believe the Government of Canada has to do it all directly. If the private sector can do a job as well and cheaper, why not?

Will the minister please answer how much money will be saved by closing the express stations as opposed to bringing in by carrier? What is the dollar saving? There was a meeting in the Battlefords with Mr. Dawson of Winnipeg who told us that a great deal of money will be saved. He stated that the reason for closing the express stations was to cut the deficit of CN. How much money will be saved?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, 1 do not know exactly how much money will be saved in the Battlefords. However, the general impression I have gained is that there will be a reduction in losses when the program is complete. I am advised $50 million.
I do not know exactly what these figures mean. I would like a bit more discussion on this subject. The figure I have in mind is $57 million, and increasing. Presumably CN Express hopes that by getting out of small parcels and remaining in the less than carload trade, it can cut its losses. Because it hopes to cut losses, it is in a position to be rather generous to its employees who will be affected by this move. As I said, the employees will be pre-pensioned, relocated or retrained. I have repeated ad nauseam that the information I have is that up to 90 per cent of those affected will be so treated. It is difficult to stop the world, to prevent change or transformations from taking place. This is one of them. CN Express is trying to do it in as responsible a fashion as possible.

I think I have time for one final question. I sincerely believe there is a problem. We understand the railways are losing money. With the loss of passenger service, express service and mobile operators, all the railways will do is haul grain, and they do not do that very efficiently. Will the minister, under section 262 which he referred to and the member from Regina West referred to, hold a hearing in the Battlefords area into the lack of services not only for the Battlefords but for places like St. Walburg, Turtleford, Med-stead and Meadow Lake to see what the people in those areas have to say and what their concerns are about the loss of services? The area is going through an economic boom right now. They are into heavy oil, they are into mining. It is an area of the country that is developing. We need better rail service and not a deterioration of that service. Will the minister consider holding a hearing in The Battlefords-Meadow Lake constituency, preferably in the Battlefords, so that the people there can express their concerns to the minister and to the Canadian Transport Commission?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
speechtext:
The Canadian Transport Commission knows what it has to do. I do not have to give them instructions on these matters. 1 will not contradict myself to the point of asking the Transportation Commission to do that. I have been standing on the floor of the House today, and last week, defending what CN Express is doing. Since they cannot compete, they want to get out of the transportation of small parcels
December 4, 1980

rather than defend the way they are doing it. It will have to take place.
As a general proposition, CN are not in business to lose money. They have CN Express, on which they always lose money, so they want to lose less money so they can pay the Government of Canada better dividends next year than they were able to pay last year. That is what I meant when I talked about CN being both a business and a responsibility. This is where the balancing act takes place, and no one has written a description of that because it varies from one circumstance to the other. If CN find out that there are a number of things they do not do well and others that they do better, then they should do what they do best.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
It is somewhat novel for me to be speaking on a matter of substance rather than procedure or points of order, or questions on the order paper. It reminds me of the old days when I was vice-chairman of the transport committee. I want to inform the House, for those who do not realize it, that the members of the transport committee, over the years, have worked very well together and basically co-operated with one another on a very non-partisan basis. I would draw the attention of hon. members to the fact that the member for Vegre-ville, the former minister of transport, the member for Regina West, and the member for Dartmouth-Halifax East are here. All of us worked together on a non-partisan basis to improve passenger rail service in this country.
1 am not that immodest that I would not take credit along with those individuals I have mentioned for the fact that VIA Rail was created in 1977 at the behest of myself and other members of that committee who have been concerned about the deterioration of passenger rail services, for years and years. I think that credit must be given where it really falls, and that is to all members of this House who have supported passenger rail. I might say to hon. members, Mr. Chairman, and to the minister, because he was not here between 1974 and 1979 when we had that really tough fight to get passenger rail service re-established, that it was a tough fight. It was a fight that was won, over the resistance of people within the Department of Transport.
I commend the minister's predecessor, Mr. Lang, and those senior officials in his department who recognized that the formation of a totally dedicated passenger rail corporation would be in the best long-term interests of this country, and was long overdue. I commend to the minister certain parts of the speeches made by the hon. member for Vegreville and the hon. member for Regina West on the subject of VIA Rail, and I can say to him that I share some of their concerns.
I share the concern of the hon. member for Regina West about the unenviable position VIA Rail was put into when it was first started, in that it had to take CP and CN equipment which was not maintained properly or well. In the case of CP it was in an absolutely disastrous state. The locomotives were so run down that I believe many of them were actually written off. And we expected a passenger rail corporation to do a
Supply
credible job! I think Mr. Roberts and the people at VIA Rail have done an excellent job over the last three years, but they are going to need a lot of help from all hon. members on this side of the House because, as the hon. member for Vegreville pointed out, with the escalating energy costs and with the shortage of oil something must become apparent to the government and the officials in the Department of Transport. It certainly has been the case with me for many years.
What must become apparent is that the future for transporting large numbers of people in this country has to be passenger rail in the corridor areas. I know that the government gave about $200 million to VIA for the purchase of the new LRC equipment which will be coming on-stream next year but, with all due respect, that is not enough.
Right on.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Mr. Roberts, the president of VIA Rail, wrote a letter to me. I have regular correspondence with him. We should write a book. I try to keep up my interest in passenger rail, and I have the letter here. I have Mr. Roberts' permission to make this public, and at the end of my remarks I propose to have it appended to Hansard, if there is the unanimous consent of the House. Some of the things Mr. Roberts says in his letter are quite startling and contrary to the given line-when I say the "given line", I say that with all due respect-by the department over the years as to why we cannot have in this country a truly rapid, viable, passenger rail service in the corridor. I will not read the letter now because I hope I will get the consent of hon. members to append it to Hansard-
Agreed.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
-but the president of VIA Rail talks in terms of plans which are now on the drawing board of VIA Rail. VIA Rail would like to realize within the next five years a travel time between Quebec and Montreal of one hour and fifty minutes; Montreal and Ottawa, one hour; Ottawa to Toronto, two hours and forty minutes; Toronto to Windsor, two hours and thirty minutes; and Montreal to Toronto, three hours and forty minutes. This is the first time I can recall that the president of VIA Rail has actually been pinned down to the fast service members of this House have been advocating for years.
In his letter Mr. Roberts went on to explain to me how this is to be done. It is to be done largely through a solely passenger dedicated track operating from Quebec City right through to Windsor. This involves using part of the special tunnel in Montreal, the Mount Royal tunnel, and negotiations have to be undertaken with the railways. It involves using the CP line from Vankleek Hill, which I understand was built about 80 or 90 years ago by Canadian Pacific to take trains, in those days, at speeds of up to 95 or 100 miles an hour and which has been allowed by that railway to become run down over the years. Only one train runs over it just to keep the company's options open. I think that is "The Canadian"

December 4, 1980
Supply
passenger service which has now been taken over by VIA Rail. That goes through Vankleek Hill, Ontario. That is one aspect.
The other aspect would be going through Smiths Falls, and we all know about that problem. It is absolutely ludicrous to visitors to this country who take rail between Ottawa and Toronto. It is fine from Toronto to Brockville, but then they have to be switched. It takes about half an hour to switch them on to the track. I believe it is a CP track to Smiths Falls. I may have it the wrong way around, but the track between Brockville and Smiths Falls has a slow order of 25 miles an hour on it because the track is so rotten. I have been stuck on that train many a night. I do not know whether the tracks have seized up, or the trains have seized up.
1 think that not to have the nation's capital lined by rail to the second largest city in the country is indeed unfortunate, and something which I am sure the minister will correct, because I have talked with the minister here and there about these concerns, and I know that he really would like to see an improvement. It must be seen within the context of my remarks that I note good faith on the part of the minister and the government in trying to improve passenger rail.
Mr. Roberts also talks about building a new 60 kilometres line to link Smiths Falls with Belleville. That would be a completely new track. It would join the main line and then go right to Toronto.
I do not really want to make too much of a speech because I would like the minister to reply, and I am sure he is making notes of some of the things I say. On the main line a few years ago there was a special run of the Turbo at 142 miles an hour. That was clocked going through Kingston. Admittedly, Department of Transport personnel were involved in the test. All the crossings were closed off. It was done at a quiet time of day, but I submit that if that could have been done three or four years ago under very strict supervision, we do not have to bury all the underpasses and we do not have to build bridges and involve astronomical costs to make the main line truly viable.
I became frustrated in the Standing Committee on Transport when I heard people from the department and Mr. Lang at the time, saying it would cost half a billion dollars or a billion dollars to improve this section of track. That does not seem to be the case, because I think that with the appropriate crossings and signalling equipment we can run trains much faster.
One specific thing I would like the minister to answer is who it is who determines that no train can run more than 95 miles an hour along that stretch of track when, in the test run a few years ago, a train was clocked at about 142 miles an hour. I asked Mr. Benson a few years ago because I was always told by the minister-I am not talking about the present minister but the former minister-that the CTC was the one. The railway said it was the CTC. I talked to Mr. Benson in committee, and he said, "No, it is the railways". I would like to find out who is responsible for artificially limiting the speed of passenger trains on the main passenger rail line in this country.
Mr. Roberts also mentioned the fact that the corridor service is not limited to Quebec-Windsor. It also involves Edmonton to Calgary. I understand that there are discussions under way with the Alberta government on building a highspeed demonstration track between Edmonton and Calgary. It would be cheaper than building a new four-lane highway, with all the extra costs involved.
If it is agreeable-I know I cannot table documents other than those pertaining to official government business in my role with the Privy Council-I will ask for the unanimous consent of the House to append Mr, Roberts' letter to me of October 29, 1980, to Hansard.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: The House has heard the suggestion made by the Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council to the effect that he be permitted to append the document he has in his hand to today's Hansard. Is that agreed?
Agreed.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
So ordered.
[Editor's Note: For text of above letter see appendix.}

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I hope I get the letter back because I did not make a copy before I came here. I am sure I will because it will be in Hansard. I think the comments in Mr. Roberts' letter will be beneficial to the minister and all members of this House. As I say, I have the permission of Mr. Roberts to make that letter public.
I want to deal with another aspect just briefly, and to throw out an idea. I am not an expert on western Canada, and I defer to those hon. members here from western Canada who know their region best, but the government announced a $4 billion western development fund in the budget.
That is after you take out eleven.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
One of the premises involved is that, by virtue of the fact that more moneys will be accruing to the federal government, the oil and gas industry will in a sense be channelling money into this western development fund. The federal government has undertaken that, with the excess revenues it will get, there will be a $4 billion fund. I am in favour of that because one of the things I fervently believe in is Canadianization of the oil and gas industry.
I throw this out as a novel idea. It may get me into trouble, but I have been in trouble in the past, and I am not worried about that. I think it might be a good idea to look at it. If we expect the oil and gas industry to contribute a higher amount of moneys accruing from oil and gas-and I agree with that- then perhaps we should also-and I am sure Mr. Ian Sinclair will quiver or quake when I say this-look at the fact that Canadian Pacific was granted enormous land titles a hundred years ago. Yes, it was private capital which built that railway, but it was back here every year to John A. Macdonald and his successors, cap-in-hand saying, "Give us some more money".
December 4, 1980

I think Canadian Pacific International, Canadian Pacific Investments, CPR or whatever its official title is-I know there are a number of companies-is a great standard bearer for Canada throughout the world. I have great respect for Mr. Sinclair as an individual, and for the members of that company, but it seems to me that if we are to ask the oil and gas industry to pay a royalty back to western Canada and to Canadians in general-I suppose that is what we are doing with the extra money coming from that-then perhaps we should also look at the fact that it is long overdue for the people of this country to receive a dividend from the land we gave Canadian Pacific a hundred years ago. I think a good case could be made that that kind of dividend should be paid to the people of Canada.
I know that CPR is investing heavily in electrification and in other improvements to its track. I fully accept its plans, and I think they are made in good faith, but CP has been a successful company. I should leave a few minutes for the minister to respond. I think this might be an idea which might be worth the government's consideration.

Mr. Chairman, I rise on a point of order. The hon. member has made some points about the CPR. I wonder if he knows that in addition to 34 million acres of land and hundreds of millions of dollars, Canadian Pacific owes the people of Canada $ 1 billion in deferred taxes, that that is why CP is making a profit, and that that is why it appears to the hon. member to be successful.
An excellent point of order.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I will comment on that last remark. This subject is a popular one, as my friend the parliamentary secretary knows. It was the object of a resolution at the Winnipeg Liberal convention. An investigation into what CP has done with all the money it received way back is a popular subject.
I understand that CP has been investigated a number of times. Whoever made the decision came out with a balanced judgment that yes, indeed, CP received great favours and yes, indeed, it served Canada well, so perhaps there is a need for another one of those. 1 do not know.
On the subject of rail, the parliamentary secretary reminded us that the government created VIA and supported it strongly through the first two or three years. 1 said this morning that it was a bit too early to conclude, but I did recite a number of the good things VIA is doing now and pointed out the great aspirations the government has that it will continue to pursue. I spoke yesterday about load factors, lower losses than anticipated, and all that, so I do not want to repeat it.
With respect to Mr. Roberts' letter I will read it with great pleasure, I am quite sure, because I want to know if he has estimated what will be needed in order to reach the high speeds on the line mentioned. When my hon. friend asked who makes the decisions as to what speeds can be reached-is it the CTC, the government or VIA-I felt like shouting "the bed". The bed of the track itself decides what speed can be reached,
Supply
because I presume this is what gives out first. I questioned Mr. Marsham on the subject, and he tells me that our railway beds in Canada are freight beds. They were built for freight and not for passengers, as opposed to the beds in Europe. I am talking always about railway beds, not ordinary beds, in Europe, for example, or in Japan.
In Japan, the bullet train runs very rapidly on a specialized passenger railway bed, be that as it may. What the minister sees in all that, just to be confidential for a minute, is the competition. We had an expression of that yesterday when the hon. member for Regina West said he believes the Minister of Transport should help only the railways.
I did not say that.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
speechtext: The hon. member said it in committee, and I am quoting him with a smile on my face because I know the hon. member for Regina West was making his point with a slight exaggeration. However, there is competition between the different modes of transportation. Each of them thinks the other one has more advantages. That is what they have in common. I received representations from owners of bus companies who have said, "What the heck are you doing spending some $420 million on railway transportation when we, the people operating the buses have no subsidies whatsoever?"
Highways.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
speechtext: Yes, that is the kind of discussion that could start now. All I want to do is to make this one observation. I think that theory will not carry you very far in these matters. It seems to me that we must save the best of railway transportation and occasionally move to STOL, notwithstanding some opposition to it, because it is a mode of transportation which is convenient in certain localities and for certain tasks.
In the right place.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
speechtext:
Yes, indeed. I just want to say on this occasion that I am not being theoretical. I think there is a balancing act between the different modes of transportation in Canada. With respect to railways, I want to say that 1 am almost as romantic on the subject as are my friends.
I am the son of a railway employee who worked for 45 years in Drummondville, Quebec. It is almost unbelievable that the CN tracks go right through the town of Drummondville. They will be coming up for a relocation program one of these days. The CP goes the other way. The house where my parents lived was right in between those two, so we were woken up in the mornings by the sound of locomotives. One could say I was born with smoke in my nose, and perhaps that has something to do, although quite remotely, with the fact that I became Minister of Transport, which is obviously the climax so far as I am concerned.

Mr. Chairman, I wish to discuss, in the minister's estimates, the Sherbrook-McGregor overpass, and

December 4, 1980
Supply
to call on him once again to reimburse the city of Winnipeg for $2.5 million for the cost overrun which is the direct responsibility of the federal government.
1 wish the minister would listen because this is a rather important matter. It is the Sherbrook-McGregor overpass. I am once again calling on the minister to reimburse the city of Winnipeg for $2.5 million which is the direct responsibility of the federal government for delaying the permit which was originally to be issued between December, 1978, and February, 1979.
I want to quote from a letter which the minister wrote to the mayor of Winnipeg this week, which was received only a couple of days ago. 1 will not read the whole letter. In the letter the minister points out that the city made a request in 1977 for a permit and for financial aid in the building of a structure to span the CPR railyards, which is the Sherbrook-McGregor overpass. Mr. Otto Lang, the former minister of transport, realized that if he were to approve such a grant on a simple application for funds, he would forever after be subject to criticism for making this serious and locally significant funding decision without knowledge of the cost of the alternatives, and one example is rail relocation.
As I pointed out to the minister before, $1,100,000 worth of studies had been done prior to December, 1978. Here is one of them, and I suggest the minister read it sometime to see all the work that has been put into studying railway relocation and the overpass. There is no need for any more studies, and I will be covering that in a little more detail in a moment.
In the minister's letter to the mayor, he also stated:
Consequently, he replied that it would be normal to consider the approval of a grade separation grant only after having assurances that the alternatives had been investigated to the extent that would support the decision being requested. The response on the alternatives containing the basic decision factors was not provided by the city.
That is a false statement. The city was not asked to provide any additional information, and I will refer to the dates in just a moment.
The letter goes on to read:
As a result, the federal government was required to undertake its own study to assign a cost to the rail relocation options before taking the decision to fund the construction of the bridge. I must advise you that in this situation the federal government cannot accept any additional financial responsibilities.
That is for the cost overrun. The city of Winnipeg has good grounds to sue the federal government if the department does not reimburse it for $2.5 million. I will go into the chronology of events right now. What is disturbing to me is that the man who is aware of the chronology of events and of all the details, is the gentleman sitting to the minister's right, his parliamentary secretary who was on the city council at the time when all of this was happening. He knows all about it. He knows perfectly well that the contents of the minister's letter to the mayor are incorrect.
I will go into the chronology of events to bring the minister up to date. By December, 1978, the then minister of transport, Otto Lang, had approved the construction of the overpass, and his approval was to be forwarded to the CTC for its approval.
The $7.6 million in initial costs of the federal share was approved as well. Design work would have begun immediately and construction could have commenced two or three months later. Mr. Lang was ready to give authority to CTC to issue the permit, and design work could have been started immediately. But, as the minister well knows, it was owing to the interference of the present Minister of Employment and Immigration who put pressure on Mr. Lang that the permit was withheld. Otto Lang was ready to issue it, and he did not ask the city of Winnipeg for any further studies.
On December 6, 1978, Mr. Lang telegraphed the mayor of Winnipeg saying that the federal government was giving its approval in principle for the construction of the Sherbrook-McGregor overpass, funds to be provided under UTAP. On December 20, 1978, the mayor sent an acknowledgment to Mr. Lang expressing his delight that the overpass had finally been given approval. The mayor then asked for details on how to proceed with the project, but there was never any correspondence, telegrams, or anything else saying that they wanted an additional study from the city of Winnipeg. The hon. member for St. Boniface, who is sitting beside the minister, knows that only too well.
On February 7, 1979, Mr. Lang replied that there was little to do. All that was needed was an agreement from the province that a portion of the UTAP money would be assigned to the Sherbrook-McGregor overpass. On February 16, 1979, Mr. Mercier, the attorney general of Manitoba, wrote to Mr. Lang and confirmed that the 1979 budget included the provincial portion. This project was given top priority by the province in its 1979 budget. So there was no request at all for a further study which the minister wanted from the city.
I will now ask the minister to make an apology to the city of Winnipeg, in writing, for the contents of his letter. The information contained there is incorrect. The department never asked for any further study to be done, and I am asking the minister once again to reimburse the city.
If the minister has any evidence or proof that he sent any letters, telegrams or anything to the city of Winnipeg requesting a further study in December of 1978, it is the minister's obligation to produce that documentation. I was in touch with the mayor's office today and was told that they have never received such a request from the minister, his official, or whoever was in charge of the department at that time. As I indicated previously, the mayor was happy that Mr. Otto Lang was to issue a permit and give Winnipeg the funds to proceed with the needed overpass. They never received any request for a further study. I challenge the minister to produce the documentation.
We all know why there was a delay of the permit. It was caused by the present Minister of Employment and Immigration who was then a member of the Manitoba legislature. I refer to an article which appeared in a Winnipeg newspaper in December, 1978. It was headed: "Local lobbying stalls funding for new bridge". It had nothing to do with asking the city to
December 4, 1980

conduct another study. The caption under the minister's photograph read: "Lloyd Axworthy... wins round". In part the article indicated:
Lobbying by Liberal MLA Lloyd Axworthy .. . has killed, or at least stalled, special federal funding for the Sherbrook-McGregor overpass.
Deputy Mayor Bill Norrie said Tuesday federal Transport Minister Otto Lang told him in effect that the city's request for $3.9 million in special funding has been turned down.
This was because of the interference of the hon. member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry; it had nothing to do with the city not conducting another study.
Also I should like to point out to the minister and the hon. member for St. Boniface some of the comments made in the Manitoba legislature about this chain of events. As reported in the Winnipeg Free Press on April 29, 1980, a Manitoba MLA called "the myth of rail line relocation ... one of the cruelest hoaxes ever perpetrated b,y any level of government".
When the hon. member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry contacted Mr. Otto Lang, he should have asked him to hold the permit for one week until the minister of finance and the president of the treasury board were asked whether there was any funding for rail relocation. If he had done that, he would have found out that there was no program, no funding, and no intention of getting into a rail relocation program. Then he could have said, "That is it, you will have to issue a permit for the Sherbrook-McGregor overpass". But, instead, he interfered all the time, which cost the city of Winnipeg an additional $2.5 million.
In June, 1980, a city of Winnipeg councillor attacked the federal government for suggesting that the $168.6 million relocation project is still possible. He said:
It's a pipe dream. It will not happen, it cannot happen and it's about time we said so.
There was never any reference to the federal government asking the city for another study. Also the urban affairs minister, Mr. Mercier, as reported in the June 17, 1980, edition of the Winnipeg Free Press, said that the federal government should pay the $2 million additional cost because it caused a delay in construction. That additional cost has now risen to $2.5 million.
On September 11, 1980, Mayor Bill Norrie said:
I don't agree with what they're doing because they're not being realistic. There isn't enough money for rail relocation and they should recognize that reality.
In that instance "they" meant the federal government. Also the Leader of the Official Opposition questioned the Minister of Finance and the President of the Treasury Board a few months ago in the House about funding for rail relocation. I have never witnessed two more evasive answers in my life. They had absolutely no intention of providing any funding for rail relocation in Canada. They simply did not have the money. If it was ever given to one city, they would have to provide the funding to other cities as well.
I find it somewhat strange that while 1 am asking the minister questions in Committee of the Whole he should walk out of the chamber; it is a real "sweetheart" arrangement. I
Supply
want some answers to my questions. I hope the grinning parliamentary secretary, who thinks it is a big joke that the citizens of Winnipeg are required to pay this additional $2.5 million, will run out to the lobby and bring the minister back in here to provide some answers.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I should like to point out that the Minister of Transport has been sitting here since the commencement of oral questions at two o'clock. He has been granted permission to go and get a bite to eat.
In the middle of my question.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
speechtext:
I welcome this opportunity because I do not know how many times the hon. member for Winnipeg-Assinib-oine challenged me in the House saying that I do not speak in the House, that I will not answer, that I do not pressure the minister.
A couple of days ago I was fortunate enough to move a motion under Standing Order 43. It was challenged because members opposite felt that a parliamentary secretary should not rise to ask any questions or to move such motions in the House. The hon. member has been a member much longer than I; he knows the rules, yet he attempts to make his point in such a way that people will believe I am not doing my job. I speak to the minister in his chambers, I have his ear, and I make representations on behalf of Winnipeg and Manitoba.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
speechtext:
I was part of the Winnipeg city council. I came here with Mayor Norrie, Mayor Steen and Gerald Mercier who is now the attorney general of Manitoba. We saw Otto Lang; we made application for UTAP funds. UTAP funds are based on a per capita rate. With one million people living in Manitoba, over five years Manitoba is entitled to $10,500,000. The province of Manitoba indicated that it was willing to dedicate $7.5 million of its UTAP funds to build the Sherbrook-McGregor overpass. There was no escalation clause, it was Manitoba's per capita fund. If that province wishes to attribute it to a certain project, it may do so; but there is nothing in UTAP funding which provides for an escalation because costs have risen.
The second point is that the city of Winnipeg never conducted the pre-required studies to consider rail relocation versus overpasses. It is customary for a city to pay 25 per cent or 50 per cent of the cost of a study, yet Otto Lang's department agreed to pay $90,000 or 100 per cent of the cost of that study. The study was completed and the city received its permit from the CTC to go ahead with the overpass. Last week the executive policy committee indicated that it would go in reverse, that it would conduct a study and consult with the people to see which project should be followed-the overpass or rail relocation.
1 should like to refer to rail relocation because I think the facts should be on the table. Rail relocation was estimated at a cost of $168 million. One could say it was high or low. But, I was part of the executive policy committee which went to see

December 4, 1980
Supply
Ed Schreyer, who was the premier of Manitoba at the time, and I am able to say that rail relocation requires the consent of the provincial government. The city of Winnipeg made its case to the government of the day, and the government of the day indicated that it would consent to the relocation of the yards but that it would never consent to the relocation of the lines.
When main lines are relocated, one must know where they are to be placed and one must have the consent of all municipalities affected. One is supposed to make a study to determine where the lines are to be relocated. None of those studies was ever perpetrated. The city of Winnipeg indicated that it did not want to make the proper application, but that it would like to find out in advance. It was similar to a person going to a bank manager and saying, "Lend me some money; I do not have a plan but I will build something some day. How much will you lend me?" This was the manner in which the city of Winnipeg and the province of Manitoba approached the federal government.
The fact of the matter is that even if the federal government had $80 million or $85 million for rail relocation, the city and the province would say that it was not a priority with them. If they had the $85 million, they would spend it somewhere else. It is time the facts came out. The hon. member did not come forward as a spokesman for Winnipeg, when Winnipeg itself did not make its case.

We now have more grounds for the city of Winnipeg to commence a lawsuit, after the absolute rubbish we have heard from the hon. member for St. Boniface.
I guess he was not listening to what I was saying. He was chatting to the minister there when I spoke earlier. The $7.6 million in initial costs of the federal share was approved by the minister, Mr. Otto Lang. He was to issue the permit before the member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry talked him out of it. You were not listening when I mentioned that to you.
On December 6, 1978, Otto Lang telegraphed the mayor telling him that the federal government was giving its approval in principle for the construction of the Sherbrook-McGregor overpass. He did not ask for another study as the minister says in his letter of this week to the mayor. He did not ask for another study. How many times do I have to say that to get it across to you? He said "We are going to issue the permit."
The mayor sent an acknowledgment to Otto Lang-I must keep repeating this, Mr. Chairman, because it is so difficult to get it through to some of these people-the mayor sent an acknowledgment to Lang expressing his delight that the overpass had finally been given approval. He did not wire back and say "We will do a study" or "What study are you talking about?" He thanked him for saying that he was going to issue the permit to build the overpass. The mayor then asked for details on how to proceed with the project. Lang replied that there was little to do. He said there was little to do. He did not say, "Do another study". He said that there was little to do. All that was needed was an agreement from the province that
a portion of their UTAP money would be assigned to the Sherbrook-McGregor overpass. Do you understand that?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
speechtext: Much dearer than you do.
I am not finished yet. The attorney general then wrote to Mr. Lang-

Mr. Chairman, despite some of the inferences and suggestions by the hon. member for Winnipeg-Assinib-oine, I wish to go on record and say to the many good people in St. Boniface that they ought to be very proud of their member of Parliament. Not only does he serve them well and with distinction, but he serves this country very well as the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport.
I think congratulations are also in order for the Minister of Transport, who in recent months has had to grapple with a great many difficult issues. Many of those issues are in Atlantic Canada. I must say he has done a great job in the short period of time in which he has held that portfolio. With reference to one particular instance in my area of the country, he made a substantial allotment of funds to the Canadian Coastguard College. In making that announcement and in making those moneys available to that institution, it speaks well for our area and that particular institution.
Notwithstanding some of the positive things that the minister has been able to do in his short tenure in that particular portfolio, I take issue with one of the very serious announcements made by Canadian National Express, that is, the announced closure of various CN Express offices in Atlantic Canada. I have gone on record before, Mr. Chairman, to oppose this particular decision, and I wish to reiterate that here this evening.
Why do you vote with the government then?
Mr. Chairman, 1 hear the very paragon and defender of the little guy from St. John's West.
Why are you supporting them?
The great thing we did for this country was defeat him on February 18. I hope he continues to sit on that side of the House providing his barrage of what I would call stupid commentary.

Why are you voting to support him if you are against this move? What bluff!
December 4, 1980

Mr. Chairman, I am in opposition to this particular announcement by CN Express. I believe it is wrong in principle. If one is trying to develop Atlantic Canada this is certainly not one of the tools one should do away with. In addition to providing the service to the business community of industrial Cape Breton, CN also provides in excess of 52 jobs. Those jobs are important to industrial Cape Breton where we have high unemployment.
I would like to raise a few other concerns with the minister and his officials with respect to the urban transportation assistance program. It is my understanding there was a five-year allocation of some $8 million for Nova Scotia. I am wondering if the officials or the parliamentary secretary could indicate to me if any of that money will be going to industrial Cape Breton. I understood, particularly, that there was a proposal before the provincial government to provide some sort of bus service from the town of Dominion in the area better known as Sydney-Richmond. I am wondering if the parliamentary secretary has any better information with respect to those two areas.
In addition to those concerns I would like to raise another. It has to do with the airport which is in my constituency, the Sydney airport. The present landing systems which are being utilized at that airport leave a great deal to be desired. The present system is better known as the instrument landing system. This particular system is in competition with a new modern system called the microwave landing system.
The new system has a great many advantages, not only for the Sydney airport, and if it were utilized in other airports across the country I am sure Canadians, as well as the experts in that field, would see it would prove worth while. First, it provides high precision for zero landings and multiple approach passes for jets and helicopters. It has 200 frequency channels as opposed to the instrument landing system which has only 40. There is minimal site preparation needed, and it can be set up anywhere, from large airports to remote strips, to helipads, oil rigs, etc. I am advocating that the minister's department go for the microwave landing system.
I think it is a fact that the international civil navigation organization agreed that in 1983 they would embark upon the use of the microwave landing system and that it would be completed by 1995. This means that all airports would have the microwave landing system. I am wondering if the parliamentary secretary could indicate whether or not the airport in Sydney would be one of the first chosen and, if not, when it might happen in that area.
There are a number of other concerns I would like to raise in relation to the Sydney airport. Some of these concerns are quite appalling, Mr. Chairman. One is in relation to the baggage handling facility at that particular airport. The Sydney airport is very well maintained by the staff there. Unfortunately, the baggage faciity is somewhat old and it is not providing the type of service travellers out of Sydney should have. When you go across the country and see various airports with modern baggage handling facilities-
Supply
What about in my constituency?

The hon. member mentioned the facility in his own constituency and how great it is. But in our airport we do not have a great baggage facility. I would like to see some renovations and improvements made to it in the next few years.
Another concern of mine is in relation to the provision of a gate for passengers to use when getting on and off planes. When one goes to the airport to embark upon a trip to other parts of the country or, indeed, to anywhere in the world, one must walk 700 or a thousand feet in stormy or wet weather. We do not see why people in my constituency and the people of industrial Cape Breton have to put up with that when other areas of the country have facilities which are much more modern.
I hope the department will give consideration to these requests, particularly the baggage facilities, the gate facilities, and the request for turning toward the microwave landing system. I have some other concern in relation to the Sydney airport with regard to the extension of the runway, but perhaps I could get into that matter at a later time and make specific representations to the minister himself.
Another area of concern is with regard to the enlargement of the customs office. I am in the process of making representations to the appropriate minister. While I raise my concerns I am aware that everything cannot be done within a six-month or eight-month period, but I am hopeful that over the next couple of years we will be able to rectify some of the major shortcomings in an area which is deserving of a modern facility and which looks forward to having that facility in the very near future.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, 1 can say to the hon. member for Cape Breton-East Richmond that the Minister of Transport has made representations to CN to consider the continuation of some of its express operations in Sydney. I am hopeful that he will be successful. The minister has also made representations to CN that the express service at Charlottetown be continued. However, these matters will be dealt with tomorrow, and we should have definite results early next week.
The program to which the hon. member referred in Cape Breton comes under UTAP. Two such programs have been approved; the transit vehicle acquisition which is receiving a contribution of $800,000, 50 per cent of which is being provided by UTAP; and a transit facility which is estimated to cost $750,000, with UTAP's share being $600,000. I refer to the bus portion of the Atlantic Provinces Transportation Program. The Mount Cabot bus line is to receive assistance of $31,000. To date it has received $5,400. Further details will be forwarded to the hon. member by letter, if requested.
The hon. member spoke of improvements to the Sydney airport, which is being served by ILS. The Department of Transport has made a commitment to ICAO that it will

December 4, 1980
Supply
commence with microwave landing systems, and it is now in its early development stages. As to which airport will have priority, the decision has not yet been taken. The whole matter of the implementation of that kind of program will be taken into consideration, and then the priorization will be established.
The hon. member also spoke of baggage facilities, improving the handling of cargo customs clearance, improvements to the terminal, another runway and passenger gates at the airport. Many of the passenger gates are owned by the airlines. One of the problems which we face, for example, in Winnipeg, is that there are not enough of these passenger gates. When people come down from the north and the temperature is 30 below, they feel as though they are discriminated against because there is no gate at their facility and they must put on parkas to get from the aircraft to the terminal.
A committee on transport has travelled across the nation. The Ministry of Transport is expected to look after 24 national airports, 76 regional airports, 455 local commercial airports, and 503 smaller airports, for a total of 1,058 airports. As we made that trip, we also learned the demands and requirements of all the principal cities we visited and all the provincial governments. If we had $15 billion, we could not meet all the requests. The budget of the Department of Transport is approximately $1.2 billion, and one does not have to be a master mathematician to understand that we cannot meet all the demands in one year, that we must rely on priorization and consider all the statistics as to passenger demand, number of flights-both incoming and outgoing-and so on, and we are doing the best we can with the dollars we have. In fact, that is why we should hurry and approve the estimates and budget of this department so that we may get on with the job.

Just one final comment, Mr. Chairman. Perhaps I do not need to say so, but I would remind the parliamentary secretary that on some of the questions which I raised he was not able to give specific information. I hope that he and his officials will follow up in writing with the answers to my questions.

Mr. Chairman, I am disappointed that the minister is not here. Oh, there he is. I have some serious questions on some serious issues. I am not here to make a speech, but merely to get some information.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Communications
speechtext: That is good news.

It will be news if 1 get answers. On September 30, 1980, I wrote to the minister about the drydock and the famous synchrolift which was announced by his predecessors, Messrs. Jamieson and Horner, on December 29, 1978, at St. John's, Newfoundland. On June 20, Canadian National wrote to the Department of IT and C about proceeding with the installation of the synchrolift. On August 6, Canadian National wrote the minister about the delay and setting out the alternatives. On August 22 the minister was sent another letter from Canadian National advising him that the government of Newfoundland had provided an acceptable offer of financial assistance and stated that if the Government of Canada would
not go ahead, the province would. In that letter it was also stated that the province and CN had reached an agreement and that CN was asking for the transfer of land, and there were comments on other matters.
I also understand that the minister was sent a letter from Mr. Bandeen of Canadian National on November 20, 1980. The exchange of land with National Harbours Board has been approved. Approval is needed for certain land owned by the federal government, other than the land owned by the National Harbours Board, at the dockyard to be transferred to CN. As far as I know, Mr. Bandeen in waiting for the answers to three questions with regard to whether the Government of Canada will permit CN to go ahead, along with the province, with the project, as an alternative to the federal government continuing its direct involvement itself.
The first question is, Will the federal government provide the necessary funding as outlined in this correspondence? If the federal government will not, although of course it should, will it permit the province to provide the financing in accordance with an agreement worked out with CN? The third question, as I understand it is: In the event that the province finances the synchrolift, will the Government of Canada convey title to the dockyard at St. John's to CN to operate that dockyard, or will it give them a 99-year lease so that it may go ahead with the modernization and save the dockyard?
I would remind the minister that the Economic Council of Canada report of a week or so ago shows that Newfoundlanders receive only 53.6 per cent of the national average earned income of Canadians. One-twelfth of all total personal income in Newfoundland comes from unemployment insurance as compared to one-fortieth, which is the average across Canada. These are some of the questions of great moment which occur to me and I would like to hear from the minister on those, if I may.

And it reminds me that last night the minister referred specifically to the problems in his department. And he said very eloquently that time and patience are more productive than strength and frenzy. the electors who also feel frustrated when they see how slow the decision-making process is. Sometimes all they know about is their local administration or their local problems. People find it hard to understand why decisions are not made more quickly.
Mr. Chairman, as I said, that is the big difference for civil servants who are extremely competent men and women, who know their files. That is the big difference. I should like to tell about a little incident I experienced in 1978, when the former minister, Mr. Otto Lang, sent to the Magdalen Islands a civil servant from headquarters in Ottawa to become acquainted with the problems first hand. I should like to point out to the minister the extreme importance of reunification and the need to have a coherent policy in the field of regional carriers. In an area of the country such as eastern Quebec or eastern Canada, it is imperative that there be some correlation between the various regional carriers.
In vast areas that are sparsely populated, regional carriers are needed that can co-ordinate the means of air transport. At the present time, eastern Canada has three regional carriers. Now, when one has to cover as short a distance as 200 miles, and yet has to change carrier three times, to deal with the three airlines that serve the area, how can there be co-ordination or correlation between the three? I am sure the minister, to whom I addressed the question, will bear in mind those extremely important problems when he discusses his policy with the regional carriers.
With regard to the Nordair problem, colleagues have spoken about it even as recently as this afternoon. Our hon. colleague from Joliette mentioned it. Our hon. colleague from Montreal did so as well. Obviously, a decision will have to be made soon. The minister is perfectly aware of it. In his answer this afternoon, he pointed it out very clearly, but I find it hard to understand why there should be concern about the possibility for Quebec interests to be major shareholders in the company that might possibly take over Quebecair or Nordair? Why create problems, why ask questions about the fact that the people of Quebec, with other parties, even possibly from

So, Mr. Chairman, I do not know if you can imagine the kinds of problems we must face when we discuss a particular problem and have to deal with two separate administrations. When I am in the Magdalen Islands discussing the harbour in Cap-aux-Meules with CTMA, which operates the ferry service between Prince Edward Island and the province of Quebec, they tell me: Of course, in Cap-aux-Meules a Quebec company operates the service but its administration comes under the Atlantic region with regards to the seaport. So I must try to get explanations from two administrations. It is easy to imagine the communication problems that exist when two directors general must meet to discuss certain things. That requires a great deal more time, and despite the good will shown by Department of Transport officers, it can take months before discussions can begin.
1 would be grateful if the minister would consider, whenever it is administratively feasible, to give back to Quebec, to the Quebec region the administration of those small centres which pose no problem. For example, the harbour in Cap-aux-Meules or in Havre-Aubert, in the Magdalen Islands could come under the Quebec region. I see no reason why the administration of those two seaports could not be transferred to the Quebec region.
Mr. Chairman, I would like to touch upon another issue which is of great importance in our region, and the minister will no doubt appreciate the problems this can cause for the people in our area; I am speaking of intermodal public transportation. In eastern Quebec and eastern Canada in general there are three main means of transport: the airplanes, the railways and Voyageur bus in Quebec and other bus companies in eastern Canada.
Because of our weather, one can leave Quebec City in the morning under bright sunshine and get into Rimouski under cloudy skies and finally arrive in Gaspe in a snowstorm. If someone flies from Montreal, he or she can be told in Rimouski that he or she cannot go any further, that a snowstorm has fored the airport in Gaspe to close down. But, if there was such a thing as intermodal transportation, the traveller could hop on the bus or the train. But no, Mr. Chairman, the plane from Montreal or Quebec City arrives in Rimouski at 9.35 a.m., the bus left at 6.10 a.m. and the train at 5.20 a.m. so the only thing that person can do is rent a car and continue his or her journey.
However, Mr. Chairman, if we had intermodal transportation, that person could get there by plane then, a half hour later, take a train or a bus and continue on towards eastern Canada into the maritimes or to Gaspe. The same applies to the return leg from Gaspe to Montreal. The plane flies out of Mont-Joli at 9.15 p.m.; the Gaspe-Quebec City bus gets into Mont-Joli at 10.49 and the train coming from eastern Canada and the Gaspe peninsula goes by at 1.15 a.m. This means that once again we have three transport companies serving the same area where the temperature can change very quickly, where small towns are strung along the coast of the Chaleur Bay, both on the New Brunswick side and the Quebec side, where the population is scattered among those towns and where three companies are fighting for customers who have the means to travel. It is extremely important for the Department of Transport to discuss with these three companies, two of which are private companies, namely Voyageur and an airline, and another which is the Crown corporation VIA Rail. All of them should sit down at the same table to determine whether they can arrange their schedules so that people can take the bus and transfer to the train or board an airplane.
At the present time, those three companies are fighting to get the greatest number of customers that they can among an extremely sparse population, since there are only 120,000 inhabitants in the 600 miles around the Gaspe peninsula. These three companies now have deficits in this area and are constantly fighting to get more passengers.
I hope, Mr. Chairman, that the minister and his department will be able to study this whole issue. I know that there are certain firms which would ask nothing better than to co-ordinate the schedules of these companies. We could have plane service from Quebec City, for instance, to Mont-Joli, and then take either the train or the bus from Mont-Joli to Gaspe.
Mr. Chairman, this brings me to a third matter which is closely related to the two others, namely, the railway problem.

The trip from Gaspe to Montreal, which some people make regularly every weekend because the people in our area are not afraid of covering great distances by car in spite of the weather, this trip of 600 miles costs $390 by car. By train, it costs only $50 for the round trip.
So, Mr. Chairman, I am saying to the Minister of Transport how important the train can be in an area where, as I said before, the majority or most of the people in the Gaspe peninsula have relatives or friends living in Quebec City, Montreal or Toronto. These people badly need a low cost means of transport they could use during the Christmas holiday or the summer vacation either to go back home or to visit their relatives outside the area. That means finally how extremely important it has now become to provide these people with a means of transport they could benefit from.
