Thank you very kindly, Mr. Chairman. 1 must say it is a real pleasure and a real opportunity to stand before the Committee of the Whole to address this topic of transportation. It is a topic in Canadian history which has been fundamental to the success and to the development and certainly will be to the future of Canada, starting from the early canoe routes across the country, followed by the canals, the railways, the air services throughout the north and more recently by the ships connecting Canada to the rest of the world. Indeed, transportation has been a factor that has welded this very diverse and varied country together.
Transportation is an integral element of Canadian development. When we consider the tremendous costs associated with transportation development and the very high cost connected with infrastructure development within Canada, we are encouraged to ask where we should be spending our money. Should we be spending it in the more depressed areas of

Canada which are experiencing economic recession? Should we be spending it in the parts of Canada where development is neutral and where growth is minimal or perhaps static? Or should we be spending it in areas of Canada which are recognized as growth areas in our economy where sound economic development is accelerating on a daily and weekly basis?
I want to paint a picture of a part of Canada for the Minister of Transport. I recognize that British Columbia and western Canada are experiencing some of the lowest levels of unemployment in the country. We are generating the highest rates of real growth in all of Canada. British Columbia and western Canada are increasingly attracting labour from all regions of Canada.
We are experiencing high rates of investment in new productive capacity in British Columbia. This year investment is up by more than 16 per cent over the corresponding period last year. In western Canada and British Columbia we are experiencing tourist growth the like of which we have never experienced before. The total number of United States vehicles entering British Columbia is up by more than 30 per cent over the past year. Rogers Pass westbound traffic is up this year 14 per cent, indicating that the number of visitors from central Canada and the prairies is increasing. Of course, there is increased traffic on the Yellowhead highway. This very crucial route is often referred to now as the "route to the resources", and traffic on it is certainly up from the corresponding period last year.
Within the Kamloops-Shuswap area itself, economic growth in 1981 will unquestionably be higher than the national average. Population is growing, and there are major new developments as a result of the major newly-found copper deposits in the Kamloops-Shuswap region. The growth of the region is illustrated by the following: the value of building permits issued in Kamloops during the first ten months of this year totals in excess of $72 million compared with $34 million in the same period last year, an increase of over 100 per cent.
In the Salmon Arm area, the centre of the Shuswap area of British Columbia, the value of building permits jumped to in excess of $11 million in the first ten months of 1980 compared with $5 million in the same period last year, an increase of well over 130 per cent.
Retailing is the second largest industry in the Kamloops-Shuswap area and, as in most other parts of Canada the great majority of retail stores are small, independently owned and operated enterprises. The strength of this sector in my riding reflects what is happening throughout the west. In the 12 months ending June, 1980, retail sales in Kamloops totalled $5,245 per capita compared with the national of $3,596 per capita. By 1985, per capita expenditures in Kamloops will likely reach $8,200. This buoyant local and regional economy provides a confident environment for the establishment of new business. So far this year 770 new business licences have been issued in Kamloops and 160 in the Salmon Arm area.
The conclusion to be drawn from the picture I have painted is that a very strong local and regional economy exists in this area of central British Columbia. Yet the transportation infrastructure which is so crucial to continued development is lacking.
Back in 1969, for example, the Kamloops airport served fewer than 100,000 passengers and experienced what was at that time referred to as a major expansion. A new coffee shop was added and a few additional feet to a lobby space. Then in 1975 there was a proposal by the government for a major expansion. In 1979 the number of passengers served was in excess of 200,000. In 1980 another significant expansion occurred at the airport. An addition was made to the baggagehandling rack. Expansion has always been promised but always put off. Expansion never took place. On July 28 I received a letter from the Minister of Transport indicating that expansion of the Kamloops airport facility had been postponed again until 1983.
Let us recognize that we are talking about a part of the province of British Columbia which is experiencing tremendous growth. Access to the area and the opportunity to leave the area for business purposes and for moving labour in and out has become crucial, yet the facility which existed in the sixties remains in place unchanged. We need an airport which can handle more traffic. We need an airport which is dependable under varying weather conditions. We need an airport which can provide an adequate and acceptable level of service. We heard earlier today about problems associated with Mirabel and the tremendous sums which have gone into the Mirabel airport near Montreal. Yet the returns are somewhat questionable. One has to ask whether it is unreasonable to request that a few dollars be spent to expand and improve the terminal facility in this dynamic part of the country and to invest in the economic development of that area.
Is an improved terminal and improved landing facilities to allow access to the airport under inversion layer atmospheric conditions too much to ask? Can we ask the minister to reconsider the decision to hold off any expansion to that airport until 1983? I will put the question to the Minister of Transport: Can we ask for an acceleration? Can that date be moved up to one more acceptable to the people and the entrepreneurs of that area?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, 1 want to thank the hon. member for Kamloops-Shuswap for the very encouraging picture of his area he painted for us. Economic growth is advancing there, and that certainly reflects the need for good transportation facilities.
Since the program to upgrade the Kamloops airport is deferred to 1983, his question is whether it can be brought forward. Well, it is not in this particular budget. In 1978 we
December 4, 1980

spent $37,000 on a garage, and $44,000 on runway stabilization. In 1979 we spent $205,000 acquiring some land. The hon. member for Kamloops-Shuswap drew attention to the need for specific improvements to the terminal and to runway facilities.
Members of the Chamber of Commerce from Kamloops appeared here in delegation and pointed out that the inverted fog layer which exists over the airport prevents aircraft from landing at Kamloops-they must carry on to another airfield because of the level of the present runway. They even went so far as to suggest that Kamloops needs a whole new airport at another level which would not be subject to that kind of influence from the atmospheric buildup over Kamloops.
Some hon. members have several airports in their ridings, and individual members come to the Ministry of Transport saying that conditions at their airports warrant higher priority than others and asking that improvements at theirs be advanced. At this stage there are no reserves to include Kamloops in this year's budget, but I am sure the minister and his officials are willing to look at the hon. member's proposal to see whether there is any possibility of taking his submission into account when preparing the next budget-and they look forward to doing that.

Mr. Chairman, I appreciate those remarks, and I certainly encourage a re-examination of the priority and the timing of the expansion of that airport, in recognition, perhaps, that it is time to be investing more money in airports. Such investments would perhaps result in more money flowing back to the Canadian government than investments in other locations at this time.
Speaking along the same line, we recognize that the centre of economic gravity is moving to the western provinces. Alberta and British Columbia are becoming more important all the time in terms of the country's economic development. The Yellowhead highway is a major interprovincial route, increasing in importance, and sometimes called Canada's road to the resources. It links up the Pacific coast to northern Alberta particularly. The daily traffic counts on that highway are now higher than on corresponding sections of the Trans-Canada highway. One of the major uses of the Yellowhead route is for heavy industrial traffic in recognition of the industrial development which is taking place in the western provinces. Would the minister comment for a moment on whether or not he sees any possible cost-sharing program to provide for present and, perhaps more important, for future needs, from the $4 billion western development fund to encourage the improvement and development of this crucial highway system?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, may 1 say to the hon. member for Kamloops-Shuswap that I had the opportunity of assisting at the Yellowhead highway convention in Saskatoon about a month ago. The problem stems from highway improvement programs which were based on cost-sharing with the four western provinces. Some of these agreements were signed earlier; they were five-year programs. I do not remem-

ber the particular ones which were started in 1975 and which terminate in 1980, but there are some that have a couple of years to go. It is relevant to me that under a federal-provincial agreement, the provinces take their allocation and decide to apply it to highways which have priority in their mind. As they have not applied these funds to the Yellowhead highway, they are now hoping that the government will see it as a parallel to the number one Trans-Canada highway to the south. They put forward many arguments, they produce figures regarding the volume of traffic and other statistics, but it is a matter which has to be negotiated between the provinces, the ministers of transport of the provinces, and the federal government. When a certain program has expired and there is no allocation in the budget of additional funds for such a program, special legislation or supplementary dollars would be required in order to arrive at such an agreement with the provincial counterparts as is suggested. I do not believe the western incentive program was designed to be applied to highway programs.
When I went to the convention, I had a list of the moneys which had been made available. When I met the B.C. minister, he said to me, "You have only given us $8 million for our highway. You should have given us a lot more." That is the type of demand the Ministry of Transport receives from all the provinces. If I may digress for a moment, let me point out that one usually sees a big sign saying, "This is a provincial highway program". And on the bottom of the sign it says, "A little bit of it was funded by the federal government."

I thank the parliamentary secretary for his response. I would say, if that is what it would take to get funding for such a highway system to provide better economic opportunities to that part of Canada, I would be quite prepared to see the federal government take the top part of that sign and put it in neon lights every few hundred yards along the highway. That would be fine with me if it encouraged the federal government to provide that kind of funding. I would ask, however, that consideration be given to investing money in highway systems which would guarantee returns to the Canadian government.
I want to refer now, Mr. Chairman, to a point which was introduced earlier by the hon. member for Cape Breton-East Richmond regarding the cutbacks in the express stations particularly along the CN rail. I think one would recognize the problem clearly if one saw it in the context of the lay-offs by CN and CP over the last 20 years which have resulted in something like 60,000 positions being cut back. As a result of the decision to reduce the CN express service, we have seen a loss of about 1,100 jobs across the country, affecting places such as Kamloops, Kelowna, Victoria, Prince Rupert, Terrace, and Smithers. A similar situation has arisen in other regions of Canada. In some parts of the country this has resulted in a complete lack of express service by railroad or by highway and dependence upon very expensive air services. I wonder, if the effect of this move has been considered, what kind of impact it will have on the small community.
I would like to give one example of a small business which received a support grant from the federal government of

December 4, 1980

$150,000 to open up a modern pottery factory exporting goods out of the region. It depended upon the freight rates established for CN express service. When this service was eliminated, the cost of freight of the goods in and out of this centre doubled, which made it impossible for the entrepreneur to compete with the national and multinational firms throughout the region. As a result, we saw another bankruptcy, another small business caving in because of the cutback in the express service.
We see a cutback in rail transportation jobs. I understand that earlier the minister indicated that perhaps 90 per cent of these positions would not be lost, that individuals would be moved into other parts of the rail service. But I would like to ask him whether there is a need to continue the phasing out of this service, particularly during these crucial energy times when it is recognized that to move goods by truck costs four times as much in terms of energy per freight mile as it does by rail. To me this does not necessarily seem the most logical progression when we are concerned about the conservation of energy. Also, I should like to remind the minister that section 262 of the Railway Act compels the railway by law to handle all traffic offered for carriage, which means the government can step in and require that the express service be maintained throughout ail parts of Canada.
Will the minister explain why this absurd cutback is occurring which is costing Canadians jobs, service, and, perhaps most important of all, jobs in businesses which will fold as a result of increased transportation costs because of this particular decision?

Mr. Chairman, it is indeed a pleasure to have this opportunity to question the minister through you, Mr. Chairman. I was fascinated by the minister's answer to my colleague, the hon. member for St. John's West when he said, "money, money, money". The minister talked about the
brown envelope question which was introduced by this side. It is very interesting how easy it is for the government to find $28,400,000 for propaganda purposes just like that; it is not even in the estimates. The excuse the minister gave the hon. member for St. John's West that there is not money is just hogwash.
Also I was fascinated with the minister's answer on JETS, the radar problem or dilemma in Canada. I was told by officers of the Air Traffic Controllers Association that the JETS system is approximately eight years old and is completely obsolete. There is one installation in Moncton, and now it is planned to instal others across Canada over the next three years. Updated systems are already in place in the United States. JETS are computer simulators which predict by calculation where aircraft will be, and now there is a system of live definition of where aircraft will be. JETS are obsolete, yet they are continuing to spend millions of dollars on them. The system is so obsolete that it cannot even transfer aircraft from one zone to another in Canada.
The executive of the Air Traffic Controllers Association of Canada has invited industry representatives to luncheons so that they might understand the problem the association is having with the Department of Transport. I appeal to the minister to invite the executive to lunch so that he will hear the same lecture they are giving to industry representatives throughout the land. The minister should not lecture them; he should listen, because they have an interesting and valuable story about how our aircraft communication can be first class. It is ridiculous to continue to spend money on an obsolete system.
I should also like to question the minister about the government's offshore sickness. It seems everything is in place to serve interests offshore rather than Canadian or domestic ones. For example, the matter of tax treaties and banks lending subsidiaries of foreign corporations money from Canada was raised in the House. The interest on this money comes back into Canada tax free through various wrinkles of the Canadian government tax treaty. One matter which pertains to the minister's responsibility is the 25 per cent of one one hundred and twentieth of duty and taxes paid on dredging and other marine equipment on an as-used basis. If a Canadian corporation builds or owns a Canadian dredge, it pays all its duties and taxes up front in cash, or "baby, you just don't get it". But we allow foreigners to come in and pay 25 per cent of one-one hundred and twentieth of duty payable over a ten-year basis and on an as-used basis. How can Canadian plants compete with that gimmick?
There are foreign dredges in the country. Our own Canadian dredging plant capacity is utilized only 20 per cent. The capital is sitting with an interest burden building upon it, yet there are gimmicks which allow foreigners a preferred status. There are three foreign dredges working in the Arctic with live-aboard crews. There is tokenism. They bring four or five Canadians up to these dredges to learn the foreign technology,
December 4, 1980

but they are not allowed to touch one thing. They are nothing but deckhands. As a matter of fact, the minister might talk to a couple of them who have quit because they would not put up with it. The wages of the foreign crews are not subject to income tax. They are advanced money for expenses, little trips and holidays, but their wages are paid at home. What is happening to the country? Where are we in terms of common-sense? They are working against Canadian marine unions, and there is correspondence on file from the unions complaining about it.
I should like to refer to Mount St. Helens in Washington which blew its top. Great, massive quantities of mud came down and filled the river systems there. We saw tragic motion pictures of fish dying in the heat of the water. There was a national emergency on the west coast of the United States, and the U.S. government called for all the dredges it could get. They were brought in from San Francisco, Los Angeles, Long Beach on the west coast, from the gulf and even from the east to handle this national emergency. At that time there was dredging equipment in British Columbia which was not being used. It was available; it was absolutely ideal to bail the mud out of these rivers in Washington. But, the Jones act of the United States would not allow the use of any of that equipment, so the emergency situation did not provide any revenue to Canadian companies.
Moving from that situation on the west coast and the protectionism of the United States to the Miramichi bids which opened on December 3, I should like to indicate that four out of the five bids were foreign ones. Apparently a brand new company called Ledin is the low bidder. If a person in the dredging business was asked about the company, he would not have heard of it; it is a new company, and no one has ever heard of it. The low bid this year is $1 million higher than the Canadian bid of last year, but I am told by a responsible official that the bid is based on the leasing of a United States dredge. So, the United States piece of equipment will come here and take work away from a Canadian plant which is working at only 20 per cent capacity. I understand the dredge is being leased from Great Lakes Dredge and Docks Company.
What are we doing to ourselves? Let me deal with Roberts Bank which is close to my home. Canada has entered into coal contracts with Japan, but we do not have in place the dock capacity on the west coast to fulfil the coal and delivery contracts with that country. If there had not been a depression or a recession in the Japanese steel industry, we would have been called on for lack of delivery. We desperately need a second pad at Roberts Bank. This has been known for some years. It would put in place enough capacity in order to handle the contracts that already exist, yet it is not done. It was almost arranged and in progress a year ago, but what troubles me is that Canadian companies do not have the inside track. Who has the inside track on Roberts Bank? It is a foreign company. Somewhere in the system the definition and the terms for dredging contracts are such that Canadian dredging companies just cannot do the job within the time-frame set.

This is absolute insanity. What is the matter? Canadian equipment and crews are available. All of a sudden a design turns to a contract and our equipment is not big enough; only a foreign company from Holland can do the job. Is that not interesting?
I have in my possession one of the most amazing telegrams I have ever read. If the minister doubts me, let him listen. This telegram was received on December 3 from Holland. It is addressed to Sceptre Dredge and it is entitled "Subject- Vancouver, Roberts Bank Tender for Dredging and Reclamation". It is from Amstelveen, Amsterdam Ballast Dredging, a division of Ballast-Nedam Groep. That is the largest group of dredging operators, I guess, in the world. It says:
Amsterdam Ballast Dredging, a division of Ballast-Nedam Groep, N.V. is interested in establishing a suitable partnership to execute the above works.
Can you imagine the audacity of this?
It is our intention to carry out all or (of) the major part of the dredging and reclamation works and whereby your share would be the slope protection and servicing works.
Isn't that nice, Mr. Chairman? A foreign company says it is their intention to do the major part of the dredging work and "your share would be . . ." Mr. Minister, what the heck is going on in this country?
Who is advising the minister?

The telegram continues:
Please advise us of our willingness to co-operate either on a joint venture or on subcontractor status, preferably by phone-
And the phone numbers are listed. It goes on:
-or by return telex. We are primarily interested in the alternatives to complete the dredging in one season.
Isn't that fascinating? We had to go and set the terms for a big dredging contract to get a great big turning circle inside for the ships to turn around in so that we could dredge up three or four new pads. The turning circle on the inside basin was the reasoning behind that.
The secondary reason was that no Canadian company could do this within the limited time-frame the Department of the Environment set down since they say the dredging shall be done between this period and that period otherwise the crabs will get hurt. I am also told that the crabgrass they are trying to protect started to grow after the first dredging. Perhaps it is time we looked at some of these applied biologists and began to apply some common sense in terms of the total picture before us.
The point I am making is really an appeal: what the heck is going on? There are many Canadian dredging companies for the Arctic, Roberts Bank and Miramichi, yet we get into deals like this where somehow or other outsiders have the inside track, where they can make requests of Canadian companies such as this. I think something is very wrong.

It smells fishy, too.

I would like the minister to answer these questions. What are we to do about dredging in the Arctic? Why cannot Canadian equipment be used in the Arctic? Why must we have foreign crews aboard who are not paying their full share of taxes? How long do you think the Canadian maritime unions are willing to put up with this kind of nonsense? We have all this unemployment. We know what our needs are. We are dredging knowledge, yet find it taken over by foreigners. Mr. Chairman, once again, I am pleased to take part in this exercise. I think it is one of the better functions of the House of Commons. I certainly associate myself with the hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain in praising this particular exercise. It seems to me the people of this country who are interested and who are watching the proceedings on television are seeing the House in one of its better moments. It is a good deal better than the question period, which is really a case of one-upmanship. In this exercise we get down to business, and individual members put national and local interests in front of the minister and receive replies.
I am pleased with the replies of the minister, both throughout today and yesterday. Transport is probably the most difficult department in any government and certainly in the government of Canada. It deals with a very large number of issues and a great deal of diversity, all of which makes it extremely difficult for the minister. In the few months in which the minister has held this portfolio, he has handled the problems extremely well. It may be very trite to say that transportation is of vital importance to Canada, but it is important to remind Canadians, again and again, of the importance of the industry.
There is probably no other country in which transportation is so important and so complex. I challenge anybody to name a
Supply
country in the world in which transportation is as complex for a population of 25 million. The distances are great and there are all kinds of regional problems. A sophisticated transportation system is necessary to link those regions which are interdependent, if not totally dependent on such links. Canada has a high growth, sophisticated economy and there is a high volume of goods and service equipment moving across the country.
On a per capita basis no country in the world has as much export trade as Canada. Certainly, we are the world's number one exporting country. When I refer to transportation on a national plane, I am also thinking of my own community because it is one of the few constituencies where the national interest almost invariably applies directly to the constituency. So when I talk about transportation in Thunder Bay, I am usually talking about a key national interest, because that community is key to the whole movement of goods and services in this country.
Thunder Bay is located almost at the centre of the country geographically or, as we say, at the heart of the country. The distances to other parts of the country from Thunder Bay are very great. Without a doubt, that community is the largest exporting community on a per capita basis in Canada. No other community has the export trade in grain, pulp and paper, transportation of equipment and so on, at least on a per capita basis. This year was a record year for the port of Thunder Bay in the movement of grain. It was probably the greatest amount of grain moved through any port in the history of mankind in one year. It is a vital port in the movement of goods and services throughout Canada.
I would like to cite some of the problems which I foresee for Thunder Bay. The port came very close to its capacity this year. The Lakehead transportation study, which was part of the Central Access study of three or four years ago, said that Thunder Bay would not reach capacity for 20 years. But three years or four years hence we have already come very close to that capacity.
It is important that we begin to devote attention to Thunder Bay. One must not forget that almost two-thirds of all Canadian grain moves through it, and will continue to do so. We must begin to look at ways in which we can improve the situation if, indeed, we are coming close to capacity. I refer hon. members to a comment which was made by Doug Radke, the deputy co-ordinator and the acting co-ordinator at present of the Federal Grain Transportation Authority in the Montreal Gazette on October 7. He says there are problems with regard to turn-around time and sorting out trains in Thunder Bay and that action must be taken to improve the situation. He goes on to say that the turn-around time for most grain trains is approximately 14 days to 16 days, and comments:
Reducing Thunder Bay's turn-around time is as good as adding more hopper cars to the system,. .. For instance, a 15 per cent reduction in the port's turn-around time would represent the same boost in grain shipping capacity as the addition of 4,000 hopper cars by 1985.

He goes on to explain in this article why Thunder Bay is not as efficient as it should be and how it can become more efficient.
I presented to the minister earlier this year a proposal designed to improve the movement of grain. I did not ask the minister for more money. I was suggesting that if the government intended to spend $1 billion on hopper cars and other items, it should look at spending $30 million at Thunder Bay as a better alternative. And Mr. Radke, three or four months later, supports me in this particular article.
The proposal which I made in the spring, Mr. Chairman, has been reviewed again. Comments have been received, some of which were adverse, from the department and from the grain companies. We are now looking at another proposal which we think will achieve some of the same results-perhaps it is a better proposal. This new proposal tries to solve the same problems as were outlined in the other, and it deals with the fact that most of the shunting by CPR is done on the main line. We went back to a proposal brought forward by CPR in 1969 or 1970 when it acquired land to the west of the city in order to build a yard so that the movement of grain and other goods could be improved. I bring this subject to the attention of the minister with the idea in mind that in the next two or three months a new proposal will be presented, and we hope it will receive very close attention.
As Mr. Radke says, a 15 per cent improvement in turnaround in Thunder Bay is as good as 4,000 hopper cars. We believe this would cost $30 million or $40 million, whereas
4,000	hopper cars would cost many times that amount. The community of Thunder Bay has become far more aware of its potential as a major port. It has set up a civic transportation committee to study these matters, and we hope we will be able to have the support and attention of the minister, with the idea that someone will appear before the committee or become part of that committee in the near future as we consider these larger problems.
We are also concerned about the future of the St. Lawrence Seaway. The transport committee had a meeting with Mr. Turner in Regina in September and it was very interesting. He put it to us that one of the problems the grain industry was really concerned about was the future of the Seaway. This was the line of reasoning that was used: They said, "Look, the Americans are going to increase their grain shipments and their exports in other areas very, very considerably, and their Mississippi waterway system is operating nearly at capacity. They are going to require much more of the Seaway. We will have to increase our tonnage through the Seaway considerably, particularly of grain; also, as energy problems develop, far more coal and other goods will he shipped, and so the pressure on the seaway will be very considerable."
The key problems are, I think, twofold: one is the Welland Canal, which is a bottleneck. I know the ministry is looking very carefully at this because we have had testimony to this effect in committee. The other problem is, of course, that we
must keep the system competitive; Seaway costs cannot be allowed to grow any more than the market will bear. Those are two very significant concerns the grain industry has and which I share as a member interested in the movement of grain, along with our community of Thunder Bay.
In the two or three minutes I have left before I ask the minister to respond, I would like to say something pleasant about VIA Rail because so much is said about VIA Rail that is unpleasant. I think a lot of it is said by people who just do not use the service. I have had occasion in the last couple of months to use the Transcontinental and the Ottawa to Toronto rail service three or four times, and I have been very pleased with the improvement in the service. There is no doubt in my mind that we made the right move when we took the two major railways in this country out of passenger service and put the project into the hands of people who wanted to run a passenger service, and whose business is running a passenger service. I can tell you that the attitude, the cleanliness, the whole approach to the service shows great improvement.
Now, there are all kinds of problems, and I will admit that. There are problems with terminals not being clean and so on. But I think that on balance, in two or three years, we have come a long, long way, and that praise is due to Mr. Robertson, the whole VIA group, and all of the employees. With that I will give a minute to the minister to comment.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
speechtext:
Our colleague from the constituency of Thunder Bay-Atikokan has agreed that I can answer his question.
We are very interested in his proposal regarding improvements that could be effected in Thunder Bay but since he has indicated that the proposal is under review and is being studied further, there will be no comment at this time, but we look forward to receiving that proposal.
On the subject of the seaway, research and development is perfecting its technique to keep the grain berths ice-free. We hope this will lengthen the shipping season through the St. Lawrence Seaway, and to that end an icebreaker, the Alexander Henry is based in Thunder Bay. It will be there, as required, at the close of the run. We will co-operate with all the grain shippers to achieve the earliest possible opening in 1981. He has our concurrence that the cost of shipping through the Welland Canal will be kept down. It is evident that this government is supporting VIA Rail in improving the service to passengers and it will continue to do so.

Mr. Chairman, I want to spend, if I may, about ten or 15 minutes going into a subject that I discussed with the minister previously. I probably will discuss it with him again, and unless I get different answers, I definitely will. A few weeks ago I asked the minister a series of questions about general aviation. In fairness, I spoke rather quickly, and I rhymed off about eight separate questions in that exchange. I probably passed them by the minister so fast that he did not get a chance to answer them properly. He latched on to one of them and gave the stock answer that we have been given for some time.
December 4, 1980

This evening, Mr. Chairman, I would like to go back over those questions, which are all related to general aviation. Frankly, I intend to press again the concept that I put before the minister previously-that within the last decade the Department of Transport has taken an adversary position with regard to general aviation, a position that did not exist earlier. In the regulations it set down, in the manner in which it has dealt with organizations and groups within the general aviation, with reckless abandon the private aircraft operators in this country-country that has more private aircraft per capita than any other company in the world-it has incurred the wrath of a group of men and women who are, by and large, pretty law-abiding citizens, who normally pay their own way, and ask for nothing free from the government.
The first item, which I know the minister will want to answer in exactly the same way he has in the past, has to do with this confounded $5 landing fee that was imposed on private plane operators about five weeks ago. I contend now, as I have contended in the past, that it was put on for one purpose only-to deter private aircraft from going into four airports in Canada. Private aircraft operators and owners do not object to the user-pay principle. Rather, they object to the method that the department uses to collect the fee. Private operators are quite willing to pay their fair share through gasoline tax concession fees or taxes, but not by landing fees. I have been the recipient of those landing fee invoices. They are expensive to produce. Obviously, the $1.65 that was collected did not come near to covering the cost of them. The $5, it seems to me, will barely cover the cost of those multicopied computer-produced, sometimes erroneous invoices. I suggest, Mr. Chairman, that this is the wrong way to go about things. Surely, if any motorist driving through a major city in Canada were faced with a barrier at the edge of that city, and had to pay a $5 fee every time he drove in, he would raise particular hell. And you could not blame him for that. Private aircraft in this country fulfil an identical utility transportation function. I see no reason at all why they should not all be treated similarly. Motorists pay taxes on their gas. Private aircraft owners are already paying a much larger amount on the gas they buy. In fact, the amount right now is about 13.1 cents per litre. Unless that is changed, the tax on motor fuel is about two-thirds of that. If that is the case, why should we have to pay a landing fee, one that is difficult to administer, expensive to collect, and obviously a deterrent to landing at major airports?
Those of us who fly feel very strongly and, as a matter of public policy that this usurious fee should and could be dropped. I shall ask the minister to keep this in the back of his mind and remember that point because I am afraid of what his answers might be.
I shall go on to one or two other points on the long list I have and see what kinds of answers I get to them before the minister comes back to this one. One factor which supports my request those fees be dropped is that the ministry is not providing any alternate service. If, for example, at Vancouver there was an adequate airport at Boundary Bay or if at
Supply
Toronto there was an adequate service at Toronto Island, there might well be a case. They are only a few miles apart. In an answer given to me some time ago, I heard that we should look at Hope airport. I am not in British Columbia very often, and I am sure my British Columbia colleagues will correct me if I am wrong, but the last time I drove from Hope to Vancouver international it was a very long drive. 1 would never consider it as being a substitute.
There are other things which bother aircraft operators. We are told that Toronto international is extremely busy. I have read it is the third, fourth or fifth busiest airport in Canada in terms of landings and takeoffs. But in the north end of Toronto international, runway 1028 is rarely used. In most majo1-airports there are taxiways which would be perfectly adequate for light aircraft, up to and including the twins of the major manufacturers. There is no reason at all why those taxiways could not be used. These aircraft can land, unless they are extremely heavily loaded, in 1,500 feet to 2,500 feet and take off quickly. It would not take a great deal of expertise to have that happen. Yet, unlike many airports in the United States, the ministry in Canada will not allow this. Aircraft are used in Canada to a much greater degree than they are in any other country. I see the minister and his parliamentary secretary writing away feverishly, so I think I will go through my list. I will let them answer my questions and then I will make one final request at the very end.
One thing that bothers private pilots excessively is the extremely arbitrary system used when a pilot is discharged for medical reasons. There is no way a pilot can get a good second opinion and convince the ministry of his ability to fly. Pilots must use those medical officers-admittedly they are usually good doctors-who have been politically appointed. Pilots are not allowed to go to an independent specialist, particularly a cardiologist, to get a second opinion which would perhaps convince the department of their ability to fly. Surely the minister will recognize that probably one of the safest pilots is one who has had a problem and is taking proper medication, exercising properly and eating a proper diet. After all, that pilot has no desire to have a heart attack at 2,000, 10,000 or
20,000	feet.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext: The hon. member for Brandon-Souris is one of those.

My colleague, the hon. member for Yukon has made a point that the hon. member for Brandon-Souris had a serious heart operation two and a half to three years ago. By looking after himself, he is probably in better physical shape now than he has been for many years.
Another item which plagues Canadian pilots concerns the regulations covering instrument ratings. The regulations in Canada are so difficult that there are more than 60 times as many instrument-rated pilots registered per capita in the United States than there are in Canada. Yet we have more pilots per capita in Canada. We have need of instrument rating because of our weather and because of long distance flying. We allow U.S. trained pilots to fly in our air space but

December 4, 1980
Supply
we do not allow Canadians to become instrument-rated without complying with a particularly difficult set of regulations. Let me at this point toss in a little item-it exemplifies the type of thing which makes me state over and over again that the ministry has become an adversary to general aviation when it should be the support of general aviation. The department requires encoding altimeters at about 14,000 feet but the regulations with regard to installing an encoding altimeter in one's aircraft are maddeningly difficult and unreasonably expensive. It is not impossible, but it is very difficult to comply with them. Again, these are regulations with which they are not faced in countries where the aircraft are built.
1 think I am getting close to the end of my allotted time, Mr. Chairman, but I want to put just one more question before the minister, his staff and his parliamentary secretary. It concerns the matter of emergency locator transmitters. I have been on my feet in this House about ELTs for all the time I have been here but I have not had a good straight answer to that question yet. The minister, and certainly his staff, will remember that private pilots were forced to put ELTs in their private aircraft. In principle, perhaps it was not a bad idea. If at that time the minister had admitted they had been warned that lithium batteries would cause difficulties, we could have made some representations. The Ministry of Transport was warned by manufacturers in the United States that the lithium batteries they were about to make mandatory in Canadian aircraft would cause difficulties, but the department neglected to heed that warning and went ahead and forced Canadian owners to put ELTs in their aircraft with lithium batteries.
When those batteries gave rise to difficulties and, indeed, caused a couple of serious crashes, the ministry backed off and said pilots were not required to have an ELT in their aircraft. I repeat, we are a country of people who fly. These pilots were forced to put in these ELTs at a cost of never less than $250. They were then told they could and should take them out.
We are now faced with a conflicting set of regulations. Frankly, as one who flies regularly, I do not know specifically what those regulations are. I put an ELT in my aircraft with other than a lithium battery. I hope it will work. The Ministry of Transport should take advantage of the size of this country and the number of aircraft here and develop an electronic locator transmitter which would be the envy of the world. We certainly have the brains and the technology to do that. The department deserves to do it and should do it for all pilots who fly in Canada. However, they are not doing it. I expect that very shortly we will again be told to put those ELTs in and pay for them again. I hope the minister will tell me this evening that if pilots are again forced to put in ELTs, the department will at least help pay for them.
I could go on and elaborate on this theme but I know my time must be running out. I ask the minister to tell me why the ministry has taken on the adversary position it has with the general aviation public in Canada.

speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I rise on a point of order. This exercise is an examination of the estimates for which the minister is accountable to the committee. That is the name of the whole exercise, the accountability of the minister. He should be answering the questions, not the parliamentary secretary. That is why he was given all sorts of notice for his department to be called. That is why he is here. It is the minister, not the parliamentary secretary who is accountable. Our practices and procedures require him to account to us on the questions that are put to him.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I do not have to teach you or the member for Yukon any constitutional law and practices. The member knows and Your Honour knows that the fact that I sit here makes me responsible for what my parliamentary secretary says. That is a customary practice and I would not think the member for Yukon would bother to raise that. It is anchored in our practices. I have seen it hundreds of times, as has he. If he has not, it is because he was not looking. It is done regularly. Therefore, I do not see why I should have to defend myself.

I only want to invite my colleague to read the Parliamentary Secretaries Act. It is very short and only says that the function of a parliamentary secretary is to assist the minister in his parliamentary duties. So I wonder why my colleague blames the parliamentary secretary for doing his duty. The minister is present in the House and the parliamentary secretary is assisting him in his parliamentary functions.
The hon. member is very lucky to have at the same time the minister and his parliamentary secretary to answer his questions as completely as possible. If he is really sincere, if he really wishes to obtain detailed information, he should be happy to get the red carpet treatment because he has here tonight to answer all his questions a minister and a parliamentary secretary who respect the law and three department officials. I wonder what more the hon. member wants. I wish I could understand the motives of his complaint. Is he sincere? I have some doubt about his real intent, but I give him the benefit of the doubt. I only tell him that he is treated royally and that he has no reason for complaining.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Mines)
speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Chairman. I think it is particularly appropriate that I should have an opportunity to speak on the subject of the Department of Transport because while we all recognize-and it has been said often during the debate-that transportation is vital to Canada it is especially so to the port of Thunder Bay. Thunder Bay is, as we know, the transportation hub of Canada. We are on the mainline of Air Canada, we are on the mainline of CP Rail, there are extensive CN operations in our area and we are an ocean port
2,000	miles from the sea. I was particularly pleased to note that at the beginning of this discussion on transport the minister mentioned the great growth which is taking place in the west and the anticipated growth which will be taking place there. We take a very special interest in that matter because by and large the grain from the prairies flows through Thunder Bay and, I am proud to say, very efficiently. We are also pleased to note that potash from Saskatchewan is being shipped more and more to the port of Thunder Bay and thence various points around the world. Coal from the west is used in Thunder Bay, reaching our port via rail. The coal which is not used in local plants is shipped elsewhere.
Built in 1959, the seaway showed a profit this year for the first time. It is certainly vindication for those men and women of vision who advocated the building of a project which has meant so much not only to Thunder Bay but to Canada as a whole. I also know that Transport Canada is eagerly awaiting, as we all are, a report from a seaway task force. The department recognizes that this mighty avenue to the world of commerce must be as efficient as possible. We need studies of this kind and we need this harmonious relationship between the federal government, the provinces and the ports themselves to make sure we have the transportation system we need and which we will need more and more in the future.
I remind the minister that we must continue to improve and upgrade our port facilities, our storage facilities and our cargo-handling capability. All ports in this country must be looked at including the port of Thunder Bay, the east coast, the west coast and the Arctic ports such as Churchill and so forth. We must be alert to maintaining our ice-breaking fleets, and we must improve our technology. I believe the parliamentary secretary made reference to that. We must continue to improve our technology to make sure that we can extend the shipping season through the cold Canadian winters. It has been proved that water transportation is still the most energy-efficient means of transporting volume goods, and therefore we think it is in the interest of the country to maintain programs
December 4, 1980

which will allow us to extend the life of the seaway and the use of our ports closer to a year-round basis.
While I have talked a great deal, as did my colleague, the hon. member for Thunder Bay-Atikokan, about our port, I would like to make a quick comment about the rail service which comes into Thunder Bay. Rail, of course, was our first major way of linking the country together from sea to sea, and 1 am happy that we as a government are continuing to look to the rail service and giving it its due. As we all know, more money has been allocated to the rail service in the budget to make sure that the system works effectively, and I think when we see and note that Thunder Bay had a record season in grain shipment this year, we must acknowledge that the rail system is indeed working, and working well. I just suggest to the minister that we continue our studies and our improvements, that we look to ways to improve the efficiency of rail handling and that we also look to the subject of rail relocation in the many communities in Canada which want things done to correct the lack of planning of years gone by or to catch up with the changes in our modern communities. Those are long-term projects, and certainly no one would expect that we would see those things happen in a day or a year, but I hope we are looking at plans which will put us in such a position to set policies which will lead to that desired end over time.
The air service we receive in this country is also very vital to keeping this country together. I am proud that Air Canada is showing a profit. I believe we have a great Canadian airline; I believe it is being recognized and will enjoy a very prosperous and good future.
I note that the federal government is working in northwestern Ontario on the northern Ontario aviation master plan. This means that the Ontario government and the federal government are working closely to improve the air safety situation in the north. Northwestern Ontario counts very much on feeder airlines and small private planes flying about to cover the vast distances involved.
I hope that we continue the work we have been doing in Timmins, and the Thunder Bay airport, the Kenora airport, and at Dryden. The new air navigational aid which has been installed at Wawa gives us an even greater safety factor.
I have talked much about Canada's water, air and rail services, and 1 am proud that Transport Canada serves all of Canada so well. We can all suggest changes and find fault in individual situations, but I think that if we are honest with one another, we must encourage the Department of Transport to continue giving us one of the best transportation systems in the world.
Finally, I will give the minister a brief reminder and ask him to be sure that his department is looking ahead and planning for the future because long-term planning is required in these vital functions. I know that the minister will want to be sure to advise his department to look at the transportation needs of the country in a long-term way so that when we need additional services and improved services, they will be provided.

Mr. Chairman, 1 would like to make a few comments about prairie branch lines and then pose a few questions to the minister.
The minister is aware that under his predecessor some 1,000 miles of line were given protection by order in council, 600 to the year 2000 and some 400 with the intention of doing a study of off-line elevators. After the minister took over I found it rather interesting to listen to some of the comments he made as he travelled about the west. The indications seemed to be that he was the one who saved these lines. 1 have also noted that the former member for Assiniboia has spent some time suggesting that he and his party saved these lines. More latterly members of the NDP in Saskatchewan have been saying that they saved the lines. I think it is rather important to make it perfectly clear for the record that the 1000-odd miles of line which were protected were protected by the Conservative government under the then minister of transport, the hon. member for Vegreville.
Some hon. Miembers: Hear, hear!

It was interesting as well to listen to the comments of the minister, who said that he himself did not think the lines should be saved, but after talking to some of his colleagues he felt it was in the political interest of his party to do so.
After the minister came to power he examined the order in council of his predecessor and did in fact leave the guaranteed lines alone, but he took steps to pass an order in council to the effect that those 400-odd miles of lines which were set aside for off-line elevator purposes were taken off the protection list. In newspaper reports and on the radio the minister's comments with respect to the off-line elevator concept were to the effect that there was no evidence of any kind before him which he could study to determine whether the off-line elevator concept should be considered.
I found this rather interesting because there is a public document in existence. It was put out by the research branch of the Canadian Transport Commission, and it is entitled "Economic Feasibility of Off-track Elevators". The date of that report is January, 1980, yet the minister said there were no studies and nothing to indicate that the off-line elevator concept should be considered. I hope the minister will take steps to obtain a copy of this public document. I hope he will read it and give consideration to try the off-line elevator concept at least on one line. The former minister suggested the Fisher Branch line, which goes some 80 miles without an elevator or a station on it. The cost of rehabilitation, as I recall, would be about $10 million. There is grain at the top end of that line which has to be delivered to the elevator. In our minds it made sense that the off-line elevator concept should at least be given a try on that line. However, the minister simply threw the suggestion out on the basis that there was no study. He had nothing on which to base a decision, so he arbitrarily passed an order in council to refer those 400-odd miles of line to the CTC for consideration and abandonment.

The minister is aware, of course, that the steps taken by his predecessor were based on certain recommendations made to him in a report. I know he has said publicly on several occasions that he did not have access to that report and was therefore not in a position to really understand the reason for the recommendations. But if the hon. gentleman had been watching the news releases which came out of the office of the Minister of Transport, he would have found that on December 20 of 1979, the department issued a news release setting forth several recommendations which the then minister said he was prepared to act upon. One recommendation was to the effect- I hope the minister will consider it

that an advisory committee should be set up composed of representatives of the various elevator companies, the railways and the office of the grain transportation co-ordinator to determine priorities for the rehabilitation of the lines. The minister is aware that until this time the consideration of the priorities is a matter for consultation between the railways and the minister's office. The basis of the recommendation which the former minister was prepared to accept was that the elevator companies should have a part in the decision-making because their decision as to which elevators on which lines would be upgraded or where new elevators would be built had to be based on a decision with regard to rehabilitation. The minister accepted that recommendation. I should like to ask the minister whether or not he is prepared to consider that recommendation.
The other point I should like to make also concerns a recommendation adopted by the former minister. Many people throughout the prairie provinces have been concerned about the validity of the charges set by the railways when they are rehabilitating their lines. The recommendation accepted by the minister was to the effect that when the rehabilitation work could be done by contractors in cases where the engineering skill of the railroads was not required, public tenders should be called. If the railway wished, it could submit a tender, and if it happened to be the lowest tender, the railway would be entitled to do the job. The calling of tenders would mean that the public and the government would know they were getting value for their money in the rehabilitation of the rail lines.
My final question to the minister is with respect to the time-frame and the money to be spent on the rehabilitation of lines. I understand that, in 1979 dollars, the total cost of rehabilitation was estimated at some $1.2 billion. The government recommended the expenditure of some $700 million for rehabilitating the lines. I am told that the cost of rehabilitation appreciates at the rate of 10 per cent a year. So it seems to me that, at the present rate of expenditure, it is doubtful we will ever catch up with the rehabilitation of the lines which have been guaranteed to the year 2000. So my third question to the minister is: what are his intentions with respect to the financing of the rehabilitation. I hope he will not say to us that we will be using that $4 billion which was announced a few months ago by the government as moneys which would be made available for economic development in western Canada. That $4 billion is money coming from the west, and if it is
going to be used for economic development, I suggest to the minister that economic development does not mean rehabilitation of lines.
I have posed my questions and I will now sit down. 1 would appreciate hearing from the minister in response.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, let me say briefly that the reason I did not accept orders 16, 17 and 18 approved by my predecessor relatively late in his tenure was that there was no overt, known or public justification for what had been done. I found that to be rather strange and that was why I hesitated. I also hesitated because there has been quite a lot of debate on other ways of transporting grain. A number of people have come out in favour of off-track and off-line elevators, transportation by truck, and so on, and I thought that this issue should be aired and that a debate should take place before a decision was reached on the spending of hundreds of millions of dollars. However, what happened is that I went round consulting a great number of people. I did not talk about studies having been made. I just happen to have the notes that I used and the communique which I issued at that time. It says specifically that my recent extensive discussions with almost all the grain handling companies in the west have led me to the conclusion that the subsidized hauling of grain by truck, which was considered by some as a possible alternative to rebuilding the rail lines, is not generally accepted.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
speechtext:
There is so much division on those things that you are happy when you have a few friends around. That is what I said. I did not say that there was no study, I just said that my experience demonstrated that there was no great, passionate movement in favour of the subject. That is why I did not pursue order 17, inclusion in the basic network for a period of five years, which was based on the concept of off-line elevators.
On the selection of branch lines for rehabilitation, it is as my friend described it. The selection is essentially decided by the railways and the department. I presume it is still the case. I am told, and I assumed repeatedly that it was being done, that the department consults with grain companies before taking a decision, and now, presumably, it does so with the grain co-ordinator. My hon. friend knows so much more about it than I do, or he can easily claim he does, so he must be aware that very often the grain elevator operators are not too keen to let it be known that they intend to close an elevator in a certain place. They are keener, of course, to let it be known that they intend to build a new one, which is the popular thing to do. Closing an elevator is not as welcome. That is why the process and the procedure are informal. When grain companies or pool operating elevators want to make it known that they want the government to rehabilitate a branch line, they find a way. I have been exposed to that process. So unless my hon. friend insists, and talks to me afterwards about it, 1 see no major difficulty there.
December 4, 1980

With respect to the contracts that lead to branch line rehabilitation, I understand that a great number of them, or parts of them, are open to bidding on a local basis on some of the less specialized jobs. But when it comes to the more specific railway work which needs to be done, generally it is done by the railways themselves for a good number of reasons. One of them is that there is what I would call a respectable agreement between the railways and the unions that the railways will go to their own employees to do the work before contracting it out. So, my friend will have to make a decision-to whom does he want to be friendly?
I think the regular employees of railways deserve some consideration when it comes to specific technical work; 1 do not take objection to it. But this is not the debate. The debate really is-who will do best the technical railway work? I think the railways would do it best.
There is no question about that.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
speechtext:
Also there is the element of protecting the regular permanent railway employees, which is why more of the work is not contracted out. As far as I am concerned the explanation is justified. I hope it is justified to the hon. member as well.
With respect to the size of the budget allocated to branch line rehabilitation, the hon. member knows better than I that $240 million has already been spent. The total amount has not changed since the hon. member for Vegreville was the minister. It is $700 million over a period of eight years. The point raised or implied is a valid one. If we had more money, it would be a good thing to accelerate the process, for a great number of reasons, one being the advantage of concentration. There is no doubt if more work was being done over a shorter period of time that there would be sizeable advantages. But, things have not really changed. The same amount of money has been allocated, and one thinks about what one might be able to do if it could be accelerated.

They do not have a line now.

1 am my own adviser on a number of aspects with respect to grain here tonight. With respect to hopper cars, it is well known the government has purchased 8,000 of them since 1973. I am sure the hon. member is aware of this. The question is: where do we go from here? By the way, the strike at Hawker-Siddeley in Trenton may be over and there are 600-odd cars which can be built there.
What about the future? We have asked the grain co-ordinator to look at it. He has produced a report in which there is a suggestion made that we will need, if my memory serves me correctly, 1,700 per year from 1982 to 1985. So we are
considering three times 1,700. There is discussion as to whether it is too much or too little. Most people say "How do we predict it?" The situation for this year is very good, as everyone knows. If I may finish my assertions on this subject, this is closely related to the Crow question, with the modernization of the Crow issue. Obviously there is a relationship between the compensatory price and the purchase of hopper cars. If the railways were taking responsibility for the provision of hopper cars that would affect the compensatory price. But the general mood in the west is that one way or another the Canadian government, the Wheat Board and the provinces should continue purchasing hopper cars in order to make up for the neglect which has taken place in the past.
I do not know where you heard I made the suggestion that the $4 billion be used for the purchase of hopper cars. I did not make any such suggestion.

Mr. Chairman, I want to raise a few questions that are of vital importance to my constituency and they follow along the same lines as those of the previous speaker.
On August 15, I received a notice of hearing from the CTC informing me that the CNR had made application to abandon the operations of the Yarmouth subdivision from a point near Liverpool, Nova Scotia, to Yarmouth, Nova Scotia, a total distance of 135.68 miles. The reason given was that the line was operating at a loss and the losses for 1975 were listed at $2,181,000: for 1976, $1,831,000, and for 1977, $1,769,000. It stated that the losses for 1978 and 1979 would be given at the hearings. Naturally when these facts became known, numerous briefs from outraged businessmen were forwarded to me as their member of Parliament, and, of course, these were sent on to the minister. Unfortunately, as I stand here tonight, to date, I have not received a concrete response from the minister, so my first question to him is to ask why there has been no answer to the questions I have raised concerning this matter.
What is happening, Mr. Chairman, in my riding, is a far cry from the promises that were made by the Prime Minister when he was campaigning in my province on Friday, January 25. At that time he was full of promises for our people, promises which were endorsed by Liberal supporters and repeated ad infinitum up and down the various constituencies of Nova Scotia. On the front page, for example, the Halifax Chronicle-Herald, on January 26, we read among other things, these words as stated by the then leader of the opposition, now our Prime Minister:
We will use revenues raised through energy taxation to make big projects happen-railway building, pipeline construction, a western electrical grid, and coal liquefaction are only a few of the projects that the energy boom could produce.
I ask you, Mr. Chairman, how you can equate that promise with the actual facts. If you would call removing 135 miles of railway line railway building, I do not know what you would call railway destruction.
To add insult to injury, on November 5, the province of Nova Scotia received another body blow from the CNR. The Canadian Transport Commission at that time, and I am quoting from their order No. R-31558, stated, in the matter of the application of CN Railways to phase out certain services in the province, that the applicants were authorized to remove the agency positions located in eleven listed locations. I would point out, Mr. Chairman, that seven of these are in my own constituency. The order goes on to say that the station buildings in eight locations will be put up for sale. Seven of these are in my riding.
I raised this matter in the House on November 18, as reported at page 4802 of Hansard, only to be told at that time by the minister that the action was necessary because CN Express was losing money. He had previously stated that the
December 4, 1980

CN had lost $14 million in 1970 and will lose $57 million this year. When I asked him if he planned to close down Mirabel, which is also losing more than $50 million annually, he said no one should compare the two. 1 agree with him; for once he is right. He is right because the CNR in its express service is serving a vast area throughout the province of Nova Scotia, while Mirabel serves only one area. 1 say to you, sir, that if $50 million needs to be saved, the minister should close down Mirabel and use the money to upgrade and continue its CNR services in the entire province of Nova Scotia.
This is what the Chronicle-Herald said in part in a lead editorial, about the cut in our express service:
It has been announced that Canadian National is to cut back its express service right across the country. As a result of this decision, about half of its offices will be closed and 1,100 of a workforce of 5,500 will join the ranks of the unemployed. In the Atlantic region, it is estimated that some 254 jobs will be lost and 15 offices will go out of business.
In other words, this government, which is loud in its promises when it is campaigning in Nova Scotia, has now adopted a policy of "sock it to them. Sock it to the bluenoses." Close down the express service. As soon as they are in power that is the course they follow. Almost one-quarter of the personnel in all of Canada will be laid off in my province alone. Think of the economic impact that will have in a province which has less than one million people. I submit to you, sir, that this will be very disastrous.
The Deputy Prime Minister and the Minister of Labour-I regret that neither is in the House at the present time-also represent my province. They should hang their heads in shame, for supporting this type of measure which cannot help but be harmful to the people they were elected to serve.
Tonight, sir, I make a plea to this minister to call a halt to these disastrous measures. Canadian National must be faulted for applying for abandonment of unprofitable lines, while not putting forward its good case for continuing the lines it has in service. Once in a while we see an occasional advertisement on TV which shows one man pulling a freight car which reads, "Very low friction, a railway is energy efficient." It is a very good ad, but when I see it I cannot but ask: have we no energy problem in Canada, or does the left hand of CN not know what the right hand is doing? CN officials should be reminded that all Canadians-and that includes Nova Scotians, Mr. Chairman-have paid their share to forgive a CNR debt of many millions of dollars. This was done only recently, and now CN, through its present financial arrangements, can boast of large profits.
I submit, sir, that an obsessive drive for profits at any cost cannot excuse CN from its obligations to provide needed service. In my view, and in the opinion of my constituents, the profitable parts of CN's operations must carry the less profitable ones.
Finally, in support of my plea-and I hope my time permits me to do this-I wish to place on the record the brief prepared by the South Queens Chamber of Commerce concerning the proposed abandonment of service along the South Shore. I quote the following:

The South Queens Chamber of Commerce takes strong exception to the proposed abandonment of service, by CN Rail, of their Liverpool, Nova Scotia to Yarmouth, Nova Scotia, rail line. Local automobile repair businesses are thriving on the undercarriage damage to cars using these crossings. The railway bed has deteriorated to the extent that trains travel at a reduced speed. (Roughly 15 miles per hour.) The cost to ship goods by rail is unreasonable considering the slowness and unreliability of the service.
It is my suspicion that CN through their neglect of this line, have created the inequity that they claim exists. To put it simply, if the line is losing money and has become unattractive to its potential users, CN must accept the blame and criticism.
Of particular importance to our county are the Bowater Paper Company and Steel and Engine Products Limited, our two largest employers. Both companies rely on rail service. With regard to Steel and Engine, abandonment of the rail line would probably cause this industry to relocate. The president and general manager of Bowater, Mr. Robert Weary, has suggested to me that the rail service is vital to that paper mill.

To threaten these businesses along the South Shore by abandoning this rail line, would appear to me, to defeat the political philosophy of our government. Although I disagree with many of the give-away practices of our federal government, this must be viewed as a necessary deficit situation. The people of the South Shore are proud, hard-working individuals who boast a low unemployment rate. We need the help of our government-sponsored Crown corporations in fostering growth for our communities.
Submitted by John L. Murray, president.
With the fuel problem in the world today, one which is predicted to become increasingly more severe, rail transportation is obviously a most attractive alternative to our petroleum-based highway service. Incidentally, many European countries enjoy efficient rail service and have had for many years. Could we not learn from their experiences?
The County of Queens and Town of Liverpool have begun to formulate a philosophy that will promote development in our area. Local and provincially sponsored plans have been studied and both councils have agreed to co-sponsor a development officer.
