Mr. Chairman, I have a few questions for the minister. The first one is as follows: The CN had given a contract to Marine Industries Limited for the construction of 1000 hopper cars for grain transport. Some time ago, the CN said that it wanted to back out of this contract and offered compensation to Marine Industries Limited. I would like the minister to tell us whether this commitment and the contract signed between Marine Industries Limited and the CN for the construction of 1,000 hopper cars still hold.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
speechtext: I should say first of all that I have received letters from the hon. member for Richelieu giving me some background information. Of course, the situation of Marine Industries cannot be changed, and this contract was extremely important for the company and the representative of this constituency. I have spoken many times of this contract to Mr. Bandeen, and he told me this afternoon that he was now able to confirm that he would maintain his order for 1,000 cars. The order was for 1,000 hopper cars to transport goods other than wheat even though they could be used for wheat, and the CN and Marine Industries are discussing the possibility of changing this order to 700 hopper cars and 300 gondola or open top cars. I am happy to give this good news to the hon. member.

Mr. Chairman, I now come to my second question. There is a coastguard depot in Sorel. There was a rumour some time ago that this depot would be moved to Quebec City or Montreal. Can the minister confirm that this coastguard depot, where buoys and boats belonging to the coastguard are repaired, will remain in Sorel? It has been there for over 150 years.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I know that I have already written to the hon. member about this. I sign about 25 letters every day, but if my memory serves me right, some changes were made some months ago, and if I am not mistaken, some boats have been moved and this has brought about the transfer of personnel. Unless I am mistaken, there have been shifts between Sorel and Trois-Rivieres, but number one in the maritime division of my department tells me that he does not foresee-or at least his big books make no mention of any- any unpleasant changes for Sorel.

Mr. Chairman, I now wish to speak about the merchant marine. Naturally, it is of great interest to me since we have a well-reputed dockyard at Sorel. Does the minister believe that Canada might have a merchant marine in the relatively not-too-distant future? We already have one but it should be enlarged to enable us to ship our goods abroad, especially the heavy material, and also to pick up abroad the goods we need for the well-being of our people; something should be done in that regard. Naturally, it is a major problem but I feel that Canada should have a high seas merchant marine as well as a coastal fleet. The present situation is a scandal. We have to hire foreign vessels to handle our inshore trade. It will probably be possible to build a coastal fleet for the St. Lawrence River and our coastal waters along the Atlantic. Might that be possible for the not-too-distant future?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I dealt with the subject in my opening remarks yesterday-is it yesterday only or a few days ago-but I would hesitate to deal with it in depth because I would not be doing it justice; still, one thing must be kept in mind and that is that Canada has quite a sizeable merchant marine in the Great Lakes, the St. Lawrence, etc. When we speak of the need for Canada to have a merchant marine, we are really thinking especially of the high seas, of international shipping; one of the main things I have learned is that ships belonging to Canadians carry 90 per cent of the freight handled on the Great Lakes. That really impressed me. We must therefore not underestimate ourselves as Canadians to the extent of thinking that we have no merchant marine; when we express the wish of having one, we are really thinking in terms of ships registered in Canada and built in Canada. That is an objective; to sum it up in one sentence only, I doubt that such an objective can be settled philosophically because our main rivals with regard to an international merchant marine, a deep sea fleet, are the manufacturers, the shippers. And what they fear is that they may be forced some day to use ships registered in Canada and that because of that it will make them less competitive on the world market because they will have paid a higher price for the advantage of using ships built in Canada and manned by Canadian crews.
The main opponents of a high sea Canadian merchant marine are the manufacturers: they will have to be convinced that such is not the case and this is now being done because the owners and the Canadian shipbuilders, thinking and in my
December 4, 1980

opinion partly rightly so, that the future calls for a Canadian high seas merchant marine, have started educating their friends in the manufacturing sector, have met with the Canadian Export Association to make them aware of the usefulness of a high seas merchant marine. That had to be said and I thank the hon. member for his question.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member for Richelieu may put one last question.

In Sorel, we have a gravel airstrip. The pilots of planes and jets do not want to land, they are afraid a stone will hit the engine or something, I do not know exactly. Even the pilots of propeller aircraft are afraid that a piece of gravel will hit the propeller, and apparently the cost of repair is prohibitive. Does the Minister of Transport foresee that in the near future that strip could be paved, and I am thinking not only of the Sorel strip but also of the one in Dolbeau where I landed last winter and which is full of potholes. Those strips should be paved so that jets could land safely and easily?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
speechtext: Unfortunately, the department cannot deal with that in the same way as it does with Mirabel, Moncton or Dorval. In that sort of case, the department does not really feel it has to take action for the simple reason that, unless there are reasons I am unaware of, it cannot force the people to maintain the strip after it has been paved. I would advise the people in Sorel to think this over carefully, to consult the people in Trois-Rivieres, the people in Sherbrooke, especially, who are having trouble with their airport these days and who might be in a good position to give some advice to the people of Sorel on what not to do.

Mr. Chairman, I would like to talk to the minister about the Fraser River Harbour Commission. As he knows, the commission ports pay no tax or grants in lieu of tax. I would like to know when he is going to bring in the ports act so that the commission ports will stop bilking the municipalities out of thousands of dollars each year. Please do not use the argument that the commission ports bring socioeconomic benefits to the community. If they do that, and 1 do not argue that they do, so do all the other industries in the area which pay taxes. It is about time the commission ports pay either taxes or grants in lieu of taxes. But they will not do it and cannot do it until the ports act is passed. We see the anomaly of the Fraser River Harbour Commission with an annual report showing a profit of $1 million and freeloading off the municipality at the same time. I wish the minister would give me an answer to that question.
Second, in the case of the Fraser River Harbour Commission, there is a port for fishermen called Gunderson Slough. The chairman of the commission, Mr. Chris Brown, has been telling me for the last couple of years with a very benign and beatific smile, how much he plans to do for the fishermen, how
Supply
he plans to improve the harbour and how he cannot wait to get all of the riparian rights so that he can build this great harbour for the fishermen. He has not yet turned a spade or put in a plank. He will not even have the harbour dredged. However, he insists on hanging on to the Gunderson Slough. He loves to control it, but he does not want to do anything concrete for the fishermen. I might point out to the minister that I have a private members' bill abstracting Gunderson Slough from the Fraser River Harbour Commission and turning it over to the minister of fisheries who might take a little more interest than the Fraser River Harbour Commission does in Gunderson Slough.
1 met with Mr. Brown last spring. He promised to bring together two other departments which have an interest in this, fisheries and public works. They were to have a meeting in the spring and Mr. Brown was to report back to me. Of course, I never heard from him again. The meeting took place. I did hear, though, from the Public Works office in Vancouver. They said, and I quote from a letter of June 19:
The current policy of Small Craft Harbours was developed in 1975 and is applied to "scheduled harbours" only. This schedule could be enlarged but in the case of Gunderson Slough it would require an agreement with the Fraser River Harbour Commission.
In order for Gunderson Slough to qualify as a public scheduled harbour there would have to be a sizeable public float installed, say in the order of 400 lineal feet.
That is still, and probably will be for a long time, under the control of the harbour commission which refuses to do anything. When the fishermen left the harbour last spring, they grounded; $20 million worth of boats had a hard time getting out of the slough. Public Works dredged 1, 2 or 3 feet out of the slough. When the fishing season was over in the fall, the boats grounded again when coming back into the harbour.
A boat that draws five feet was bottomed. It stuck. Public Works should take notice there are no navigation buoys in the harbour. Mr. Brown wants to control the harbour, but he does not want to do anything for the fishermen.
I would like to know the minister's department's attitude and policy toward that aspect. Is the minister going to take the Fraser River Harbour Commission to task and make sure that he delivers service to the fishermen who deserve it, or is he going to turn it over to public works or small craft harbours so that at least one department of the government will assume responsibility rather than have confusion among three departments.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I thank the hon. member for Surrey-White Rock-North Delta for the information he has given me. It is the first time I have heard about the Gunderson Slough. I am not even sure I can pronounce the name properly. I will rehearse tomorrow.
With regard to the status of the harbour commission, under the 1964 act, the hon. member said they were neither paying taxes nor grants in lieu of taxes. I am suspicious that Mr. Chris Brown will not be particularly grateful for the intervention tonight. It is an advantage that he is not too keen to

December 4, 1980
Supply
proclaim. I will not continue because I do not want to incur his wrath.
Be that as it may, Mr. Brown's argument is that the harbour commission makes a very important contribution to the development of the surrounding area in economic terms. Ele feels that is the way the harbour makes its contribution to municipal taxation.
How was that again?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
speechtext: I am not commenting on it. I am just passing on the message with some conviction on my part because this is a good case. As is well known in maritime circles, that is one of the reasons Mr. Brown has never been particularly keen to pay allegiance to the National Harbours Board. He has always expressed great satisfaction in being under the Harbour Commissions Act. When I met Mr. Brown again recently, I referred to him as "64". He understood very well what I was talking about. He is a legendary character in the area. We all like his cherubic smile, as my hon. friend referred to it, and praise him for the great job he is doing in the area. Be that as it may, 1 will look into the problem raised by the hon. member.
Can the minister tell me who the wharfinger is for the harbour commission? Second, will he agree that Mr. Chris Brown is not only the commissioner but the port manager as well?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
speechtext: Yesterday 1 appointed a list of wharfingers. I can assure the hon. member that they are all believers in free enterprise, the future of the country, peace, harmony, good government, stability of laws and other virtues.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. minister for Surrey-White Rock-North Delta.
Oh, oh!

I appreciate the promotion, Mr. Chairman, but not to this government. I would like a clear and unequivocal answer to this. Why is it that the Surrey municipality has been denied an opportunity to appoint a nominee to the commission?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
speechtext: The situation with the Fraser commission is that a number of municipalities got together to appoint a member for all of them. If memory serves me well, there was a bit of a problem the last time.
Oh, oh!

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
speechtext: How can a guy remember all that? There was a bit of a problem because one of the municipalities did not want to go along with the others. Finally, 1 had to take the bull by the horns or the horns by the bull-
You should have taken him by the tail.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
speechtext: In accord with the principle of democracy, I had to decide for them, for the majority.
Hear, hear!

Thank you, Mr. Chairman. I would like to direct my questions to the issues of railway safety and air transport. About two years ago there was a serious railway accident involving robot trains in which some 76 cars were derailed. I think the average speed they were supposed to be travelling was around 18 miles an hour yet their speed was over 60 miles an hour. The Railway Transport Commission studied this wreck and about six months ago they made recommendations and expressed certain views as to how things should be done. Can the minister tell us whether those recommendations have been implemented yet or whether they are considered serious enough to be brought in?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
speechtext: I must admit I am not familiar with this particular case, but I know of similar cases. For example, the last difficulty at MacGregor, Manitoba, led to an inquiry by the CTC. The CTC made a whole series of recommendations some of which involved the CTC itself, some the Department of Transport and some the railways. I know how the system works.

I am not asking that question. I am talking about the Revelstoke mountain subdivision of CP Rail in the Revelstoke to Golden areas. These recommendations were made to the effect that when snow reaches-three inches or more on the rails-ploughs would be run and so on. While this investigation was going on there was a reduction in the tonnage to be hauled. Instead of hauling 14,000 tons, I think they reduced the weight of this train to somewhere around 9,000 or 10,000 tons. Before the report came in they allowed CP Rail to increase it to 14,000 tons. Two days ago in Elkford, on a piece of track that allows trains to go ten miles an hour, a robot train with 14,000 tons and approximately 76 cars went out of control and derailed.
Is the minister prepared to recommend to the Railway Transport Commission that they immediately request a reduction of tonnage on these trains until the reports come back on this accident?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
speechtext: I am quite prepared to have a discussion with the CTC on that subject. I am not prepared to commit myself and tell the railways how to run the railways.
It's about time someone did.

May I remind the minister that less than three weeks ago I wrote to him after the investigation was made into the labour problems in Revelstoke? Some very significant problems were brought out in that report as to the operation of trains on this piece of track-not this specific piece but the piece on the Revelstoke Mountain subdivision. I requested that the minister consider sending some railway transport commissioners in to investigate the reports which came out of the labour relations investigation at Revelstoke. To date I have not received a reply although I had a very brief discussion with Mr. Charles Turner who has, I believe, made a suggestion to
December 4, 1980

the minister's department. 1 am concerned about this matter and would urge the minister to look into it immediately.
I will go on to another area, if I may. During a health and safety standard tour by our party to Nova Scotia and New Brunswick we visited the air traffic controllers' building in Moncton, a new building which I think the minister opened a few months ago.
Some of these air traffic controllers were working double shifts-and in a brand new building-because there were not enough adequately trained people to do the job. Is the minister planning a major training program to train air traffic controllers so that the public does not have to travel in aeroplanes when air traffic control officers are working these extended hours?
The Montreal airport is short 60 controllers, Toronto is short 34, Vancouver is short 27, Moncton is short 25 and Gander is short 20. Is the minister not concerned that we are operating aircraft with these staff shortages? Is he prepared to start immediately setting up a major training program so that we can begin training people to handle the strenuous job of operating control towers?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the figures provided by my hon. friend are from the union, CATCA, and they tend to exaggerate, as we all do occasionally. The hon. member for Regina West does occasionally, and so do I.
The figures stated with respect to the need for more controllers at the airports mentioned are slightly exaggerated, which does not mean that 1 and the department are fully satisfied with the situation now, particularly when it comes to bilingual controllers, in which case there has been great difficulty simply because of the number who have left Quebec and gone to other provinces. However, that is not the main subject.
I now have the actual numbers with respect to what is needed. If the hon. member used the figure of 30, the department thinks seven might be adequate. As far as I am concerned this is an important subject. I think there should be more controllers to make the profession more open, and we should not be in the situation where we have to depend on these gentlemen to the point we do now. The department devotes much attention to the training of controllers, and I can only assure the hon. member that this is a subject with which I am preoccupied.

The figures I have given are from a report given to the inquiry into aviation safety. It was given by the Canadian Air Traffic Controllers Association which testified yesterday.
It was made very clear to us during our visit that there is a tremendous amount of stress and strain involved with this work and strain on the families of these people, who are called in to work extra hours and double shifts. This is something the Canadian people cannot tolerate. We must have a better
Supply
system of training and more up-to-date facilities. The control tower to which I referred is tremendously updated, and to have such a facility understaffed is not acceptable.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I take these recommendations quite seriously. I have said that the figures might be exaggerated, and I have given other figures to demonstrate that view. This case has been put to the Dubin commission of inquiry. Mr. Dubin will begin to report in the new year, and I will give much attention to his report.
One of the difficulties with respect to the profession of air traffic controller is that the Canadian government is the only employer. This makes it rather more difficult to attract people to the profession. It makes competition a bit more difficult to bring about.

Mr. Chairman, I have a series of questions to put to the minister. For a number of years the federal government has been a tremendous help to every province in Canada through the grade-crossing fund, and because of the joint efforts of the federal government and provincial governments-and municipal governments in some cases-we have saved hundreds, probably thousands, of lives across this country. For some reason the federal government is now cancelling any contributions to the grade-crossing fund for separations. In the short time allotted to me I would like to endeavour to indicate to the minister that this is a very bad policy.
In 1978 there were 65 deaths at rural railway crossings. Thirty-nine of those, or 60 per cent, were at unprotected crossings. In the same year at urban crossings there were 25 deaths and injuries, and 19 of them were at crossings where there was no protection. At every place where there was a grade separation-either over or under the railway tracks- there were no deaths or injuries. In other words, 90 persons were killed in that one year because there was no protection at those level crossings.
If the federal government continues to follow the policy of not contributing to separations, it will really be adopting a very tragic course because contributing funds to lights and bells only does not do the job. In 1977 at places where there were lights and bells 12 people were killed. In 1978, 25 people were killed. We do not have figures for 1980, but it appears that the figure for 1980 will be even higher. Lights and bells are not doing the job. The only way to make a level railway crossing completely safe is to put in a separation, so I urge the minister to go back to the policy which helped for many years to keep people alive, namely, that of contributing, through the grade crossing fund, to separations over level crossings. Seventy-five per cent on replacements and 50 per cent on new ones is a far better investment than contributing only to lights and bells. Why is the government cancelling its contribution to separations at level railway crossings?
The Greeks had a great hero by the name of Achilles. Achilles had one weak spot, and that weak spot led to his downfall. I am suggesting that the Achilles heel of transportation in Canada today is roads and highways. All the other modes of transportation are receiving more help than the

December 4, 1980
Supply
provinces are with respect to highways and roads. Because of that, we are paying in one way or another. We pay for roads whether we build them or not. We pay for them in lost lives, in crippled bodies, in lost jobs and in repairs to our vehicles. 1 suggest that the Canadian government was wise when it contributed to the construction of the Trans-Canada highway, to the roads to the north, to DREE, to roads in some other parts of the country and, to some degree, to the Yellowhead highway and other highways across the country. The Canadian government, by withdrawing funds from all these highways, is holding back expansion, holding back jobs, and so on. 1 am not saying that too much is going to the other modes of transportation but highways are not getting a fair share of the dollar going to transportation. I ask the minister whether he would review the moneys spent on various modes of transportation with a view to giving highways a better deal. My third point concerns highways such as the Howse Pass highway. The David Thompson highway which goes west to the Banff-Jasper highway where an extension to Howse Pass is required. Part of the cost would come from the B.C. government and part from the federal government. It is relatively few miles long but it would make a splendid access for traffic, particularly for trucks going from central Alberta to Vancouver. I ask the minister to consider the construction of the Howse Pass highway.
My fourth point is on twinning. I should like to ask the minister whether he is really serious about carrying out the promise of the Prime Minister to twin the railways from Winnipeg to Vancouver. There may be parts of that railway which it would be sensible to twin. To stick to the promise and to twin the whole railway would be exaggerated, ridiculous, foolish and would be laughed at in the west. It would be folly indeed. The money could be spent otherwise much better. There is one place, however, where money could be spent wisely on twinning, and that is on the Banff highway. The provinces built it right up to the Banff gates and from there on it is a two-lane highway where thousands of cars are locked bumper to bumper every weekend and sometimes on work days. I wonder if the Minister of Transport, in conjunction with the Minister of Public Works and the Minister of the Environment, could take a very careful look at expanding and twinning that highway from the Banff and Jasper gates west. There, too, we would save lives and get the traffic moving faster. 1 would appreciate hearing the hon. minister answer those four points.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, first of all, the Minister of Transport is always serious. Never ask him whether or not he is serious because even when he smiles a little he is serious. The first point I want to make is that one should not sound the alarm too easily on the number of railway accidents. I have the figures here but I do not think I have time to put them on the record. They indicate that notwithstanding increases in volume and activity, the trend in the number of incidents of derailment, injuries and death reported to the CTC is down. I am just trying to correct an impression which the hon. member might have left with members here and the audience at large.
He said also that payments for railway grade separation had come to an end. That is not correct. What happened in 1977 was a move from the railway crossing grade separation fund to the UTAP fund. The money which used to be in the railway crossing grade separation fund was partially moved to the
UTAP fund, as I explained the other day, in order to give provinces with urban transportation needs other than grade separation access to money for other purposes. That is how the UTAP program became somewhat of a grab bag.
Also I indicated the other day, we may have to return to more strict federal responsibility in the UTAP program. If this takes place, more money would be going to grade separation and less to other urban transit, which 1 am sure other people will resent.
With respect to the department not paying enough attention to highways, essentially highways are a provincial responsibility, as I am sure the hon. member is aware, but I agree with him that the multimodal approach should be more generally accepted in Canada, so that we will not witness situations where railways are being improved at the same time as an adjacent highway is the subject of expenditures.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member for London East.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: It looks like I am in trouble, Mr. Chairman.
Are you retiring, Charlie?
Oh, oh!

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I respect and admire the minister and the officials of the Department of Transport.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
But I must question the actions and policies of some of the giant corporations which operate under the jurisdiction of the Department of Transport.
I want to cite three recent examples of derailments or fires of serious consequence on the CPR: last November at Mississauga when the city had to be evacuated; last June 9 when again the CPR had a derailment and fire at Komoka, Ontario and the subdivision of Kilworth Heights was evacuated; then about a month ago when a freight car exploded on a CPR line at Thamesville, Ontario.
We can thank the police and firemen that there were no casualties at Mississauga and Komoka-which is precisely all the firemen from Lobo Township, Delaware Township, London Township and Westminster received for their efforts at Komoka when they responded to a mutual aid call, evacuated a subdivision, brought the fire under control, and remained at the scene until such time as there was no longer any danger to the community or the train. Mr. Chairman, these were
December 4, 1980

volunteer firemen who lost pay from their jobs. They risked their lives to control this fire and when they submitted a bill to the CPR for their services they were advised that CPR has an assessment in Lobo Township of $4,900, they pay taxes and they pay $14.38 for fire protection, therefore, "we wish to thank you for your excellent service but we will not pay your account."
When further inquiries were made it was pointed out to the CPR that the normal ratepayer only makes .0285 calls per year while the CPR made seven in nine years. Are they a normal ratepayer? What was the value of that train and its cargo? A locomotive engine costs nearly a million dollars. How many engines were on that train? Two or three. What was the value of the boxcars, tankers, hopper cars and the cargo? I suggest to you, Mr. Chairman, that the rolling stock was worth several millions of dollars. And they pay $14.38 a year for fire protection and "thank you, volunteer firemen, for the excellent service. We will probably need you again soon. Be ready."
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: I could not help but notice in a report by Dr. Mclsaac and the Hon. Leon Balcer that the president of CPR receives a total salary of $568,515 per year-
Shame!

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
Perhaps this explains why this railroad cannot afford to pay these volunteer firemen for their services to extinguish fires on rolling stock. I believe if his salary were reduced to $528,515 and the difference in salary were used to pay these firemen, they would be happy and continue to provide the protection to the trains passing through their communities. This would, in turn, give peace of mind to both the president of the CPR and the insurance companies.
Mr. Chairman, if these firemen are not compensated for their work under such dangerous conditions then 1 would suggest the CPR and the CNR be forced by legislation or regulation to provide their own fire equipment to safeguard the public interest.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
While these volunteer fire departments do receive a degree of compensation from their municipalities to purchase equipment they usually have fund-raising events to purchase lifesaving equipment, uniforms, etc. They are paid if they make a call to a fire on a provincial highway or a county road, and although they charged the same hourly rate for that near-disastrous call on June 9 to the CPR they are still waiting for the pay. In the meantime, the equipment maintenance requires funding. The volunteers have still not recovered lost wages but the president of the CPR still remains on the payroll at the rate of $10,932 per week.
Mr. Chairman, I say thank you, volunteer firemen, for your excellent work.
Supply
This is an outrageous situation. Surely a corporation as large as the CPR can be held accountable, not only to these volunteer firemen from the respective communities of Canada, but also to the farmers of western Canada. I hope when the Crowsnest Pass rate problems are past the persons involved will study the value of services provided against the current value of concessions made 83 years ago.
But in spite of these three accidents-I do not wish to comment on the causes until reports are tabled and translated-the number of accidents is diminishing, primarily due to roller bearings replacing friction boxes on the axles of the cars. In addition, the number of crossing accidents has dropped from a high of 1,074 in 1974 to 654 in 1980. This dramatic drop is due to the efforts of the federal government and the Department of Transport to create overpasses which eliminate grade crossings.
Recently 1 received the following letter from a railway engineer on the subject of dangerous commodities. It reads:
Since the Mississauga derailment the movement of dangerous commodities has generated a great deal of interest. At present it could very well cause regulations of such complexity that they would be very hard and expensive to comply with.
As an operating engineer I will attempt to give my views as to what I would like to see accomplished in the regulations as to my responsibility in the movement of these commodities.
There is no reason why I should know the name or components of any cargo. 1 should know if the cargo is inflammable, toxic, corrosive, radioactive, explosive.
At present, our dangerous commodity placards cover all such cargo. To change the cards and brackets would be expensive and unnecessary. A visual identification method would be more efficient and safer than our present "696 book" which is the rules and regulations given to crews, and the master red book which we do not have. At present we often find we have either overprotected or underprotected the shipment. This is how the colour and number code system could work. In the case of a dangerous commodity with no special handling or immediate health hazard, the present card could be used. An inflammable commodity should carry the present card with a large red "one" stamped on it. The red would indicate inflammable, the "one" would indicate the marshalling requirements. With this method it would be possible to use five or six numbers and cards colour-coded red, orange or black to cover the requirements at the head-end.
The head-end crew should be able to identify the requirement of a dangerous commodity while pulling by at 15 or 20 miles per hour. This method would be simple, easy to apply by the crews and involve little or no additional expense either by the railway or the shipper. The simplicity of this method is probably its drawback. Experts have a habit of talking over people's heads and recommending regulations which only experts can understand. Crews should only be subject to regulations that are thoroughly understood and easy to apply.
In closing, I received a letter from a conductor who says that in form 696, general operating instructions, they are told that the response forms are not required for import traffic and that

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I want to thank the hon. member for London East for his brilliant participation in this debate. The reception which he received when he entered the chamber was prime ministerial in dimension and very well deserved. I will, of course, communicate the purport of his speech to the presidents of the two railways and obtain specific answers to the question he raised at the end of his comments.

I do not know if the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre was aware of that fact.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader
speechtext: Yes, but it is not enough.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
speechtext: I have those figures in front of me now. CN has recently announced a lump-sum payment to pensioners and survivors to compensate for the increase in the cost of living, and the adjustment for retirees in 1972 and earlier. It will mean increases ranging from $65 to $226 per year. Survivors will receive 75 per cent of that figure. speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader

speechtext: -and comment on the reaction that he had this evening which was indicative of a staunch defender of railway employees and transportation people in general. The sort of reaction he had was worthy of a distinguished member of Parliament.

Mr. Chairman, I have already given my questions to the minister's officials. I want about seven minutes of good, solid responses.
I am very pleased to see you all out here tonight to listen to me-
Hear, hear!

I will make just one observation, Mr. Chairman. It was like watching an exercise in New Brunswick togetherness, to see the member from Restigouche trying to steal from the member for Saint John the little pittance that Transport bothers to give to that beleaguered city.
The principal purpose of my speaking at this point is to ask the minister if he would care to respond to several questions which are very pertinent and important to this whole matter of dredging and the capacity of Canadian firms to participate in dredging, for the government account. Specifically, I have given to the minister a number of questions in writing asking whether or not any senior officials in his department have at any point in the past been associated with, or were employees of, any of the firms which may be tendering for work in Canada. I want to ask the minister what response he intends to give to the telex dated December 1, signed by the SIU in which they set out these points. They make the protest in the strongest possible terms, and I will just read it, as follows:
We wish to protest in the strongest possible terms at the inequity of this treatment, as the Canadian dredging industry is obliged to pay all duties and sales taxes on imported components at the time of purchase and construction.
They are responding to information which has come to their attention that foreign vessels will be allowed into Canada on a ten-year pay-out of duties and sales tax, this assessment being levied, as was pointed out earlier by my colleague, only when the vessel is operating.
They go on to make their point that this is not in the interests of Canadian entrepreneurship, nor is it in the interests of Canadian labour. Foreign labour is employed on these vessels, eliminating, as I say, the use of Canadian labour which is available. There are no personal income taxes, if any significance derives from this. The corporation tax, under the treaty is not payable in Canada by the foreign country. Many of these foreign vessels, for example, are registered in tax-free havens. As Canada is one of the-

This is vital to the continued growth of this country. There are presently three vessels of Dutch origin operating in Canadian Arctic waters. What does the minister intend to do about these questions? How does he intend to respond to the SIU, and how does he intend to respond to the telex dated December 2, 1980. I quote from the second paragraph of the telex, signed the SIU and the Canadian Marine Officers Union, as follows:
The labour movement in Canada can no longer allow foreign labour to take away the bread and butter of the Canadian worker and we will do everything legally possible to disrupt the operation of any foreign dredges operating in Canadian waters.
That is a serious charge, and one that the minister, whether he is familiar with it or not, cannot let go unanswered.

VIA Rail Canada Inc.
J. Frank Roberts Chairman and President P.O. Box 8116 Montreal, Quebec H3C 3N3
October 29, 1980
Dear Mr. Collenette,
Thank you for your letter of September 9, 1980, and particularly for your comforting comments on the efforts of VIA Rail Canada Inc. to improve railway passenger services in this country.
In your letter, you refer to improved services between Ottawa and Toronto as well as between Montreal and Ottawa; I would like to explain our short and long-term strategies in this regard. On the short term, we are proposing to make schedule and frequency improvements while for the long term we are planning a high performance passenger line between Quebec City and Windsor. I might add that the same philosophy applies to another area of the country with similar potential, namely, Edmonton-Calgary.
The railway passenger service has tremendous potential for being the most popular mode of transport for distances of 100 to 500 miles. Between Quebec City and Windsor, for example, we are contemplating for the long term, a single passenger-dedicated line from Quebec City to Windsor going through Montreal, Ottawa and Toronto. Such a high performance line would allow speeds of 200 km per hr and could provide travelling times of approximately:
Quebec City-Montreal	1 h 50
Montreal-Ottawa	1 h
Ottawa-Toronto	2 h 40
Toronto-Windsor	2 h 30
Montreal-Toronto	3 h 40
Travel durations of this nature coupled with frequencies of one train per hour throughout most of the corridor would undoubtedly have a very high impact of the market. This would give central Canada a transportation infrastructure with virtually unlimited capacities with regard to the present and expected population densities.
The possibility to link Ottawa to Mirabel in about 45 minutes as well as Toronto to Mirabel in about 3 h 25 also
opens all kind of opportunities for ground transportation acting as a feeder to large airports.
There are still many obstacles to overcome to effect these improvements such as: our relationship with CN and CP, the use of the Mount Royal tunnel as an integral part of this corridor, the construction of a new stretch of line of about 50 kilometres between Smiths Falls and Napanee and the yet to be determined detailed routing between Napanee and Windsor. Nevertheless some of the work could start as early as 1981 should the federal government approve our capital budget. There is still, however, some reluctance on the part of the department and the central agencies to invest in the railway passenger mode to the extent required to make it successful.
With regard to the work being done for improving the Ottawa-Montreal service, we have commissioned Canadian Pacific Consulting Services to perform a study on the rehabilitation of a stretch of line between Vankleek Hill and Ottawa. This segment is common to all routing alternatives of the high performance corridor. We expect to start some line upgrading in 1981 should we receive capital budget approval from the Federal Government soon.
The Ottawa-Toronto service is one that requires improvement as quickly as possible. The high performance line would require line construction as I mentioned above. I would hope that this could be started out in 1982 or shortly thereafter if capital funds are made available. We are also looking at a couple of short-term improvements to reduce travel time between these two capital cities but it is too early to give results; we will consider your alternative.
Your point about seeking parliamentary support for this important project is very well taken. We will be preparing a public relations program in this regard very shortly.
Thank you again for your comments and for your support and interest in railway passenger services.
Yours sincerely,
J. F. Roberts
Mr. David Collenette, M.P.
